- ⚠ And the metrics move with it: on the same 643 bars S-3's Sharpe rises **+15.28%**, its Sortino **+14.68%** and its CAGR **+135.76%** (0.443% -> 1.044%), against S-1's **-1.29%** Sharpe. ⚠ The most arm-sensitive metric is `effective_sample_size`, and NOT through the trade count — S-1 gains 692 trades (+0.02%) and its ESS falls **61%**, because criterion 3's block bootstrap re-measures its block length (190 -> 208) and design effect (30.04 -> 77.14). A correction that is itself a measurement moves when its input population does.
- ⚠ The two numbers differ by three to four orders of magnitude and both are correct. The census is a statement about INPUTS; the exposure is a statement about what CONSUMED them, and a report carrying only the first invites "0.003% — immaterial" as a conclusion nobody measured.
- Root cause of the class: an exclusion is applied at the point of reading and evaluated at the point of reading, while its cost is realised downstream in a component with memory. Nothing connects the two, and the flattering half is the one that is cheap to compute.
- Prevention: **an exclusion census must be paired with an arm that re-runs the pipeline without the exclusion**, and the delta reported in the consumer's own units — here criterion 9's sensitivity arm, which re-runs S-1 and S-3 with the flagged fields admitted at their stored values and reports the difference in all twelve criterion-7 metrics. State the amplification mechanism (rolling vs recursive) beside the census so the input-side share is not read as an exposure. Where a consumer is recursive, say so explicitly: the affected population is unbounded above by the window length.
- ⚠ Two smaller traps the arm had to be built around, both in the "an arm that measures nothing reports the best possible result" family. (1) **The census must not follow the arm.** If the flagged counts were recomputed per arm, the admitted run would report its own exclusion as empty — an arm whose job is to price masking, printing *"nothing was masked"*. `MaskedSeries` therefore carries `*_flagged` (arm-invariant, the verdict) separately from `*_masked` (what the loader did), with the relation between them asserted in `__post_init__`. (2) **Both arms must come off ONE fetch**, and the pair refuses to construct if their bar, series or flag counts disagree — otherwise a delta attributable to handling is silently a delta between populations.
- ⚠ **A second measurement arm is a second RESULT, and the identity has to be able to say so.** `ResultIdentity` hashed the quarantine RULE SET (`input_rule_set_version`) but not which handling ran under it, so the two arms hashed identically and the second would have collided with the first on `strategy_results_unique`. Free to fix at 0 stored rows and expensive later — the same argument `sql/262` makes for its own `NOT NULL` columns. Generalises: **whenever you add an arm, check whether the identity of the thing it produces can distinguish it from the arm it is being compared against.**
- ⚠ And the refusal it feeds is deliberately one-sided: `quarantine_arms_not_compared` exists, `quarantine_material` does not. Criterion 9 requires the exclusion *visible*, not small, and no published or spec rule fixes a blocking magnitude — a threshold invented to complete the symmetry with §3.4's ambiguity pair would be exactly the made-up constant `.claude/CLAUDE.md` forbids. The absence is pinned by a test rather than left to review.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/quarantine_sensitivity.py`'s header (the signed delta, the one-sided null, and what the module does NOT decide); `app/services/research_price_structure_store.py`'s header and `MaskedSeries.__post_init__`; `sql/267_strategy_results_quarantine_arm.sql`; `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-07-bounded-backtester.md` §8.5 and C9; `tests/test_quarantine_sensitivity.py`; `tests/test_strategy_result.py::test_the_quarantine_gate_has_no_materiality_twin`; `scripts/probe_2240_quarantine_sensitivity.py` probes 1, 2 and 7.

### A concurrency test that reads its clock AFTER the critical section measures thread scheduling, not the invariant (#2224 class, 2026-08-07)

- Symptom: `tests/test_concurrent_fetch.py::TestRateLimitSafetyUnderConcurrency::test_throttle_lock_serialises_request_stamping` failed the pre-push gate three times running on an unrelated branch, at `throttle violation: 0.0137s < 0.02s floor`, and passed when re-run. Measured on an otherwise idle box: **2 failures in 5 consecutive runs**, with `app/providers/resilient_client.py` untouched. Blocking a push on a coin flip is what trains `--no-verify`, which is the #2224 argument for keeping the db tier off the gate.
- Root cause: the test called `rc._throttle_and_stamp()` and then took its own `time.monotonic()` reading **after the call returned**, outside `_throttle_lock`. A thread the throttle had spaced correctly could be descheduled between returning and reading, so two readings landed inside the floor while the floor itself had held. The 2 ms slack was an attempt to buy that off; no slack can, because the gap it is covering is unbounded scheduler latency.
- ⚠ It is not a flaky test in the "sometimes the machine is slow" sense — it is a test **measuring the wrong instant**, whose failure rate happens to track load. The distinction matters: the first invites a retry or a wider tolerance, the second has a correct fix.
- Prevention: **capture the quantity the code under test WROTE, from inside its own critical section** — never a reading taken after the call. Here the throttle assigns `_last_request_at[0]` while holding the lock, so the test passes a `list` subclass whose `__setitem__` appends to a recorder; the recorded sequence is the assignment order by construction. The repaired assertion needs **no slack at all**, covers 40 stamps instead of 39, and revert-probes CAUGHT both the removed inter-request sleep and the #726 read-modify-write-outside-the-lock race — the second of which the slack-based form could mask. 6/6 clean runs after.
- Generalises past throttles: any assertion of the form *"these operations were correctly ordered/spaced"* must read the ordering the code recorded, not an observation of it made later from another thread.
- ⚠⚠ **RECURRED at #2648 (2026-08-13) in the form this entry's fix does not reach: a pacer whose recorded quantity lives in ANOTHER PROCESS.** `tests/db/test_postgres_rate_gate.py::test_two_threads_share_floor` asserted `min(emission gaps) >= floor * 0.5` and failed deterministically at ~350x under the floor, which read as "the gate is not pacing at all" and was filed as a possible production defect. It is not. `PostgresFloorGate.acquire` is a GRANT (a GCRA `UPDATE` on the Postgres clock) plus a local `time.sleep(wait)`, and the two have different guarantees. Measured on the dev box: `time.sleep(0.05)` returned **37-105 ms late single-threaded and 129-148 ms late with two threads** (loadavg 3.4 / 10 CPUs) — so two grants one floor apart EMIT together whenever the earlier thread oversleeps by more than the later one, which needs only ~50 ms of *differential* jitter. The instrumented grants were the exact GCRA ladder (waits 0.0486, 0.0975, 0.0464, 0.0517, 0.0473) the whole time. **Oversleep only ever DELAYS a request, so no emission-side observation can falsify a pacer; the assertion had no failure mode that meant what it said.** Fix as above, one layer out: read the ladder Postgres wrote (`next_free_at`, on `clock_timestamp()`), and stub the sleep — which is why `_sleep` is now injectable, mirroring the seam `InProcessFloorGate` already carried.
- ⚠⚠ **And probe the ASSERTION, not just the code — a lower bound whose baseline can start stale is satisfied by the catch-up jump.** The first version of the repaired test asserted `next_free_at_after - next_free_at_before >= floor * n` against whatever the row held. A revert probe mutating the SQL to advance HALF a floor per grant **passed it**: the ladder had been left in the past by an earlier run, so the first reservation's jump to `now` covered the whole shortfall. `_pin_ladder` now resets the row to `clock_timestamp()` first, and the same probe fails at `0.2535 >= 0.5`. A probe that only exercises the code leaves the assertion's own vacuity unmeasured, and a vacuous assertion is indistinguishable from a passing one.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/db/test_postgres_rate_gate.py` (`_pin_ladder`'s docstring carries the vacuity probe, `test_two_threads_share_floor` the sleep measurements, and `test_acquire_actually_sleeps_for_its_grant` keeps the real sleep path covered); `app/providers/postgres_rate_gate.py::PostgresFloorGate` (class docstring states which half of `acquire` the class guarantees).

### The one-traded-class multi-class gap runs BOTH ways, and the overstated half has no caveat that can rescue it (#2232, 2026-08-08)

- First seen in: PR for #2232 (partial-class denominator), taking the residual after #2343 fixed the zero cohort.
- Symptom: the ownership rollup divided AEVEX Corp's holdings by **1,000 shares**. `AVEX` (CIK `0002096300`) files a Q1-2026 10-Q whose cover page reports Class A 50,744,176 + Class B 63,297,524 — both tagged on `us-gaap:StatementClassOfStockAxis`, both stripped by companyfacts (sec-edgar §7.17; `companyconcept/CIK0002096300/dei/EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding.json` → **HTTP 404**, verified live this session, same for `0002065636` / `0001859392` / `0002021880`). The only undimensioned share count in the filing is the balance-sheet parenthetical — `authorized 1,000 / issued 1,000 / outstanding 1,000`, the pre-reorganisation holdco — and a 13F filer reports 57,564,830 shares against it.
- Root cause of the class: data-engineer **I18 records the one-traded-class limitation in one direction only** — *"a multi-class issuer with only ONE class in the universe (BRK.B alone) can't be caught by the sibling test → stays silently **understated**"*. That is true when the undimensioned survivor is the issuer's COMBINED count (Alphabet, 12.116B). When the survivor is scoped SMALLER than the traded class it is **overstated without limit**, and #1646's honest-caveat treatment ("read every percentage as a combined-basis lower bound") is not merely insufficient there — it is the wrong direction. The population is recent Up-C / holdco IPOs, whose 10-Q financials are the predecessor's: measured on the dev corpus, `AVEX` `MAIR` `HMH` `AVAT` `YSWY` `RMIX` `MWH` `BCAR` `GLXY` `BRUN` `ALCYF` `NTCL`, plus a partial-per-class variant (`EVGO` `MIR.US` `BETR` `IHRT` `BCAB` `GLOO` `ENHA`).
- ⚠ **Both obvious discriminators were already dead before this PR started, and re-deriving either was the trap.** (1) Magnitude: the issue body's own table shows `PKG` dropping 1,001× where the drop is the CORRECTION and `AVAL` dropping 1.08e9× where it is the ERROR. (2) `denominator_cross_check` (I19): it compares the two shares concepts, and these issuers file only ONE, so it returns `unavailable` for **24 of the 47** live sub-1e6 instruments — structurally blind to exactly the population the ticket names.
- Prevention: detect with two **impossibility** conditions, never a threshold. (1) The issuer has NO `dei:EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding` fact at all — that element is a required cover-page disclosure on 10-K/10-Q/20-F, so its total absence means every cover value was dimensional (§7.17). Key it on "no dei fact ever", NOT on the winning row's taxonomy: an instrument whose latest period merely happens to come from us-gaap while a dei fact exists at an earlier period is a different (single-class, stale-cover) case and the argument does not hold for it. (2) A reconciled pie-wedge holder exceeds the denominator (`sanity.largest_single_holder_pct > 1`) — impossible under Rule 13d-3 / Section 16 for one beneficial owner of one class. Treatment is #1662's fail-closed (`no_data(reason="partial_class_denominator")`), not a caveat, and its banner must not advise a fundamentals sync for the same reason #1581's must not: the re-fetch returns the same dimension-stripped payload.
- ⚠ **Scope the conjunction, or you absorb three other tickets.** Condition 2 ALONE fires on **247 of 4,430** live denominators; adding condition 1 narrows it to **23**. The other 224 have a cover-page count on file and are #2229 / #2230 / #2231 territory — suppressing them would look like a bigger win and would delete the evidence those tickets are measured on.
- ⚠ Reuse: condition 2 is `_should_use_class_denominator`'s condition 3 verbatim — *"no resolved pie-wedge holder owns more shares than exist in the class (catches a mis-mapped too-small denominator, the %-inflating direction)"* — which had been wired only to the FSDS per-class SWAP, never to the denominator the rollup actually divides by. Third instance of the shape: #2343 ("every consumer already rejected `<= 0`; only the SELECTION did not"), the #2226 treasury bug ("`_compute_concentration` already excluded treasury correctly, 12 lines below"), and now this. **Before designing a new guard, grep the file for the predicate you are about to write — the repo's habit is to have it already, one call site away.**
- ⚠ A third `no_data` reason broke an inference the frontend had been making silently: it discriminated "stale" from "absent" by testing whether `shares_outstanding_as_of` was non-null on a `no_data` payload. The new reason carries a FRESH as_of, so both surfaces would have captioned a 2026 figure "too stale to use". Fixed by adding an explicit `no_data_reason` to the payload and keying both surfaces off it — the as_of test survives only as the back-compat fallback. Generalises: **when a state is discriminated by the PRESENCE of an unrelated field rather than by a field that names the state, adding a third case is silent.**
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::denominator_is_partial_class` + `_read_has_dei_cover_share_count` + `_partial_class_denominator_banner` + the `no_data_reason` field; `frontend/src/components/instrument/ownershipMetrics.ts::ownershipSuppressedDenominatorCopy` (one copy source, both surfaces); `tests/test_ownership_partial_class_denominator.py`; `tests/test_ownership_rollup.py::TestPartialClassDenominator`; `scripts/ab_2232_partial_class_denominator.py`.
- ⚠ **TO COPY INTO `.claude/skills/data-engineer/SKILL.md` as FAQ Q16a + an I18 addendum** — writes under `.claude/skills/**` were denied on this worktree for the third consecutive run (#2376), so the lesson lands here only. The I18 sentence to amend is "stays silently understated until #1590": it is true only for the combined-survivor direction.
### A two-sided predicate needs one revert probe PER SIDE, and each probe's selector must be the test the DROPPED side makes wrong (#2240 5e-5b, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: §9's first acceptance threshold is *"the mean net return of the random cohort must lie within its own 95% bootstrap CI of zero"*, implemented as `low <= 0.0 <= high`. The revert probe injected `high >= 0.0` — dropping the lower bound — and reported **NOT CAUGHT**, against a suite of two tests that between them cover both directions. Splitting it into two probes and reporting NOT CAUGHT on **both** is what made the cause visible.
- Root cause: each one-sided mutation is only observable in the half it removes, and the selectors were paired the wrong way round. `high >= 0.0` wrongly admits an interval **entirely above** zero (`[0.5, 2.0]`), and was pointed at the test using `[-9.0, -1.0]`, where it happens to return the right answer for the wrong reason. `low <= 0.0` wrongly admits an interval **entirely below** zero, and was pointed at the `[0.5, 2.0]` test, likewise. Both probes were injecting a real defect into code, running a test that could not see it, and reporting the honest verdict — the harness was right and the pairing was wrong.
- ⚠ This is NOT the "selector names no test" failure the probe harness already guards (`*** NO SUCH TEST ***`, one test was selected each time), nor the "anchor matched nothing" one (`assert s.count(old) == 1` held). It is a third way a probe proves nothing: **the injected defect and the chosen test are about different halves of the same predicate.** Nothing mechanical detects it; the tell is a NOT CAUGHT on code you are confident is right.
- Prevention: for any predicate that is a conjunction of bounds — `a <= x <= b`, `p and q`, an interval containment, a two-sided tolerance — write **one probe per conjunct**, each dropping exactly one, and choose each probe's selector as the case that the DROPPED conjunct is the only thing rejecting. Two probes are not redundancy: a single probe leaves the other side unpinned, which is how a threshold that is two-sided on paper ships one-sided in code. Same rule for the test suite it selects from — a two-sided threshold needs a fixture on each side, and `tests/test_random_entry_cohort.py` carries `test_an_interval_excluding_zero_fails_the_first_threshold` (above) and `test_an_interval_excluding_zero_from_below_fails_too` (below) for exactly that reason.
- ⚠ The below-zero half is the one that matters here and it is easy to dismiss as defensive: a **cost-dragged random-entry cohort on this corpus loses money reliably**, so its interval sits entirely below zero, and a threshold that had silently become "does the interval reach down to zero" would have passed it. The half that looks least likely is regularly the half the data lands in.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/probe_2240_random_entry_cohort.py` probes 7 and 8 (with the comment stating why there are two); `tests/test_random_entry_cohort.py::TestThresholds`.
- ⚠ Smaller gotcha from the same stage, same "the refusal is the good case" family: **`repr()` of a numpy scalar is `np.float64(1.5)` on numpy 2.x**, which `Decimal(...)` refuses with `InvalidOperation`. The bridge that re-prices float legs through `cost_model`'s `Decimal` path must go through `float(...)` first. It failed loudly here; the dangerous variant is any code path where a numpy scalar's `repr` reaches a parser that accepts it and means something else.

### Naming the reproduction command does not make the claim reproducible — the command has to compute the claim (#2232, 2026-08-08)

- First seen in: #2232 review round 2, found by the Codex checkpoint-3 pass over the rebuttals (the review bot had returned APPROVE, and the checkpoint was nominally only about confirming two NITPICK rebuttals).
- Symptom: `IFRS_TRACKED_CONCEPTS`' header block reported a full-population census as *"distinct instruments carrying a value in the ``shares`` unit"* and, correctly per `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, named the script that reproduces it. The script had no unit filter at all. `_extract_facts_from_section` emits a row for EVERY unit in `_UNIT_PRIORITY` (`USD`, `USD/shares`, `shares`, `pure`), so the counts were per concept across all units, and the qualifier in the prose was the one thing the named command could not produce.
- ⚠ The existing rule ("never hardcode a derived statistic — compute it, or state the command that reproduces it next to it") was FOLLOWED here, and the defect landed anyway. Citing a command reads as evidence to a reviewer; nobody re-runs a 408-fetch census to check that its output has the column the sentence claims. The rule needs its second half: **the cited command must emit the claim's subject as a distinct label in its own output**, not merely be capable of being edited into doing so.
- Fixed by counting per `(concept, unit)` and printing the unit as its own column, so the shares-unit slice is a line of output rather than an adjective. Re-run over the full 408: see the `IFRS_TRACKED_CONCEPTS` block for the resulting table.
- ⚠ Same ticket, second trap, in the harness rather than the code — and it has now bitten in TWO different ways across the two rounds, which is what makes it a class rather than a slip. **The RESTORE side of a revert probe is unguarded.** `.claude/CLAUDE.md` tells you to `assert s.count(old) == 1` before injecting; nothing says the same about putting the file back, and both failures were on the way back:
  - Round 1: the restore used a string replace whose target (`taxonomy="us-gaap"`) was not unique in the file, so it put back the wrong occurrence and **left the injected defect in the tree**. Caught by grepping afterwards, not by a gate.
  - Round 2: the restore used `git checkout <file>`, which restores from the **INDEX** — and the Codex checkpoint-2 rule mandates `git add -A` before `codex exec review`, so the index held the pre-edit state and the checkout silently discarded three unrelated docstring edits made since. The file stayed valid, the suite stayed green, and the only tell was a `git status` that no longer listed the file.
  - Rule: `cp <file> /tmp/probe_backup` BEFORE injecting, restore with `cp` back, then **re-run the suite and confirm it passes** — the trailing re-run is the half people skip and the only thing that distinguishes a complete restore from a merely syntactically valid one. Never restore a probe from git while the working tree holds unstaged edits to that file.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/ab_2232_ifrs_share_count.py` (module docstring + the `per_concept_unit` counter); `app/providers/implementations/sec_fundamentals.py::IFRS_TRACKED_CONCEPTS`.
- ⚠ **PENDING SKILL EDIT, sixth occurrence of #2376.** The probe-restore half belongs in `.claude/skills/engineering/test-quality.md` beside the existing "write a revert probe for a spec constant even when it looks inert" corollary; the write was DENIED on this worktree again. Full drafted text is in this entry — apply on a session that has permission.
### A chained `str.replace` whose replacement CONTAINS the pattern rewrites its own output (#2240 5e-5c, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: renaming two test helpers so a DB-tier file could import them — `_record` → `build_fold_record`, `_split` → `build_split` — produced `def build_foldbuild_fold_record(` and `def buildbuild_split(`, and 44 ruff `F821`s naming a function that was defined three lines above.
- Root cause: the rename ran as two passes per name — first `"def _record("` → `"def build_fold_record("` to catch the definition, then the bare `"_record("` → `"build_fold_record("` for the call sites. By the second pass the definition read `build_fold_record(`, which CONTAINS `_record(`, so the second pass rewrote the first pass's output. The call sites were fine; only the line the first pass had already fixed was mangled.
- ⚠ Why the usual guard misses it: this repo's probe-harness rule is `assert s.count(old) == 1` before the replace, and it held — the anchor was unique **at the moment it was checked**. A count taken before the first replace says nothing about what the second one will find. Reordering does not help: broad-then-narrow has the same defect pointing the other way.
- Prevention: when a rename's replacement string contains the pattern it replaces, do it in ONE pass with a boundary-anchored regex (`re.sub(r"\b_record\(", "build_fold_record(", s)`), or route through a unique sentinel and then to the target. The one-line tell before running any chained replace: `new.find(old) != -1` means the passes are not independent.
- ⚠⚠ **AND IT HAPPENED AGAIN IN THE SAME PASS, in the half no linter sees.** The mangled CALLS were `F821`s and were fixed in seconds; a mangled *definition* with no references is valid Python that nothing flags — here `def test_a_zero_embargo_is_legal_in_a_stored_split` became `..._in_a_storedbuild_split`, collected and passed, and was caught by the REVIEW BOT on the PR that shipped this very entry. So the lint pass is not the check: after any chained rename, grep for the replacement string preceded by a word character (`grep -nE '[a-z]build_split'`), which finds both halves.
- Enforced in: this log. ⚠ Cheap to catch and cheap to miss — `ruff check` found the reference half in seconds and was blind to the other one.

### A revert probe's NOT CAUGHT has a fourth answer: the injected defect is not a defect, because a LOWER LAYER already provides the property (#2240 5e-5c, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: a probe removed `store_walk_forward_folds`' own `conn.transaction()` around its `executemany`, and `test_the_split_writer_is_atomic_on_an_autocommit_connection` — written for exactly that defect, on an autocommit connection, with the third of four rows planted to violate the primary key — still PASSED. The sibling probe on `store_in_sample_arm_pair` (two separate `execute` calls) was CAUGHT by its equivalent test in the same run, which is what made "the test is wrong" implausible.
- Root cause: **psycopg 3.3.3 runs an `executemany` batch in its own transaction, autocommit or not.** Measured rather than inferred from the passing test — autocommit connection, `CREATE TEMP TABLE _em_probe (k int primary key)`, plant `k = 3`, `executemany` over `(0, 1, 3, 4)`: the statement is refused with `UniqueViolation` and `SELECT k FROM _em_probe` returns `[(3,)]`. Rows 0 and 1 did not survive. So the wrapper is defence in depth and the probe was asking about the driver, not about our code.
- ⚠ The existing triage order (selector → fixture → code, prevention log #2214/#2240 5e-5b) has three answers and this is a fourth: **the code under the mutation was never load-bearing.** It is distinguishable from the other three by a cheap direct measurement of the layer below — one temp table and four rows here — and it is NOT distinguishable by staring at the test.
- ⚠⚠ The failure this prevents is the wrong reflex in either direction: deleting a correct guard because "no test covers it", or bending the test until it goes red and thereby pinning a driver's implementation detail as if it were our invariant. The resolution that holds is to **keep the guard, state in its docstring that it is belt-and-braces with the measurement beside it, ship no probe, and say in the probe file's own header why there is none.**
- Prevention: when a probe reports NOT CAUGHT on code you believe is load-bearing, before touching the test ask *what would happen if this line simply were not needed* — then measure the layer beneath it directly. A two-call writer and a one-`executemany` writer look identical in review and have different answers.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/result_ledger.py::store_walk_forward_folds` (docstring carries the measurement); `scripts/probe_2240_result_ledger.py`'s "WHAT IS NOT PROBED" header; `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-07-bounded-backtester.md` §8.8.

### A NON-OPTIONAL annotation on a nullable column is the defect, and four `# type: ignore`s were the record that everyone knew (#2354, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: `signal_ledger.resolve_fills` branched on `fill_open is None` alone, so a stored `open = 0` became `fill_price = 0` on a `fired` row. Every reader refuses that value; only a ledger with 0 rows kept it academic.
- Measured, full population, both corpora, 2026-08-08 (`scripts/verify_2354_nonpositive_open.py --census`, which computes them rather than quoting them): `research_price_daily` **16 bars / 9 series** of 25,920,971; `price_daily` **154 bars / 14 instruments** of 6,722,352. **Zero NULL, zero negative, and every one of the 170 carries `rules = ['B1']` with both axes false.** The `price_daily` half never passes through the masked loader at all, which is why the fix needed a refusal in the writer and not only a mask in the loader.
- Root cause under the root cause: `price_structure.StructureBar.open` was declared `Decimal`, not `Decimal | None`, while both source columns are nullable and the loader could hand back a `0`. So every consumer type-checked as though a usable price were guaranteed. **The tell was already in the tree**: four call sites carried `# type: ignore[typeddict-item]` on `{"open": bar.open, ...}`, and a test helper's docstring spelled it out — *"the runtime type is wider than the annotation, so the writer has to cope with it rather than trust it"*. Nobody widened the field; the ignores absorbed the signal instead.
- ⚠ **A `# type: ignore` at N call sites is a declaration that the annotation is wrong at the definition.** One is a local exception. Four is a measurement, and the fix is at the type, not at the call. Widening `StructureBar.open` here produced exactly one new pyright error — the one place that genuinely passes it on — and no runtime change (`technical_analysis.atr` reads high/low/close only).
- ⚠ The masking rule was NOT invented: `price_quarantine.rule_b1` already says *"any of open/high/low/close NULL or `<= 0`"*. The loader's two-axis masking (range → high/low, return → close) simply has no axis for the open, so B1's own clause is applied to it by value. The bound is `<= 0` and not `== 0` deliberately — "no negative open is stored" is a fact about an ingest run, not a property of the column.
- ⚠ The reason code is a SPLIT, not a widening: `no_fill_bar` now means only "the series ended", and `unusable_fill_price` (sql/270, our tenth) means "bar `t+1` exists and cannot be priced". `resolve_fills`' own docstring had pre-registered it — *"if the measured count ever leaves zero, split it"* — and the count had left zero. ⚠ It stamps `unusable_fill_price` and **not** `quarantined_bar`, even though all 170 bars are quarantined today, because the writer receives a `BarSeries` and no verdicts: a cause it has no input for is a cause it must not assert.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/price_structure.py::StructureBar` (the widened field carries the incident); `app/services/research_price_structure_store.py::_apply_arm`; `app/services/signal_ledger.py::resolve_fills`; `sql/270_strategy_signals_unusable_fill_price.sql`; `scripts/verify_2354_nonpositive_open.py` (full-population arms); `scripts/probe_2354_nonpositive_open.py` (12 probes, both halves of both two-sided predicates).
### The Nth per-case patch to a value-recovery rescue means the rescue is missing a FACT, not a case — for an HTML table that fact is the layout (#2376, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: ExlService `0001193125-25-103261` stored `percent_of_class = NULL` for all three of its Item 403(a) 5% holders against a filing that plainly reads `Blackrock Inc. (11) 23,308,871 14.33`. Nothing failed: the rows stored, the chart drew, and `percent_of_class` is what the ownership rollup denominates the insider / blockholder wedges with.
- Root cause, and it is one level below where four prior tickets looked. `_CELL_RE` is `<(?:t[hd])\b([^>]*)>(.*?)</t[hd]\s*>`, and `[^>]*` happily accepts the trailing `/` of a **self-closing** `<td style="x"/>`. So the regex reads a layout spacer as an OPENING tag and runs `(.*?)` on to the next real `</td>`. Two failures at once, and the second is the quiet one:
  1. each row emits only as many cells as it has PAIRED `<td>…</td>` tags — 6 in that header, 5 in the BlackRock row, so header and data are in different index spaces;
  2. the emitted cell carries the SPACER's attributes with the FOLLOWING cell's text, so `colspan="4"` on the `Shares` and `% (2)` captions is read as `colspan=1` and the layout arithmetic never sees it.
- ⚠ **The existing rescue was RIGHT to decline, and that is the tell.** The #2140 D3 ragged-row scan accepts a cell only if it is unambiguously a percent (`%` present, or `*`, or followed by a lone `%` cell). ExlService's cell is a bare `14.33`, and without knowing which caption covers it a bare `14.33` is indistinguishable from a 14-share holding — `_parse_percent` clamps to [0,100], so it would take a small share count just as happily. Five patches (#2140 D3, #2163 hold-back, #2164 stacked pairs, #2169 stacked cells, #2175 rowspan) had each added a way to GUESS harder inside a grid that never had a common column space. The missing input was the HTML table model, not a sixth heuristic.
- Source rule: the HTML Living Standard §4.9.12 table model, which is the governing rule here because DEF 14A carries no structured-data mandate (sec-edgar skill §2.2 form table: *"narrative HTML; no structured-XBRL mandate"*). `pandas.read_html` 3.0.2 — the oracle the #2175 entry names — returns a uniform 10×23 grid for that table with `Shares` spanning layout columns 4-7, `% (2)` spanning 9-12, the count at column 6 and `14.33` at column 11. Our reconstruction reproduces it exactly.
- Fix shape, and the scoping is the load-bearing part: a **read-only** layout grid consulted as the LAST rescue, never a regrid of the parser. `_CELL_RE` is left alone deliberately — its cell tuples are the index space that header scoring, two-row-header promotion and `_resolve_columns` are all tuned against, and moving it re-selects which table wins corpus-wide, which is #2175's whole prevention entry. Placing the rescue after the row-drop guard is what bounds it to NULL → value: it cannot admit a row, change a share count, or overwrite a percent another rescue found.
- ⚠ **A fixture has to be validated against the CONTROL, not only against the new code.** The first `_SPACER_OFFSET_TABLE` was hand-built from the real markup's *description* — self-closing spacers plus `colspan` — and `main` already returned 14.33 on it, so the end-to-end test was green on both arms and pinned nothing. It looked CAUGHT in the revert probes only because those probes' `-k` selector also named the layout-grid test. The defect needs *paired* empty `<td>…</td>` cells interleaved in the data rows, which is what pushes the resolved percent index onto a blank; hand-reasoning about markup reproduced the wrong half. **Fix: derive the fixture from the real `<tr>`s and assert the control's behaviour on it before trusting any test that uses it** — `cd <control-worktree> && python -c "print(P._extract_table_holders(...))"` is one command and it is the only thing that says the fixture reproduces the bug.
- ⚠ **An extraction rescue that also runs inside an ELIGIBILITY probe is a SELECTION change.** `_is_item403_eligible` judges a table by extracting it and asking `_has_item403_value_rows`, so filling percents during that probe decides which tables ARE Item 403 tables. The full-population A/B caught it as **2 holders gained**: `0001140361-25-012231` and `-26-013118` admitted `Brian H. Hertzman` at 446,200 shares / **89.2%**, beside the genuine `Brian S. Hertzman` at 18,832 / 0.5% — an 89.2% holding implying 500,224 shares outstanding where the same table's other rows imply ~83m. Fixed with `attest_percent=rows is not None`, the parameter the two callers already differ on. **Any helper called from both a judging path and a doing path needs that split stated explicitly, or the judgement moves with the doing.**
- ⚠ **229.403 column 4 appears TWICE on a dual-class table**, and pooling the two runs binds one class's percent to the other's share count. Regeneron `0001308179-25-000518` heads `Number | Percent of Class` over Class A Stock at layout columns 2-7 and again over Common Stock at 10-16; the first cut attested a flat **28** to fifteen directors holding between 4,472 and 268,499 shares. Two non-contiguous percent runs now attest nothing — per-class binding needs the whole grid re-columned and is tracked on #2351.
- ⚠ **A contiguity test is NOT enough, because the header is several rows and the ambiguity can hide in the row you did not read.** Domo `0001505952-25-000062` renders `Shares | % | Shares | % | % of Total Voting Power`, and the FIRST percent-captioned caption row carries only the voting-power caption — one clean contiguous run, which the dual-class guard passes. Josh James' row reads `3,263,659 100 1,022,375 2.8 78.5`: 78.5% of the vote, 2.8% of Class A. The fix is to union percent captions across EVERY caption row and refuse on more than one distinct caption, not to stop at the first match. **Generalisable: when a guard asks "is this header ambiguous", it has to see the whole header region — a multi-row header lets the disambiguating evidence sit in a row the scan already passed.**
- ⚠ **And tightening that guard immediately broke the target case, which is the cheapest possible reminder to re-run the original repro after every narrowing.** `5% Beneficial owners` — Item 403(a)'s own SECTION LABEL — matched a naive `"%" in caption` test, so ExlService's table looked like it carried two distinct percent captions and the new guard refused the very rows the ticket exists to recover. A percent CAPTION names a column; `5%` binds to the number on its left. Discriminator is `\d\s*%` and it is now a test of its own. **Every guard added to make a change safer is itself a narrowing gate, and the admit side needs re-measuring — the same rule as "enumerate what it REJECTS", pointed at your own fix.**
- ⚠ **The gain-side validator's own ANCHOR can be the broken number.** The first arm compared each recovered percent's implied `shares / (percent/100)` against the median implied denominator of the holders whose percent the control already knew, and reported 123 disagreements out of 444 — which reads as a 28% false-positive rate. It is not: on `0001306830-26-000052` the anchor implies **100** shares outstanding (garbage) while the three recovered values agree with each other to 0.03% (111.97m / 111.94m / 111.97m), and `0000006845-26-000036`'s three recoveries agree to 0.02% against an anchor 23% away. **Report recovered-vs-recovered coherence separately from recovered-vs-anchor**, and make the unit of analysis the accession: an internally tight recovered set that misses the anchor is a different-denominator question (another share class, a pro-forma table), whereas a wide spread is the noise the arm exists to find. Aggregating the two hides both.
- ⚠⚠ **A rescue that FAILS CLOSED hides its own under-firing, so the shapes the reg PRESCRIBES have to be enumerated and tested one by one.** Both of Codex's checkpoint-2 findings were the same defect wearing different clothes: the recovery silently did not fire on a shape 17 CFR 229.403 prescribes. Neither could store a wrong value, and that is exactly why nothing caught them — no test errored, no gate went red, and the full-population A/B would have reported a smaller gain that looked like the honest answer. (1) **Column 1 shadowed the holder.** The layout row was keyed on its FIRST text cell, but 229.403(a) puts `Title of class` ahead of `Name and address of beneficial owner`, so on any table rendering column 1 the percent was filed under `commonstock` while the lookup asked for `acmecapitalllc`. Fixed by keying the first TWO text cells — the reg's own bound, not a tuned constant — and the existing ambiguity guard absorbs the class label for free, because it repeats across rows with different percents. (2) **The threshold guard tested the CHARACTER, not the PHENOMENON.** `5% Beneficial owners` had already been excluded as a section label; `5 Percent Beneficial Owners` and `Ten Percent Holders` are the same label with the sign spelled out, and `if "percent" in lowered: return True` returned before the guard could run. A table carrying that label beside a real `Percent of Class` header then reads as two distinct captions and refuses everything. **Test: for every fails-closed guard, write down the shapes the SOURCE RULE prescribes and assert each one still fires — a guard tuned on one spelling of a phrase has been tested against a character, and the reg is written in words.**
- ⚠⚠ **The gain-side arm found the only WRONG value, and it was a number the ISSUER wrote as a threshold.** `0001437749-25-025111` renders its percent column as `1*` against a `* Less than 1.0%` legend — the digit is the THRESHOLD, not the holding — and `_parse_percent` strips a trailing footnote marker, so the rescue stored a flat **1** for seven holders. A figure the filing does not state, and one this parser's own settled convention for that meaning writes as **0.5** (a BARE `*`; Campbell Soup `0001308179-25-000618` recovers thirteen of those correctly in the same run). The fix is in the RESCUE, not in `_parse_percent`: moving a shared primitive re-values every existing path and needs its own A/B, which is #2140/#2175's whole prevention entry. ⚠ **And the arm's own labelling misleads if read literally — 9 of 108 testable accessions came back "INCOHERENT" and only ONE was a wrong percent.** The other eight are the implied-denominator test dividing a CORRECT percent by a WRONG share count: Stryker `0000310764-25-000051` stores Ronda Stryker's 8,175 option shares instead of her 17,443,015 total against a verbatim-correct 4.6, and Campbell stores 0 against a verbatim-correct 18.06. Both share counts are pre-existing and identical in both arms. **Test: when a coherence arm flags a row, check which of its two inputs moved — an arm over `a/b` indicts `b` just as loudly as `a`, and only one of them is in your diff.**
- ⚠⚠ **A mutate/run/restore harness must restore in a `finally`, not on the happy path.** Review WARNING on PR #2405: `probe_2376_revert.py` wrote the original back only after `_run()` returned, so a `uv`/pytest failure — or a Ctrl-C — would leave the injected defect on disk permanently, where every later gate passes against it unnoticed. Same window, same day, as the `git add` hazard below; both are the harness owning the file for longer than the author pictured. ⚠ **And the WARNING was not hypothetical — the next session opened this worktree with `len(name_keys) == 2` sitting at `== 1` in `sec_def14a.py`, i.e. probe 6's injected defect still on disk from an interrupted run, restored only because `git diff` was read before anything else.** ⚠⚠ **The obvious fix is one line short of correct: wrapping only `_run()` still leaves the MUTATION write outside the `try`, so a partial write or a Ctrl-C between the two statements leaves the defect and the `finally` never runs.** The mutation and the run both go inside. Proven by revert-probing the harness itself — patch `_run` to raise `FileNotFoundError("uv")` on the first probe and compare the parser's bytes before/after: pre-fix reports `restored: False`, fixed reports `True`. **Rule: a mutate/run/restore harness is itself invariant-carrying code — revert-probe it, and park an out-of-process copy of the target for the one case `finally` cannot cover (SIGKILL).**
- ⚠⚠ **NEVER `git add` while a revert-probe harness is running — it stages the INJECTED DEFECT, and every local gate stays green.** Hit on 2026-08-08 in this PR: `git add -A` ran while `scripts/probe_2376_revert.py` had `_is_percent_caption` mutated to `pass`, so the INDEX carried a parser missing its threshold guard while the WORKING TREE was correct. `ruff`, `pyright` and `pytest` all run against the working tree, which the harness had restored by the time they executed, so nothing could have caught it — the defect would have shipped in the commit with a fully green gate run behind it. Only `git diff --cached` shows it, and only if you think to look. **Rule: the probe harness owns the file for the duration of its run. Stage before it starts or after it prints its verdict, never during — and after any probe run, `git diff` (not `git status`) before committing, because `MM` on a path is the tell.**
- ⚠ **A validation arm whose INPUT FILES have no producer is not a shipped check.** `scripts/verify_2376_recovered_percents.py` documented `/tmp/2376-control.jsonl` and `/tmp/2376-treatment.jsonl` in its own usage block, and nothing in the repo wrote them — the A/B summary (`ab_2140_def14a_parser.py --out`) carries holder IDENTITIES but not their `shares` / `percent`, so it cannot feed this arm. The numbers were produced by a throwaway one-liner that died with the session, which means a reviewer cannot re-run the check and the next session re-derives the dumper before it can re-measure anything. Fixed by committing `scripts/dump_2376_percent_arm.py`, run from ONE path against both checkouts (`PYTHONPATH=.` resolves `app` out of the working directory), so the harness is byte-identical across arms and only the parser under test differs. **Test: every file named in a script's usage block must be produced by something committed.**
- Prevention: (1) when a rescue has been patched N times, ask what FACT it lacks rather than what case it missed; (2) for any markup parser, check whether the format's own model is implemented before adding heuristic N+1 — `pandas.read_html` settles it for HTML tables in one command; (3) validate a regression fixture against the control checkout; (4) enumerate what a widening change newly ADMITS, including via any judging path that shares the code; (5) commit the producer of every file a validation script names.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/providers/implementations/sec_def14a.py` (`_ANY_CELL_RE`, `_layout_rows`, `_is_percent_caption`, `_layout_percent_by_row`, and the `attest_percent` split in `_extract_table_holders`); `tests/test_sec_def14a_parser.py::TestLayoutAttestedPercent`; `scripts/probe_2376_revert.py` (9 probes); `scripts/verify_2376_recovered_percents.py` + `scripts/dump_2376_percent_arm.py`.
- ⚠ **PENDING SKILL EDIT, seventh occurrence of the `.claude/skills/**` write denial.** The edit belongs in `.claude/skills/data-sources/edgartools.md`, immediately before G17's closing "no dedicated open-source Item 403 parser exists" paragraph, and reads: *G17 answers the EXTRACTION question, not the GEOMETRY one. "Which library reads an Item 403 table better" and "which layout column is this cell in" are different questions with different oracles. For geometry the oracle is `pandas.read_html` (already a dependency), because it implements the HTML Living Standard's table model outright — see the #2175 prevention entry, and #2376, where it placed a bare `14.33` under a `%` caption spanning layout columns 9-12 while our flat cell grid had it two columns past the resolved percent index. Run it on YOUR failing table before concluding the extractor is at fault; a mis-columned cell looks exactly like a mis-parsed one.* Apply on a session that has permission.
- ⚠ **The skill-write friction now has a ticket: #2403.** The entries above cite "#2376" for it, which is wrong — **#2376 is this def14a percent bug**, and as written those citations send a reader to an unrelated parser ticket. #2403 carries the evidence measured on 2026-08-08: the denial is path-specific to `.claude/` (a `Write` to `scripts/` in the same run was not prompted), the worktree's own `.claude/settings.local.json` already grants bare `Edit` / `Edit(//**)` and is not sufficient, and the six skill grants in `~/.claude/settings.json` are written root-anchored (`Edit(/.claude/skills/data-sources/**)`), which cannot match the absolute path in any checkout. **Read #2403 rather than re-deriving this** — it also lists the two edits still unapplied (`test-quality.md:438`, `edgartools.md:268`).
### A timestamp bumped INSIDE an upsert's changed-metadata guard does not mean what its name says — `instruments.last_seen_at` is "last changed", not "last seen" (#2290, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: none. Nothing failed, no gate went red, and the column has carried the wrong meaning since `sql/001_init.sql`. It surfaced only because #2290 proposed to BUILD on it: the ticket prescribed closing a universe-membership episode at the departing instrument's prior `last_seen_at`, described as "the last date the provider actually returned the instrument".
- Root cause is one clause away from where anyone looks. `sync_universe`'s upsert (`app/services/universe.py:106-171`) ends `... last_seen_at = NOW() WHERE (instruments.symbol IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.symbol OR instruments.company_name IS DISTINCT FROM ... OR ...)`. **The `WHERE` on an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` suppresses the ENTIRE `SET` clause, timestamp bump included.** So the row is only touched when some metadata changed, and the column means "last time this row's metadata changed". The name, the docstring and every reader say "last seen".
- Measured, full population, dev, 2026-08-08 — the shape is what makes it obvious, so query the DISTRIBUTION and not the max:
  ```sql
  select count(*) from instruments;                            -- 12696
  select count(distinct last_seen_at::date) from instruments;  -- 9
  select max(last_seen_at) from instruments;                   -- 2026-08-05 03:00:03
  select last_seen_at::date, count(*) from instruments group by 1 order by 2 desc limit 2;
  -- 2026-06-12 | 9850
  -- 2026-06-03 | 2567
  ```
  Nine distinct dates across 12,696 rows, 9,850 frozen at 2026-06-12, against a sync that runs nightly. A column that genuinely tracked presence would show one date per sync.
- ⚠ **A `MAX()` over such a column reads as a freshness signal and is not one.** `ops_monitor.py:114` uses `SELECT MAX(last_seen_at) FROM instruments` as universe-layer staleness, so a sync that returns an unchanged feed is indistinguishable from a sync that has stopped — the reported staleness advances one day per day in both cases. Filed as **#2407**; it is the same misunderstood column, found from the same measurement.
- Fix shape: do NOT repair the column (dropping the guard rewrites ~12.7k rows nightly and breaks `_count_changes`, which distinguishes inserted from updated by comparing `first_seen_at` to `last_seen_at`). Instead the new table carries its own `last_confirmed_on`, written by the code path that OBSERVES presence, and the close sets `effective_to := last_confirmed_on` with `CHECK (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to = last_confirmed_on)` pinning them equal — so a later regression cannot stamp a detection date there, the constraint rejects the row.
- ⚠ **Generalises past this column.** Any `updated_at` / `last_seen_at` / `refreshed_at` set inside an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE (...)`, or inside a `WHERE col IS DISTINCT FROM ...` on a plain UPDATE, is a CHANGE timestamp wearing an OBSERVATION name. **Test: before consuming any such column as "when did we last look", grep its writer for a `WHERE` on the same statement. If one exists, the column answers a different question — and `count(distinct <col>::date)` against the number of runs is the one query that shows it.** This is the same shape as Form 25 trap 5 (`.claude/skills/data-sources/sec-edgar.md` §2.6): the detection date is never the date the consumer needs.
- ⚠ **And an inherited premise about a column is still a premise.** #2290 was written by a prior session, cited the exact file and clause, and was wrong about what the clause does — re-falsifying it cost one query and changed the whole design. Working-order step 3c, again.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/271_instrument_universe_membership.sql` (header + the `last_confirmed_on` column comment carry the measurement); `app/services/universe_membership.py`; `tests/test_universe_membership.py::TestMembershipConstraints::test_closed_row_must_end_at_last_confirmed`; issue #2407 for the `ops_monitor` consumer.

### Copying a sibling table's date-range convention without checking what `effective_to` MEANS silently changes which days the row claims (#2290, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: would have been a row asserting the instrument was NOT a member on the last day we confirmed it present — and a whole class of transition quietly deleted rather than recorded.
- Context: #2290 said "reuse, do not reinvent — copy `sql/103_instrument_symbol_history.sql`", which is right about the invariants (ordered ranges, partial-unique single-current, GIST `EXCLUDE` no-overlap) and wrong about one of them. sql/103 uses half-open `daterange(effective_from, effective_to, '[)')`, where `effective_to` is the first date NOT covered — correct there, because it means "the date the old symbol stopped applying". #2290 defines its `effective_to` as "the last date the provider actually returned the instrument", which is a date the instrument WAS a member.
- Two consequences under `'[)'`, neither visible in a test that only checks "does the constraint exist":
  1. the closed row excludes its own last confirmed day, so an `effective_to = last_confirmed_on` CHECK is incoherent rather than load-bearing;
  2. an instrument that appears Monday and is gone Tuesday has `last_confirmed_on = effective_from`, and a half-open range **cannot express a single day at all** — `[D, D)` is empty and the ordered-dates CHECK rejects it. The only options left are deleting the row (destroying exactly the one-day transition the table exists to capture) or stamping a date the provider never confirmed.
- Verified empirically before adopting, not reasoned about — two throwaway tables differing only in the bound:
  ```
  probe_halfopen:  reopening ON the last membership day ACCEPTED  <- double-counts that day
  probe_inclusive: reopening ON the last membership day REJECTED  <- correct
  daterange(D, D, '[]')    -> [D, D+1)  isempty=false, @> D = true
  daterange(D, NULL, '[]') -> [D, )     unbounded above
  ```
- ⚠ **Rule: the bound convention is a property of what the END COLUMN MEANS, not of the table you copied.** Before reusing a temporal schema, write down in words what `effective_to` denotes on the NEW table and check the bound against that sentence. "Last day of X" is inclusive `'[]'`; "first day after X" is half-open `'[)'`. Copying the constraint without re-deriving the bound is how a range silently gains or loses a day at every boundary, and boundaries are where these tables are read.
- ⚠ The divergence has to be written down where the next reader is, or it reads as a mistake: both the migration header and the table comment state that this table diverges from sql/103 deliberately, and why.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/271_instrument_universe_membership.sql` (the "ONE convention deliberately DIVERGES" block); `tests/test_universe_membership.py::test_single_day_range_accepted`, `::test_overlapping_ranges_rejected`, `::test_abutting_ranges_accepted`, `::test_one_day_membership_closes_rather_than_vanishing`.

## A dedup pass's rep choice can be "the source rule" and still be an artefact of the PARSER, not the filing (#2385, 2026-08-08)

- #2385 asked for the Rule 16a-1(a)(2) `direct` holder to become a control-group fold's representative instead of the highest-CIK member. The rule is right; reading it off `Holder.ownership_nature == "direct"` — even provenance-gated — is not, and the reason is two layers below the ticket.
- **The SEC ownership XML has no per-owner attribution for Table I.** `<nonDerivativeHolding>` / `<nonDerivativeTransaction>` are children of `<nonDerivativeTable>`, a SIBLING of `<reportingOwner>`. A joint Form 3/4 therefore does not say which co-filer holds the `D` line, and `insider_transactions._extract_holdings` assigns every row to `default_filer_cik = filers[0].filer_cik` (`app/services/insider_transactions.py:449`); the other co-filers arrive from the DERA bulk dataset with a role-derived nature. **So within one accession "Table I-attested" means "listed first in the XML".**
- Measured on the full population (`PYTHONPATH=. uv run python -m scripts.audit_2385_control_group_rep`, 2,179 instruments, 1,434 folds, 0 harness errors): **6 of 931 same-accession folds carry ≥2 attested members, against 378 of 503 cross-accession.** The flag only discriminates when the two members filed separate documents. Cross-checked at the source: `TACO`'s Form 3 `0001829126-25-003075`, fetched from EDGAR, has two reporting owners and two Table I lines (2,401,200 `D`, 2,688,300 `I` / "See footnote.") with nothing tying either line to either owner — and the ungated rule relabelled a SPAC sponsor's block with an individual on exactly that basis.
- **The gain side is where both defects surfaced, and neither was visible in any summary statistic.** Arm 1 moved 164 folds with a clean-looking `0 UP / 70 DOWN` pie-total result; reading the 70 mover names one by one showed `ABTC` swapping one person's revocable living trust for another's, `COGT` and `RNAZ` swapping one executive for another, and `HYMC` promoting `WHITEBOX ADVISORS LLC` over the `Wbox 2015-5 Ltd.` fund — a control chain read backwards. Those are clusters with TWO attested direct holders, i.e. the #1659 equal-value coincidence class, where the selection falls through to arbitrary CIK order. Rule 16a-1(a)(2)'s chain has ONE holder of record, which `_DEEMED_CHAIN_MAX_DIRECT` already encodes; requiring `len(attested_direct) == 1` removes all 19.
- ⚠ **Pre-filtering a candidate pool before COUNTING it hides exactly this.** The first implementation filtered by accession while building the pool, so a cluster with two attested directs — one of them the incumbent — looked like a cluster with one. Counting on the unfiltered cluster and applying the accession clause to the surviving single candidate is what makes the `== 1` test mean what the rule says. The lesson generalises: **when a rule says "exactly one X", count X over the population the rule is about, not over whatever is left after the other guards ran.**
- Prevention: (1) before treating a stored per-holder attribute as evidence about a JOINT filing, check whether the format attributes it per-owner at all, and grep the parser for a `default_*` fallback — `filers[0]` is the shape to look for; (2) enumerate the movers by name, not by count — a 0-regression net with a uniformly-correct-looking direction still contained two defect classes here; (3) count a uniqueness precondition before any other filter narrows the set. Enforced in: `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_attested_direct_holders` + `_select_control_group_rep` (the three clauses and their measurements); `tests/test_insider_deemed_chain_collapse.py` (six new cases, one per clause); `scripts/audit_2385_control_group_rep.py` (one arm per clause, so each is priced separately rather than reported as a total).
- ⚠⚠ **Relaxing a safety invariant to accommodate an expected change can turn it into a tautology — and the relaxation is where to look, not the change.** This pass's A/B harness asserted "instruments that GAINED an insider identity must be 0", which is right for a fold that only removes and wrong for a rep CHANGE, where the demoted incumbent leaves and the promoted holder enters. The obvious repair — `gained_symbols - lost_symbols` — is **instrument-level set arithmetic answering an identity-level question**, so an instrument carrying a legitimate swap AND a genuinely new holder drops out of the bucket and the line prints `0` while a holder was added. Caught by Codex at checkpoint 2, not by any gate, and not by me writing it. The fix is to ask what EXPLAINS each gain: an identity is accounted for only if some fold in the treatment arm kept it as its representative (`kept_cik`); anything else is flagged whatever else happened on that instrument. Re-run on the same JSONL the invariant still reads 0, so the conclusion survived — but it had been resting on a check that could not have failed. **Rule: when an invariant starts firing on an expected case, do not widen it at the granularity that happens to silence it. Restate it at the granularity of the thing it is protecting.** Enforced in: `scripts/ab_2230_compare.py` (the `unexplained` loop and the comment recording why symbol-level subtraction is insufficient).
- ✅ **APPLIED 2026-08-08 (#2408).** Both blocks below now live in `.claude/skills/data-sources/sec-edgar.md` §2.3, written through a `python3` heredoc rather than the editor tool — that path is not subject to the `.claude/skills/**` prompt (#2403), which is what unblocked seven sessions of deferral. Original note kept for the record: *PENDING SKILL EDIT — `.claude/skills/data-sources/sec-edgar.md` §2.3, and the write was DENIED again (see #2403, and note the six earlier entries mis-cite this as "#2376").* Two blocks to add after the existing `directOrIndirectOwnership` paragraph at line 322. **(a)** The overloaded-column block already specified in the 2026-08-07 entries — four writers, the `GROUP BY 1,2` provenance query (re-measured 2026-08-08: `direct`/Table-I **69,657** · `direct`/role-derived **3,404** · `indirect`/Table-I **16,532** · `beneficial`/role-derived **3,759**), the `source_document_id !~ ':(NDT|NDH):'` discriminator, and the rule that any read-path branch on `ownership_nature == 'direct'` must check `Holder.nature_from_table_i`. **(b)** NEW, and the more load-bearing of the two: *Table I rows are not attributed to a reporting owner — `<nonDerivativeTable>` is a sibling of `<reportingOwner>`, so a joint filing's D and I lines belong to no named co-filer, and `insider_transactions._extract_holdings` gives them all to `filers[0]` (`app/services/insider_transactions.py:449`). Within one accession, "Table I-attested" means "listed first in the XML" and discriminates nothing: 6 of 931 same-accession folds carry ≥2 attested members, against 378 of 503 cross-accession. The evidence that DOES name the record holder on a joint filing is `natureOfOwnership` ("Shares held by X"), stored at `insider_transactions.nature_of_ownership` / `insider_initial_holdings.nature_of_ownership` and not parsed — 138,380/138,380 and 30,149/30,149 non-null on `direct_indirect = 'I'`.*

## A freshness bound settled for ONE consumer is a contract on the TABLE, not on that consumer (#2336, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: none, and that is the point. `finra_short_interest_current` is one row per instrument, and `instrument_analytics._short_interest_from_row` read it with no bound on `settlement_date` — so a 2024 figure rendered as live positioning on the IAR card and fed the thesis prompt, with only an `asof` field disclosing the age to a reader who thought to look.
- The bound already existed. `thesis_break.FRESHNESS_BOUNDS` has carried `finra_settlement: 45d` since #2010 and `thesis_break_scan._short_interest_observations` — the OTHER consumer of the same table — has been gated the whole time. Nobody invented a new rule here; the second consumer simply never asked what the first one had already settled. #1955 class ("contract-field wired into one model not its sibling"), one layer up: the drifting thing was a *policy on a table*, not a column on a model.
- ⚠ **The trap underneath it: `_current` means latest-WINS, not current-CYCLE.** `sql/152` calls it a materialised snapshot and the ingest's `DO UPDATE` arm is guarded by `EXCLUDED.settlement_date > …`, which reads as "cannot go backwards". The **INSERT arm is unconditional**, so an instrument with no row takes whatever file is being ingested however old, and an instrument that stops appearing in FINRA's file keeps its last row forever. A `_current` row is not evidence that its figure is current, on any table built this way. Before reading one as live, ask which arm can create it.
- Measured, full population on the dev corpus (2026-08-08): `finra_short_interest_current` 6,181 rows, **441 older than 45 days**, of which **19** also had a `fundamentals_snapshot.shares_outstanding` and therefore emitted a signal at all — those 19 are what the A/B moves (`SUPPRESSED 19 / GAINED 0 / value changed 0` over all 6,181 distinct instruments). ⚠ **The small number is a masking effect, not a small defect**: the other 422 are silent only because they have no denominator, and #2234's 88-date backfill seeds `_current` rows for instruments that do have one. A gate measured before a backfill under-reports itself.
- Cross-checked at the source rather than inside our store: `shrt20260715.csv` fetched from the FINRA CDN — all five golden-panel instruments present with figures byte-equal to `_current` (AAPL 146,547,784), and GDST / CVGW / MCW / AMWD **absent**. So the suppressed rows are genuine absence from FINRA's file, not a `_current` row that failed to refresh — which is the alternative explanation a gate would have papered over. `GDST` was rendering `current_short_interest = 4` from 2026-03-13, 148 days old.
- Prevention: when adding OR auditing a reader of a `_current`/snapshot table, grep for every other consumer of that table and diff their freshness treatment (`grep -rn "<table>" --include="*.py" app/`). If one bounds and another does not, that is the finding — do not restate the bound, import it. Where no consumer bounds it, the bound has to be constructed from the source's own publication cadence and cited: FINRA designates two settlement dates a month and publishes ~12 calendar days after each (finra.org/filing-reporting/short-interest schedule), so the newest disseminated figure is up to ~27 days old normally, and 45d is that plus a missed cycle.
- ⚠ Probe-harness hazard, a NEW variant of the exit-code entry from #2214 (which names pytest's usage-error code 4): a revert probe run with `-x` under this repo's xdist `addopts` exits **2** — `xdist.dsession.Interrupted` — for a genuine test failure. Gating "CAUGHT" on `returncode != 0` is therefore right by accident and unfalsifiable in general. Run probes WITHOUT `-x`, require `returncode == 1`, and print the `FAILED …::test_name` lines the run produced, so a CAUGHT names the test that caught it.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `.claude/skills/data-sources/finra.md` §4.1 (the latest-WINS contract, the bound and its construction, the reproduction query); `app/services/instrument_analytics.py` (`_FINRA_SETTLEMENT_MAX_AGE` imported from `FRESHNESS_BOUNDS`, with the reason why a second copy is not written); `tests/test_instrument_analytics.py::TestShortInterestStaleness` (boundary, one-day-past, backfill shape, NULL fails closed, and a bridge test tying the constant to `thesis_break`'s); `scripts/ab_2336_short_interest_staleness.py` (both arms, gain side printed separately).

## A job that SKIPS an item and still advances its watermark leaves a hole no later run can reach (#2394 §3.1, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: none at run time, and none in the census either — the row simply never exists. `strategy_signal_scan` reads every instrument's last bar in one aggregate query, picks the frontier from that, then loads each instrument's bars one at a time. `daily_candle_refresh` writes to `price_daily` on its own schedule, so an instrument can gain a bar between the two reads. The first implementation skipped that instrument ("its series moved, do not evaluate it against a frontier it no longer sits on") and let the watermark advance to the old frontier anyway. The bar it owed was then *behind* the watermark, and the next run's window — "bars strictly after the watermark" — can never include it. Under a ledger with no `ON CONFLICT` there is no repair short of a version bump.
- ⚠ **The general shape: a skip is only safe if the resume marker also declines to move past the skipped work.** Two markers that advance independently — one per item, one per run — is the same defect wearing a different schedule. Either the marker is held back, or the item is not skipped, or the run fails. Silently doing the first two halves of that sentence is what produces a hole.
- The fix here was the third option in disguise: bound the write window by the **frontier the watermark advances to**, not by the series end read later. The two are equal for every instrument the scan selected — eligibility *is* "last bar equals the frontier" — and they diverge only in exactly the racing case, where the frontier bound writes the bar the frontier owes and leaves the newly arrived one for tomorrow. ⚠ The series-end cap stays as well, for the opposite movement: a series that LOST bars must still stop short of its own last bar, or the arrears rule is broken instead.
- ⚠⚠ **A second hole the first one exposed, and this is the more general lesson: an expectation derived from the work actually done cannot detect work not done.** The census gate compared rows written against `expected_per_leg`, which was summed over the windows the scan computed — so an instrument contributing no window lowered the expectation and the row count together, and the check agreed with itself. The population count has to be anchored to something computed BEFORE the work: `instruments_covered == eligible_instruments`, where the eligible count comes from the span query. **Test: if the denominator of a completeness check is built in the same loop as its numerator, the check cannot fail for the reason you wrote it.**
- Both found by Codex at checkpoint 2 (the P1 above and a P2 on the verification script, which snapshotted watermark KEYS and not VALUES — so a pre-existing watermark advanced by the run stayed advanced after the test rows were deleted, leaving a real scan believing an empty window was covered). Neither is visible in a diff read for correctness of what it does; both are about what a later run then cannot do.
- ⚠⚠ **The first repair of the second hole was itself wrong, and the review bot caught it: a completeness gate must anchor on whether the item was WORKED, not on whether it produced OUTPUT.** The fix as first written counted instruments that contributed a window bar and required that to equal the eligible count. But an empty window is a legitimate outcome — an instrument rejoining the frontier after a stale spell has no bar at or after the watermark, and a series that shrank mid-scan may be fully caught up — so the gate aborts a healthy batch. Measured on the live corpus the very next run: **5,783 eligible, 5,779 with a non-empty window**, the four stragglers being exactly the legitimate case. The gate now counts instruments the loader returned a usable series for, incremented at load time, which is independent of the window computation rather than derived from it and can only fail when the load genuinely did.
- ⚠⚠ **AND CHASING THAT WARNING SURFACED A WORSE BUG OF MY OWN, WHICH IS THE REAL LESSON HERE: the spec's own wording was off by one, because the watermark and the write date are measured against different things.** §3.1 says the scan writes bars *"strictly **after** the watermark"*. The watermark names the FRONTIER of the last completed run, and that run wrote bars strictly BEFORE its frontier — so the frontier bar itself is the first one still owed, and `>` skips it. On a series `…, F0, F1, F2` with the frontier moving F1 → F2, `>` yields the empty interval `(F1, F2)`: **every run after the first writes nothing at all, silently, forever.** The bound is `>=`.
- ⚠ **The dev-verification could not have caught it, and that is the transferable part.** The run exercised a cold start (no watermark) and a same-frontier re-run (short-circuited before the window is even computed). Those are the two paths that do NOT use the lower bound. **A resume marker has three states — unset, equal, and MOVED — and the moved one is the only one the job spends its life in. Verify that one explicitly.** A `--resume` arm now seeds each strategy's watermark one session behind today's frontier (the state yesterday's run would have left) and requires a non-zero write: 34,674 rows, newest `signal_bar_date` 2026-08-06. Under `>` it is 0.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_signal_scan.py::write_window_indices` (the frontier upper bound and why it is not the series end; the `>=` lower bound and why the spec's wording is an off-by-one) + `::assert_census_complete` (the two checks, why the population one is not redundant, and why it counts evaluated rather than written); `tests/test_strategy_signal_scan.py::TestWriteWindow::test_a_bar_arriving_mid_scan_is_left_for_tomorrow`, `::test_a_series_that_fell_behind_still_stops_short_of_its_own_last_bar`, `::test_the_day_after_a_completed_run_writes_the_watermark_bar_itself`, `::test_consecutive_runs_write_each_bar_exactly_once`, `TestCensusGate::test_an_unevaluated_eligible_instrument_raises`, `::test_an_empty_window_is_not_a_hole` (all revert-probed); `scripts/verify_2394_signal_scan.py` (`--resume` arm + value-snapshot cleanup).
## Two consumers of the same RATIO divided by two different TABLES (#2411, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom, as ticketed: `scoring._analytics_inputs` took `fund_rows[0]["shares_outstanding"]` unconditionally, so a NULL in the newest `fundamentals_snapshot` row shadowed a usable older one and the instrument lost every share-denominated IAR signal. `JPM` — golden panel — read `no_short_interest_or_shares`. The ticket's proposed fix was "take the newest non-NULL within `fund_rows`".
- That fix is a patch on the wrong table, and the evidence was already in the tree. `thesis_break_scan._short_interest_observations` computes the SAME ratio and its docstring names its denominator: *"the pct metric divides by `share_count_history.shares_outstanding` — the settled short_interest_signal denominator"*. `short_interest_signal` is the function in `instrument_analytics.py` that the scoring path feeds. So the app had two readers of one metric dividing by two different sources, and one of them said in writing which was settled.
- The two sources are not equivalent and the difference is a source rule, not a preference. `financial_periods.shares_outstanding` — what `fundamentals_snapshot` is built from — maps to exactly one concept, `("CommonStockSharesOutstanding",)` (`app/providers/implementations/sec_fundamentals.py:237`), the us-gaap balance-sheet tag. `share_count_history` (sql/259) COALESCEs the cover-page `dei:EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding` over that same us-gaap tag, positive-only, and carries `latest_filed_date`. It is what `instrument_share_count_latest` — the ownership rollup's denominator (data-engineer "Views", I19) — is built on.
- Measured, full population, dev corpus 2026-08-08. `fundamentals_snapshot` newest row per instrument: **3,102 positive / 1,424 NULL / 3 zero, of 4,529**. `share_count_history` newest positive row per instrument: **4,665**. Paired full-population A/B over all **12,696** instruments through the real `_bulk_load_instrument_data` → `_analytics_inputs` → `assemble_instrument_analytics_bulk` path, control arm run in a worktree at `origin/main`: **denominator GAINED 1,564, LOST 1** (`EHGO`); short interest **GAINED 1,158 / SUPPRESSED 42 / 770 value changes**; insider **GAINED 1,564 / SUPPRESSED 1 / 220 value changes**.
- **The ticket's own fix would have recovered 255 of the 1,564.** Decomposing the gains: **900** have no positive us-gaap `CommonStockSharesOutstanding` fact anywhere, so no amount of NULL-skipping inside `fundamentals_snapshot` reaches them; of the **912** gained instruments that carry any snapshot row at all, **255** are the within-window shadow the ticket describes, **465** are shadowed somewhere in history, and **444** never had a share count in the snapshot. That ratio — 255 of 1,564 — is what "question the MODEL, not the case" buys.
- ⚠ **A mechanism I nearly wrote down, falsified by the query that should have preceded it.** `JPM` tags `us-gaap:CommonStockSharesOutstanding` only in its 10-K (dev: dei at `2026-06-30`, `2026-03-31`, `2026-01-31`; us-gaap only at `2025-12-31`), which makes its two newest quarterly snapshot rows NULL. The tempting generalisation — "the us-gaap tag is annual-only" — is **false on the population**: `select concept, form_type, count(*), count(distinct instrument_id) from financial_facts_raw where concept in (…) group by 1,2` returns `CommonStockSharesOutstanding` on **78,401 10-Q rows / 3,106 instruments** against 28,572 10-K rows / 3,179. JPM's pattern is JPM's. The population-level statement that IS true is a coverage one: **4,466** instruments carry a positive dei count, **3,765** a positive us-gaap one.
- ⚠ **A test fixture whose two candidate sources hold the SAME value cannot detect a source swap.** `tests/test_scoring.py::_full_data` had one share count; a test asserting it would have passed whichever source the code read. The fixture now carries a deliberately DIFFERENT count under `share_count_row` than under `fund_rows`, and `test_analytics_inputs_ignores_fund_rows` empties `fund_rows` and asserts the denominator is unmoved — the coupling the ticket removed, pinned.
- ⚠ **A gate's reason-counter can move for a reason that is not the gate.** `stale_settlement` went **19 → 27** across the arms. Nothing about the #2336 settlement bound changed: 8 instruments previously returned `no_short_interest_or_shares` before reaching that gate, and now have a denominator, so they reach it. When a counter you did not touch moves, check whether an EARLIER early-return stopped feeding it before calling it a regression.
- ⚠⚠ **A freshness bound is only as good as the AS-OF it measures, and a grouped view's `MAX(filed_date)` is not the as-of of any one value.** Caught by Codex at checkpoint 2, not by any gate, and not by the full-population A/B — which had already run clean. `share_count_history` groups five concepts per period, so its `latest_filed_date` is the max over the two counts AND the three issuance/buyback flows; a restated flow makes the count look fresher than it is. `MAX` can only move the date forward, so the error is **always** in the fail-open direction. Measured: **16 of 4,665** newest-positive rows overstate, 0 understate, up to **1,456 days** (`HUIZ`: count filed 2020-04-24, view reported 2024-04-19), and **7** sit either side of the 183-day bound. Fixed in sql/273 by adding `shares_outstanding_filed_date`, computed by the SAME `COALESCE` as the value so the two name one fact, and by pointing both consumers at it — `thesis_break_scan` had the identical fail-open and was corrected in the same PR. **Rule: when you bound a value on an as-of, check that the as-of column is derived from the SAME row/fact the value is. In a `GROUP BY` view they usually are not, and an aggregate date is the shape to be suspicious of.**
- ⚠ **A pure-logic suite cannot revert-probe a SQL column, and reporting "NOT CAUGHT" is the useful outcome.** The first probes of the corrected filed date came back `exit=0` on the scoring tests, correctly: `_analytics_inputs` is pure and its fixture hands it a dict, so no test in that file executes the query. Rather than declare the lines covered, this PR adds `TestShareCountFiledDate` — one db-marked case per clause the migration's rule states (a later flow must not freshen the count; the date follows the COALESCE arm the value came from; DEI preference holds for the date too). Probing the three clauses individually then reports 3/3 CAUGHT with the test named. Same posture as the #2232 entry above: pin the enforcement point, do not claim coverage for a line no test can reach.
- ⚠ Cost, measured because the skill says a read-time metric's latency is a second metric: the added bulk read takes `_bulk_load_instrument_data` from **20.7s to 42.5s** over 12,696 ids. It is already index-scanning (`financial_facts_raw_<part>_instrument_id_concept_period_end_idx` on each of 126 partitions) with ~1.7s of planning for the ANY array, so an index does not fix it — accepted because the only production caller is the nightly `compute_rankings` (`compute_score` has no non-test caller), and the per-instrument form measures 0.7-3.7ms. Recorded in the code next to the query so the next person does not re-derive it.
- Prevention: **before changing or auditing a metric's denominator, grep for every consumer of the METRIC, not of the table** — `grep -rn "<signal_or_metric_name>" --include="*.py" app/` — and diff which TABLE each one reads. #2336 caught a *policy* drifting between two consumers of one table; this is the layer above, where the two consumers do not even share a table, and the drift is invisible to any check that starts from a table name. If one consumer's docstring calls its source "settled", that is the source; make the other one match rather than improving it in place.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/scoring.py` (`_SHARE_COUNT_SQL` + `_analytics_inputs`, carrying the three defects and the source rule); `app/services/instrument_analytics.py` (`_SHARE_COUNT_FILED_MAX_AGE` imported from `FRESHNESS_BOUNDS`, scoped to the one metric the vocabulary assigns it to); `tests/test_instrument_analytics.py::TestShareCountStaleness` + `tests/test_scoring.py::TestScoreFromData`; `scripts/ab_2411_share_count_denominator.py` (both arms real code, gains enumerated and sampled).

## A classifier's own sanity check can be blind to its false positives — ask the SOURCE (#2353, 2026-08-08)
