- Symptom: none, ever, and that is the shape. A CUSIP the Official List publishes as an issuer's `CALL` or `PUT` class — AAPL `037833900` / `037833950` against `037833100 COM` — cannot resolve by any path we have, so it sits in `unresolved_13f_cusips` forever while every job reports success. Measured 2026-08-08 by joining the table (110,177 rows / 65,938 distinct CUSIPs) against `13flist2026q2-txt.txt`: **9,561 bulk rows** carrying a terminal `openfigi_unknown` and **8,657 legacy rows** still pending.
- **The source rule was in a PDF nobody had opened.** Form 13F Special Instruction 10 (`https://www.sec.gov/files/form13f.pdf` p.6-7) puts *"Columns 1 through 5 ... in terms of the securities underlying the options, not the options themselves"*, and 11.b.iii makes Column 3 the CUSIP. So an option-class identifier in Column 3 is a filer DEVIATION, not an unmappable security — which changes the verdict from "we lack coverage" to "the filer sent the wrong identifier", a different owner and a different remedy. The ticket had framed these as legitimate identifiers with "nothing upstream to fix".
- ⚠⚠ **The lesson that cost a round: a classifier over source text needs a check that can DISAGREE with it, and a check that correlates with the classifier cannot.** The discriminator was first written as "the description CONTAINS the token `CALL` or `PUT`", and sanity-checked against the CUSIP mod-10 check digit — 9,977 of 10,171 matches failed it, which reads as overwhelming confirmation. It is not a confirmation of anything: option classes copy the underlying's check digit into position 9, so failing mod-10 is a *consequence* of being an option class, not independent evidence about the classifier's edges. A live OpenFIGI probe of the check-digit-VALID tail — the only rows where the two signals could disagree — returned a populated `data` array for `063679427` `CALL NRGU 45`, a BMO structured note. Containment swallows **7 genuine securities**: 4 BMO notes (`CALL NRGU 45`, `CALL NRGD 45`, `CALL BNKU 45`, `CALL LKD 41`) and 3 covered-call ETFs (`ETHE CO CALL ETF`, `KWEB COVERD CALL`, `YIEL S& CALL ETF`), **all 7 passing the check digit**. Fixed to an EXACT description match. **Test: name the rows where your validation signal and your classifier could disagree, and go look at those. If there are none, the validation is a restatement.**
- ⚠⚠ **The wasted-budget framing understated the ticket by an order of severity; the real exposure was a WRONG WRITE.** These rows are not merely unresolvable — the legacy fuzzy-name resolver matches on `name_of_issuer`, which for an option class is byte-identical to the underlying's, so it would mint an `external_identifiers (provider='sec')` row binding an option-class identifier to the underlying instrument. Simulated over the full legacy pending partition (not a sample): **3,876 of 8,663 would promote**, 703 ambiguous, 4,084 below threshold, the top matches at score 1.0 (⚠ subject: that 8,663 is the pre-correction CONTAINMENT set, a superset of the 8,657 the shipped classifier claims — the simulation predates the fix and was not re-run, which bounds the claim rather than voiding it) (`13321L908` → CAMECO, `771049903` → ROBLOX, `29355A907` → ENPHASE ENERGY). Nothing had fired only because that resolver had not reached them. **When a ticket says "wasted budget", check what the wasted work would have WRITTEN if it had succeeded.**
- ⚠ **The obvious structured field was the wrong one, and the filing proved it.** `PUTCALL` is a real column in the 13F INFOTABLE and looks like the discriminator. It is not: accession `0001313360-26-000003` (`form13fInfoTable20260806.xml`, fetched from EDGAR) files `<cusip>78462F953</cusip>` — the Official List's SPY PUT class — **together with** `<putCall>Put</putCall>`. `PUTCALL` describes the POSITION; the defect is in the IDENTIFIER, and the two are independent. Both conventions are live in one corpus: AAPL holds 2,230 compliant option rows bound through `037833100`.
- ⚠ **A live-arm A/B can read `0 → 0` and still be the right change.** The bulk partition's OpenFIGI selection set measured **0 before and 0 after**, because every bulk row already carries a terminal status — the value there is latent, realised when #2304's reset returns them to NULL. Reporting only that arm would have read as "no effect"; the legacy arm moved **43,239 → 34,582 distinct pending CUSIPs (−8,657)**. **State which arm is live and which is latent rather than averaging them into one number.**
- ⚠ A revert probe on "feed the tombstoner the `D`-filtered list instead of the raw parse" came back **NOT CAUGHT** and the honest move was to say so and add the test, not to reclassify the probe as unnecessary. A delisted `CALL` class is still a `CALL` class; the backfill drops `status='D'` rows before MATCHING (correctly — a just-delisted CUSIP must not anchor a new mapping) and that filter must not reach the tombstoner. 6/6 CAUGHT after.
- Prevention: **when writing a classifier over source free text, find the check that can falsify it — usually the source's own answer for the disputed rows — and run it before shipping.** A statistic computed over the rows the classifier already accepts cannot tell you about the ones it should have rejected. And per "source-rule before design", read the FORM's instructions, not only the data dictionary: the instruction that made this a filer error rather than a coverage gap is prose in a PDF, absent from every structured artefact we hold.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `sql/274_unresolved_13f_option_pseudo_cusip.sql` (Special Instruction 10 quoted, the three narrower-than-expected traps, why the verdict is terminal and never overwrites); `app/services/sec_13f_securities_list.py` (`_PUT_CALL_DESCRIPTIONS` carrying the 7 false positives and the probe that found them, `_is_put_call`, `tombstone_option_pseudo_cusips`); `.claude/skills/data-sources/openfigi.md` §4.5 + §7.5; `.claude/skills/data-sources/sec-edgar.md` (13F Official List bullet); `tests/test_sec_13f_securities_list.py::TestIsPutCall` (incl. `test_compound_descriptions_containing_call_are_not_option_classes`) + `::TestTombstoneOptionPseudoCusips` (all revert-probed, 6/6).
## A guard written against a library's documented behaviour is dead code once the library changes it (#2394 §3.2, 2026-08-08)

- `deflate_group` refuses a "degenerate trial" — one whose per-entry-date return series never varies over the dates it shares with the others — because such a trial carries no pairwise information and equation (8)'s correlation is undefined for it. The guard was copied verbatim from `scripts/verify_2240_statistics.py`'s P11, whose comment states: *"`np.corrcoef` returns NaN for a CONSTANT series — its denominator is that series' own standard deviation."* It then tests `np.all(np.isfinite(matrix))`.
- **Measured on numpy 2.4.4 (2026-08-08), that is false.** `np.corrcoef(np.array([[0.1, 0.1, 0.1], [0.1, -0.2, 0.3]]))` returns `[[1., 0.], [0., 1.]]` — a finite **0.0**, not NaN. So the `isfinite` guard never fires, and a trial with no information is read as **UNCORRELATED**, which pushes `implied_independent_trials` toward `M` on evidence that does not exist. The direction is conservative here (a larger `N` raises the deflation threshold), which is exactly why nothing would ever have surfaced it.
- ⚠ **The general shape: a guard whose trigger is a third party's failure mode is only as live as that failure mode.** It reads as defensive code and cannot be told apart from working code by inspection, because the branch it protects is never entered. The fix is not to delete it — a future numpy could restore NaN — but to (a) test the PROPERTY on the input rather than the symptom in the output, and (b) **pin the library's current behaviour in an assertion next to the test**, so the day it changes back is visible rather than silently making the live check redundant.
- ⚠⚠ **AND THE FIRST REPAIR WAS ITSELF WRONG, in a way only a table test found: `float(np.std(row)) == 0.0` does not detect a constant series.** The mean of three binary `0.1`s is `0.10000000000000002`, so the deviations are ~1e-17 and the standard deviation is a denormal rather than a zero. The property that actually means "no variation" is that every value is equal — `np.ptp(row) == 0.0` — which is exact in floating point and invents no tolerance. **Rule: never test a derived statistic for exact zero when the underlying property is an equality; test the equality.**
- ⚠ Incidental, filed rather than fixed here: `scripts/verify_2240_statistics.py::_criterion6` still carries both the false claim and the dead `isfinite` guard, and would report a rho of 0 for a degenerate sleeve.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/backtest_run.py::deflate_group` (the `ptp` guard, why it is not `std`, and the measurement that killed the `isfinite` mechanism); `tests/test_backtest_run.py::TestDeflateGroup::test_a_constant_return_series_refuses_and_is_not_read_as_uncorrelated` (which pins numpy's current return value beside the assertion); `scripts/probe_2394_backtest_run.py` (the `std`-for-`ptp` probe).

## The invocation unit of a job is set by the STATISTIC it must produce, not by the resource it iterates (#2394 §3.2, 2026-08-08)

- §3.2 of the runner spec says the job *"runs the harness for a strategy × namespace × arm"*. Read literally that is a per-strategy job, and it would have been the natural thing to build: one strategy, six arms, eight rows, repeat. It cannot work, and the reason is arithmetic rather than architectural. Criterion 6's Deflated Sharpe deflates the observed Sharpe by `V[SR_n]`, the variance of Sharpes **across the measured trials**, and `deflated_sharpe.MIN_MEASURED_TRIALS` is 2. One strategy is one trial, `V[SR_n]` does not exist, and `deflate_sharpe` returns `None` — so every row a per-strategy invocation writes carries `deflated_sharpe = NULL` and `check_promotable` refuses it with `deflated_sharpe_not_computed`, **a refusal no amount of re-running that strategy can clear.**
- Equation (8) needs the same thing from the other side: the inter-trial correlation is measured off the trials' realised return series on the dates they BOTH traded, so one trial has nothing to correlate with.
- ⚠ **The consequence for the failure rule, which inverts the sibling job's.** `strategy_signal_scan` (§3.1) is explicit that one strategy's failure must not stop the others, and the first draft of this job copied that without checking whether it still held. It does not: `V[SR_n]` is a function of WHICH trials were measured, so a run that loses one strategy during evaluation and proceeds deflates the survivors against a smaller variance while reporting itself complete — **a more confident number obtained by losing evidence.** The phases are therefore ordered evaluate-everything → deflate-once → write, so that a strategy failing in phase 1 aborts with zero rows written.
- ⚠ **Test: before copying a per-item failure rule from a sibling job, ask whether any output of the new job is a function of the SET.** A per-item transaction boundary is right exactly when the items are independent, and a cross-item statistic is the thing that makes them not.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/backtest_run.py` module header (§2's rule) + `run_backtest`'s docstring (the inverted failure rule and why the phase order follows from it) + `deflate_group` (grouped per `(namespace, quarantine_arm)`, because a Sharpe measured on the withheld side under admitted bars is not a draw from the same search as one measured in-sample under masked bars).

## A measurement that is FREE has to be refused by the job, because no constraint can refuse it (#2394 §3.2, 2026-08-08)

- Criterion 5's whole mechanism is that looking at the withheld side is rare, deliberate and logged. The database enforces a lot of it: `sql/264` gives `strategy_results` a cascaded check option over `namespace = 'in_sample'` so the obvious writer *cannot* express a hold-out row, and the store carries a trigger refusing any hold-out row with no `evaluate` access record.
- None of that helps here, because **`strategy_result.namespace_for_position` is a FILTER over positions one corpus sweep has already produced.** Measured on S-1 masked, full population: one pass yields `in_sample 2,456,097 (78.34%) / hold_out 679,258 (21.66%)`. The hold-out arm costs nothing. A job that computes both partitions every run and writes both turns `strategy_holdout_accesses` into **a count of cron fires**, and `check_promotable`'s criterion-5 clause — every evaluation must have a recorded access — then passes on rows nobody deliberately looked at. Every constraint is satisfied and the audit means nothing.
- ⚠ **So the hold-out side is not merely left unwritten on an in-sample run — it is not COMPUTED.** The positions are partitioned, the hold-out side is counted and discarded, and the count is the only hold-out figure such a run emits. A run that computes the withheld metrics and logs them at INFO has performed an unrecorded evaluation whatever the table says.
- ⚠ **Same shape one layer up in the gate's own inputs.** `result_ledger.quarantine_arms_compared()` answers "are both criterion-9 arms stored?" and, on a `hold_out` identity, deliberately RECORDS a `read` access — *looking is the event criterion 5 governs*. A job that gated every hold-out row it had just written would add one read record per row and turn the audit trail into a count of its own automation. The job supplies the boolean directly: it wrote both arms in one transaction, so **it must not ask the database a question it is the answer to.**
- ⚠ **General rule: when a control's cost is what makes it a control, and the cost goes to zero, the control has to move into the caller.** Look for it wherever a "second, expensive arm" turns out to be a projection of the first.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/backtest_run.py` module header (§4's rule), `_absorb` (the counted-and-discarded branch), `_candidate` (why `quarantine_arms_compared` and `ambiguity_material` are supplied rather than read), and `_check_holdout_pairing` — which also refuses a **whitespace-only** `holdout_purpose`, the #2286 present-but-empty shape at a new layer: `"   "` is truthy, so a bare truthiness test admits an audit record that records nothing.

## A labelled set drawn from the channel where truth EXISTS cannot separate two spellings of a rule that differ only where it does NOT (#2408, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: none at either gate that was supposed to catch it. #2408 reads the record holder of a joint Form 3/4 block off the filing's own `natureOfOwnership` text, because the ownership XML does not attribute a Table I line to a co-filer (`<nonDerivativeTable>` is a SIBLING of `<reportingOwner>`; `insider_transactions._extract_holdings` gives every line to `filers[0]`, `app/services/insider_transactions.py:449`). The matcher asks "which of this cluster's members does the sentence name". Two spellings were live: raw substring containment, and containment anchored on token boundaries.
- **Both scored IDENTICALLY on the labelled set — 47 correct swaps and 4 wrong, of 51, on all 408 clusters — and both passed every unit test in the file.** The labelled set is the cross-accession clusters carrying exactly one Table I-attested `direct` member, i.e. the clusters where the shipped #2385 rule already decides. That is the only place ground truth exists, and it is by construction a place where the new tier never runs.
- Root cause of the near-miss: the anchored spelling UNDER-matches an abbreviated EDGAR conformed name. `LCID` accession `0001104659-24-113592` (fetched from EDGAR and confirmed against our stored rows) lists `PUBLIC INVESTMENT FUND` and `Ayar Third Investment Co` as reporting owners, and its `natureOfOwnership` reads **"By Ayar Third Investment Company"**. Anchored, the subsidiary that actually holds is unmatchable, its parent becomes the only named member, and the fold promotes the parent — moving `LCID`'s pie by **280,992,324 shares**, the largest single mover in the A/B. Unanchored, both are named, the uniqueness guard declines, and the incumbent (the correct holder) stands.
- The mirror case is real too and was what motivated anchoring: `LEGION PARTNERS L P I` is a prefix of `LEGION PARTNERS L P II`, so a footnote naming fund II also "names" fund I. **6 folds of 1,434** carry a member pair with that shape. But that failure DECLINES — a lost promotion, never a wrong one — so the over-matching spelling is the fail-closed one and it wins.
- ⚠ **Only the paired full-population A/B distinguished them.** Not the labelled set, not the census, not 9 revert probes. The A/B is where a rule's behaviour on the population it will actually run against becomes visible, and on a read path whose representative is load-bearing (#2385: the rep is the identity that survives into owner-once) it is the only place.
- Prevention: **when validation has to borrow its labels from a different channel, say which sub-population the labels cover and check whether the change even fires there.** If the answer is "it does not", the labelled score bounds the rule's ceiling and says nothing about its edges — and the edges are where two candidate spellings differ. Enumerate the movers by name in the A/B and read the largest one; here that was one line of output and it inverted the decision.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_named_record_holder` (the two failure directions, the `LCID` and `LEGION` cases, and why raw containment is the fail-closed one); `tests/test_insider_deemed_chain_collapse.py::test_an_abbreviated_conformed_name_still_matches_its_own_footnote` + `::test_a_sibling_fund_substring_declines_rather_than_guessing`; `scripts/probe_2408_record_holder_rep.py` probe I (injects the reverted anchored spelling).

## Free text in an ownership filing is per-ROW evidence — pooling it per ACCESSION lets another holding's record holder decide this one (#2408, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: a first draft of the #2408 census gathered every `natureOfOwnership` string and every footnote on a cluster's accession and asked which member they named. It read plausibly and was a category error.
- One Form 4 carries a footnote set covering MANY holdings, each naming a different record holder. `0001415889-25-017225` (Battery Ventures, dev corpus) names BV IX, BIP IX, BP IX, The Lee Family Trust, and "Roger H. Lee jointly with his spouse" across five footnotes of one accession. `0001193125-26-054947` (Berkshire) names GEICO and National Fire & Marine — subsidiaries that are not reporting owners at all, so "exactly one member named" is unsatisfiable there and must stay unsatisfied.
- The link that DOES exist is the reported amount: `insider_transactions.post_transaction_shares` for a Form 4, `insider_initial_holdings.shares` for a Form 3, and `footnote_refs` for the row→footnote edge. That is the same value the fold clusters on, so evidence is keyed `(accession, shares)`.
- ⚠ Two adjacent traps found while wiring it: `insider_initial_holdings` has NO `footnote_refs`, so a Form 3's `See footnote.` resolves to nothing and contributes only the literal field — an asymmetry to state, not to paper over. And a query against `insider_transactions` alone silently halves the evidence: **30,149 of the corpus's indirect rows are Form 3 initial holdings** (`direct_indirect='I'`, all 30,149 with a non-null `nature_of_ownership`; `insider_transactions` holds 138,380 more).
- ⚠ A separate arm, built rather than argued: matching a natural person's EDGAR conformed name (`LAST FIRST`) also in rotated `FIRST LAST` form. It is the "complete" thing to do and it is WORSE — 106 correct of 124 on the labelled set against 121 of 125 — because it makes the deemed owner matchable beside the holder and collapses the uniqueness the rule depends on. Verbatim matching therefore leans toward entities, which is right under Rule 16a-1(a)(2) but is a name-format artefact rather than the source rule, and that distinction is recorded in the code so a future "improvement" re-runs the arm.
- Prevention: **before matching free text against a set of candidates, ask what the text is ABOUT and find the key that scopes it to that.** A document-level pool is only correct when the document says one thing. Where no key exists the honest answer is to decline, not to widen the pool.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_read_record_holder_evidence` (value keying, the Form 3 asymmetry) + `::_named_record_holder`; `tests/test_ownership_rollup_record_holder_db.py` (four db-tier cases pinning the SQL a pure suite cannot probe); `scripts/probe_2408_record_holder_rep.py` probes D, J, K, L.

## A revert-probe run MUTATES the source file, so anything that reads the tree while it runs captures an injected defect (#2408, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: `git status` showed `app/services/ownership_rollup.py` modified after a clean commit, and the diff read backwards — HEAD held `candidate = _named_record_holder(...)` ordered BEFORE the Table I clause, the working tree held the correct order. The commit had captured **probe E's injection**, not the code.
- Root cause: `scripts/probe_*.py` works by writing a mutated copy of the module to disk, running pytest, and restoring in a `finally`. That is the right design — it is what makes the probe test the real import path — but for the duration of the run **the checkout is not the branch**. The probe had been launched into the background (13 injections × 2 pytest runs is well past a foreground timeout), and `git add -A && git commit` ran while injection E was on disk.
- Blast radius was wider than the commit, because the same window was used to launch other work: the paired full-population A/B (3 shards) and the golden-panel smoke both started inside it, and Python binds the module at process start — so each could have loaded any of the 13 injected variants. **The results looked coherent** (0 pie increases, the expected movers, `LCID` absent), which is exactly why coherence is not verification. All three were re-run on an idle box against the amended commit; the panel came back byte-identical and the A/B was re-measured rather than argued about.
- ⚠ The tell was cheap and generic: `git status --short` was non-empty immediately after a commit. That is the check, and it costs nothing.
- Prevention: **treat a probe run as an exclusive lock on the checkout.** Nothing else — no commit, no A/B, no smoke, no second probe — starts until it has printed its restored-suite line and exited. Concretely: `pgrep -f probe_ | wc -l` before launching a measurement or committing, and `git status --short` after any commit that followed a background job. The repo already forbids sequential A/B arms while the daemon writes; this is the same hazard sourced from your own tooling instead of the daemon.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/probe_2408_record_holder_rep.py` (module docstring states the exclusive-lock requirement).

## A "fails closed" test whose expected answer is ALSO the defect's answer proves nothing — order the fixture so the two differ (#2408, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: three occurrences on one ticket, and review caught the third. Each test asserted "the cluster is ambiguous, so the incumbent is kept". But the incumbent is what the pass returns for *every* refusal — no evidence, no pooling, a broken uniqueness guard, the feature deleted entirely — so the assertion did not separate the case it named from any of them.
- Concretely: `_named_record_holder` builds `named` in cluster order. With the incumbent listed FIRST, dropping the uniqueness check (`return named[0]`) returns the incumbent, and the test passes against the exact defect its name describes. Revert probe B reported `NOT CAUGHT` on the first occurrence; the second was found by the review bot on PR #2425 (*"the test doesn't actually verify decline behaviour distinct from normal incumbent selection"*).
- Fix in both cases was one line — list the NON-incumbent member first, so "take the first named" produces a different answer from "decline" — plus a comment saying member order is load-bearing, because it does not look load-bearing.
- ⚠ This is the same shape as the prevention-log entry on a FLAT fixture pinning neither `>` in `a>b AND c>d` (#2240 phase 5c). The general rule: **a test of a refusal must construct the fixture so that the refusal's output differs from every plausible wrong path's output.** If they coincide, the test is a tautology however precise its docstring is.
- ⚠ The revert probe is the detector that works here and it is cheap — but only if its `must_fail` list actually names the new test. The second occurrence existed because probe B was never pointed at it.
- Prevention: when writing a "fails closed / declines / keeps the incumbent" assertion, ask **"what would a broken version return?"** and change the fixture until the answer differs. Then add the case to the revert probe that injects that break. Enforced in: `tests/test_insider_deemed_chain_collapse.py::test_text_naming_two_members_fails_closed` + `::test_two_accessions_naming_two_members_fails_closed` (both carry the ordering note); `scripts/probe_2408_record_holder_rep.py` probe B (runs both).
## Re-using an engine "for apples-to-apples" imports its POLICY, not just its plumbing (#2426, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: `strategy_results_store.buy_and_hold_return_pct` read **33,706,844.28%**, and `return_vs_buy_and_hold_pct` inherited it. Every strategy therefore "failed to beat buy-and-hold" by tens of millions of points — the exact comparator #2364 was to build criterion 7's promotion refusal on.
- Root cause: `backtest_run._measure_namespace` built the benchmark by calling `equity_curve.build_equity_curve`, whose docstring correctly argues that sharing the engine is what stops *"the machinery's difference being attributed to the strategy"*. It does — for the **cost model** and the **fill contract**. But the engine also carries `SIZING_RULE_ID = equal_weight_concurrent_v1`, which **re-imposes equal weight on every event date**, so the benchmark traded: 3,292 rebalance dates and **137,477,862×** the starting pot turned over, on a portfolio defined by never trading.
- Source rule, which existed and was not consulted: **Blume & Stambaugh, "Biases in computed returns: An application to the size effect", JFE 12 (1983), 387-404** — rebalancing trades into the bid-ask noise in each closing print, and *"returns computed for buy-and-hold portfolios largely avoid the bias induced by closing prices"*. They measure it 50× larger on small firms (0.056%/day vs 0.001%), which is our panel exactly. Full-population A/B on identical legs: rebalanced **1,204,631,084.15%** against buy-and-hold **3,223.24%** — **23.2 points of annual return, manufactured**.
- ⚠ The issue's own premise was FALSIFIED and the falsifier was structural, not statistical: there is no summation anywhere on the path — `build_equity_curve` carries one `cash` scalar and returns `cash + Σ(units × mark)`. The stated arithmetic (`33,706,844 / 3,541 ≈ 9,519`) was numerically plausible and mechanically impossible. **A plausible ratio is a hypothesis about a mechanism; read the code path before accepting it.** The measured sum was 0.0141× the stored figure — 70× too small.
- Prevention: **when reusing a component so two things are "comparable", enumerate which of its decisions you meant to inherit and which you did not.** A cost model and a fill contract are plumbing; a sizing rule is policy, and policy is the thing the comparison is supposed to isolate. Concretely: if the shared component has a frozen, hashed rule id, the reuse site must say which id governs the second caller — and if the answer is "the same one", that is a claim to defend, not a default.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/equity_curve.py::BENCHMARK_RULE_ID` + `build_buy_and_hold_curve`; `app/services/backtest_run.py::_measure_namespace` (why-comment at the call site); `app/services/strategy_statistics.py::compute_metrics` docstring (which used to assert the SAME sizing rule); `.claude/skills/data-sources/market-structure.md` ("The benchmark is a construction"); `tests/test_equity_curve.py::TestBuyAndHoldComposition`; `scripts/verify_2426_benchmark.py --compositions`.

## Anything that determines a stored number must be on the identity hash — and adding it later collides with a rehash-on-read guard (#2426, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom (latent, not observed): `ResultIdentity.version` hashed `sizing_rule` — deliberately, because §5.4 says naming it *"is what stops a later sizing change reading as a performance improvement"* — but hashed nothing describing the benchmark, because the benchmark had no rule of its own. So the comparator every result is judged against could have been changed with **no version movement**: two runs with different bars would collide on one identity, and the second would be refused as a duplicate of a measurement it does not match.
- ⚠ The second half is the part that bites during the fix. `result_ledger._result_from_row` **re-derives the hash from the stored columns on every read and raises on mismatch**. So adding a hashed field is not the free "new rows get new versions" it looks like — it makes every *existing* row permanently unreadable. Found by Codex at spec checkpoint 1, against a spec whose own acceptance criteria contradicted each other on this point.
- Resolution: re-derive the stored versions under the completed payload, because the benchmark rule always WAS an input to those numbers and the old hash was simply computed over an incomplete payload. ⚠ Ordering is forced by `trg_strategy_results_holdout_access`, which fires `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE` and demands a matching `strategy_holdout_accesses` row: the access rows move to the new version FIRST, same transaction. The replacement hashes are emitted as literals by a script that **asserts it reproduces each row's OLD hash from the stored columns before emitting the new one** — without that guard an emitted literal is a guess, and a wrong one is indistinguishable from the bug.
- Prevention: before adding a field to any identity hash, `grep` for a reader that re-derives that hash and compares. If one exists, the migration owes the existing rows a re-derivation, and the re-derivation owes itself a reproduce-the-old-value assertion. And when a hashed rule is *absent* rather than wrong, ask what stored number it determines — an unhashed input is a knob nobody can see turn.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_result.py::ResultIdentity.benchmark_rule`; `sql/275_strategy_result_benchmark_rule.sql` (header states the ordering and the literal-emission rationale); `scripts/verify_2426_benchmark.py --emit-version-map` (the reproduce-the-old-hash guard).

## `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` silently DROPS the view's check option (#2426, 2026-08-08)

- Symptom: `test_the_view_refuses_to_smuggle_a_hold_out_row` failed with `DID NOT RAISE WithCheckOptionViolation` after a migration that added a column to `strategy_results_store`.
- Root cause: `sql/264` creates `strategy_results` and then applies `ALTER VIEW strategy_results SET (check_option = 'cascaded')` **as a separate statement**, with a comment saying why it must be separate. A later migration adding a result column must re-run the `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` (because `SELECT *` was expanded at creation) — and doing so resets the view's options, dropping the check option with no error and no warning.
- ⚠ The failure direction is the dangerous one: the view stops refusing an INSERT that smuggles a `hold_out` row in through the in-sample name, which is criterion 5's entire mechanism. Nothing about the column change looks related to hold-out access.
- Prevention: **`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` and `ALTER VIEW … SET` travel together.** Any migration that re-runs the former must immediately re-run the latter. More generally: re-running a DDL statement to pick up a schema change reverts every option applied to that object afterwards — grep the object's creating migration for trailing `ALTER` statements before re-issuing its `CREATE`.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `sql/275_strategy_result_benchmark_rule.sql` step 5 (re-applies the check option, with the reason); `tests/test_strategy_holdout_namespace.py::test_the_view_refuses_to_smuggle_a_hold_out_row` (which is what caught it).
## The documented escape from "never pipe a gate" is itself broken in zsh (#2240 fold wiring, 2026-08-08)

- `.claude/CLAUDE.md`'s rule — *never pipe a gate command, because a pipe returns the pipe's status* — offers three escapes, and one of them is `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`. **`PIPESTATUS` is a bash array and does not exist in zsh**, which is this box's shell: zsh spells it `$pipestatus` and indexes from **1**. So `uv run pyright 2>&1 | tail -2; echo "EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"` prints `EXIT=` — an empty string, not a status.
- ⚠ **The failure direction is the one the original rule exists to prevent.** An empty `EXIT=` reads at a glance as a gate that printed nothing, not as a gate whose status was never captured. The status being gated on is silently absent, and absence looks like success. Committed this session against `uv run pyright`, and caught only because the surrounding output happened to say `0 errors` — had there been a real type error, the same empty `EXIT=` would have been read as "fine".
- ⚠ This is a defect in the WORKAROUND, not in the rule. The rule's own preferred form is correct and shell-agnostic: **run the gate bare and read `$?`, or redirect it to a file and read the file.** `${pipestatus[1]}` is right only under a `#!/bin/zsh` shebang and `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` only under `#!/bin/bash`; neither belongs in an ad-hoc interactive command on this box.
- ⚠ Same session, adjacent: a background measurement written with `print(...)` and no `flush=True` left its output file at **0 bytes** for the whole of a ~40-minute full-corpus run, because Python block-buffers stdout when it is redirected. The archive already carries this for piped jobs; it applies equally to an unpiped redirect, and the tell is identical to a stall.
- Enforced in: this log; `scripts/verify_2240_fold_wiring.py` (`flush=True` on every progress line, with the reason beside it).

## Asserting a data-capability gap without probing the provider (#2437, 2026-08-09)

- Symptom: I stated "we have no intraday data / we only have daily candles" across a multi-session strategy-research pass. The operator corrected it **four times**, the last with visible annoyance. The claim was false the whole time.
- Root cause: three separate things were collapsed into one sentence. (1) `research_price_daily` is daily, true. (2) The eToro **WS stream** has no depth and no trade sizes — true, and the only real gap. (3) `price_intraday` exists (`sql/023_live_pricing_currency.sql`) with **0 rows and no writer**. I read (3) as evidence of *unavailability*, when it is a **build gap**. Meanwhile `EtoroMarketDataProvider.get_intraday_candles` (`app/providers/implementations/etoro.py`) has served intraday OHLCV on demand the entire time — measured reach at `count=1000`: `OneMinute` ~2 days, `ThirtyMinutes` ~1 month, `OneHour` ~2 months, **`FourHours` ~8 months**, volume populated, extended hours included.
- ⚠ **An empty table is not a measurement of what a provider can serve.** It measures what we have chosen to store. The two are routinely confused because the empty table is the artefact sitting in front of you and the provider capability requires a call to discover.
- ⚠ **The blast radius is not the wrong sentence, it is the deleted option space.** A false capability constraint silently removes a whole class of strategy from consideration, and every downstream recommendation inherits it without ever restating the premise — so nothing later in the chain can catch it. The research pass was framed around "daily bars only" for days.
- ⚠ Repeat-correction is itself the signal: **the fourth correction of the same fact means the fact was never written down.** Memory of a correction does not survive a context boundary; a skill section does. Cost of writing it: one edit. Cost of not: four corrections and a misframed research pass.
- Prevention: **a capability claim is a measurement — probe the provider before asserting a gap**, exactly as "test before claim" already requires for behaviour. Concretely: grep the provider interface for the capability (`get_intraday_candles` was one grep away), then hit it (`/_debug/etoro-candles-probe`, `app/api/_debug_ws.py:47`). When a claim about our data has been corrected once, write it into the data-source skill in the SAME turn — do not carry it as something to remember.
- Enforced in: this log; `.claude/skills/data-sources/etoro-api.md` § "⚠⚠ WE HAVE INTRADAY HISTORY" (per-interval reach table + reproduce command + the three-capability split); `.claude/CLAUDE.md` (etoro-api skill bullet).

## A structural data boundary must cover every consumer of the affected state (#2469, 2026-08-10)

- Symptom: the bounded runner loaded every unresolved `price_series_break` and prevented S-4 positions from crossing one, but only split indicator state when `StrategyEntry.exit_levels` was present. S-1/S-3 could therefore compute momentum or mean-reversion state across the old and new price scales; S-2's separate cross-sectional staging path could do the same.
- Root cause: the boundary was attached to the feature being added (S-4 level outcomes) instead of to the property it protects (every price-derived state consumer). The result looked fail-closed at the outcome layer while other strategies still admitted cross-scale inputs.
- Prevention: when adding a structural corpus boundary, enumerate every consumer of the affected series contract, including alternate per-series and cross-sectional paths. A branch-specific test is insufficient; pin at least one consumer on each distinct path and assert both the final pre-boundary bar and post-boundary warm-up behaviour.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/backtest_run.py::_signals_for` and `::_stage_cross_sectional_segments`; `tests/test_backtest_run.py::TestSeriesBreakBoundary` (per-series S-4 and cross-sectional S-2 restart cases).

## Aggregate the entity grain before joining its history (#2531, 2026-08-11)

- Symptom: review flagged strategy realised P&L and committed capital queries whose current joins are one-to-one only because `strategy_position_ownership.broker_position_id` and `strategy_trades.funding_decision_id` are schema-`UNIQUE`.
- Risk: a later legitimate history-table redesign could turn either relationship one-to-many and silently multiply money inside `SUM`, even though the query itself still looks valid.
- Prevention: establish the monetary grain explicitly before aggregation. Select distinct exact broker-position IDs before joining close events; use `EXISTS` for lifecycle-state membership when summing one funding decision's amount. Do not rely on a distant uniqueness constraint to make a money aggregation correct.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_wealth.py` `owned_broker_positions` CTE; `app/services/strategy_control_plane.py::configure_paper_pool` committed-capital `EXISTS` predicates.

## Corporate-action labels do not prove ratio direction (#2580, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: the delayed-SIP source probe accepted a `forward_splits` record whenever `new_rate != old_rate`; a reverse-split-shaped ratio could therefore qualify the forward-split contract.
- Prevention: validate the economic direction as well as the provider's category. A forward split requires positive `old_rate` and `new_rate > old_rate`; unequal rates alone are insufficient.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/alpaca_delayed_sip_probe.py::_require_tsla_forward_split`; `tests/test_alpaca_delayed_sip_probe.py::test_forward_split_check_requires_actual_matching_action`.

## A fail-closed read guard turns every existing row, and every fixture, into the refused path (#2436, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `sql/332` adds `theses.subject_identity_ok` and the consumers refuse anything but `TRUE`. Two consequences arrived from the same root, one caught by Codex and one by the test suite. (1) The migration can only add NULL columns, so on any database already holding theses a migrate-and-deploy would have silently stripped the ENTIRE historical corpus out of `portfolio.py`, `scoring.py`, `entry_timing.py` and `reporting.py` until somebody ran a Python backfill by hand. (2) `tests/test_scoring.py::_thesis_row` omitted the new column, so `test_thesis_without_targets_notes_stance_not_absence` began exercising the QUARANTINE path while still reading as an ordinary-thesis test.
- Root cause: fail-closed is right for the guard and wrong as a **deployment default**. NULL correctly means "nobody decided", but on the day the column ships that is true of every row that exists, and a documented "remember to run the backfill" is not a control. The fixture case is the same shape one layer down: a positional/dict fixture that predates the column supplies the refused value by omission, and the test keeps passing under a name that no longer describes it.
- ⚠ **The direction of the failure is the dangerous part.** Both land on the safe-looking side — no exit fires, no band is read, the test still passes — so nothing raises. The blast radius is invisible precisely because the guard is doing what it says.
- Prevention: when adding a fail-closed verdict column, ship the **populating path in the same PR and on the automatic route**, not as a script an operator must find. This repo's route is the `app/main.py` lifespan self-heal (the `ensure_*_singleton` probes, #1232/#1270 precedent) — it runs unattended, is idempotent on verdict-equivalence, and self-heals a restore-from-snapshot or a rule-hash change. Keep exactly one write function shared by the boot path and the script so they cannot drift. Then, separately: grep every fixture that builds a row of the affected table and add the column with an explicit safe default, documenting in the fixture WHY it is not optional. Verify the boot path empirically — null the column, run `pytest tests/smoke`, confirm the counts return to what they were.
- ⚠⚠ **RECURRED at #2648 (2026-08-13), and the recurrence is in this entry's OWN prevention step.** "Grep every fixture that builds a row of the affected table" was written here and then applied to the one fixture that had failed (`tests/test_scoring.py::_thesis_row`) — a per-case patch wearing a full-population instruction. `tests/test_thesis_accuracy_244.py::_seed_thesis` still omitted the column, so all three #244 entry-anchor tests seeded the refused verdict: two failed loudly (`TypeError: conversion from NoneType to Decimal`), and the third — `test_no_anchor_returns_null_target_hit` — kept PASSING while asserting nothing, because the quarantine nulls the same three columns the missing anchor was supposed to. **A fail-closed default does not only break tests, it disarms the ones that assert absence.** Census run this time (13 `INSERT INTO theses` sites across 9 test files): only this file drives a consumer that applies `is_thesis_usable` — the gate lives in exactly `entry_timing.py`, `portfolio.py`, `reporting.py`, `scoring.py` — so the remaining 8 files are unaffected rather than untested. ⚠ Note the verdict is a CONSTRAINED TRIPLE (`theses_subject_identity_triple_ck`): a fixture cannot set the verdict alone, and the rule version must come from `RULE_SET_VERSION`, never a literal, because it is a code hash.
- ⚠ Generalises: **when a prevention step says "every X", the entry is not discharged until the census is recorded with its count.** A number in the log ("13 sites, 9 files, 1 affected") is checkable by the next reader; "grepped the fixtures" is not, and reads identically whether one file or all of them were fixed.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/thesis_subject_identity.py::ensure_subject_identity_verdicts` (docstring carries both halves); `app/main.py` lifespan probe; `scripts/backfill_thesis_subject_identity.py` (audit only, delegates the write); `tests/test_scoring.py::_thesis_row` docstring; `tests/test_thesis_subject_identity_quarantine.py::TestEnsureSubjectIdentityVerdicts`; `tests/test_thesis_accuracy_244.py::_seed_thesis` (docstring states why TRUE is the default) + `::test_a_thesis_with_an_undecided_subject_verdict_is_refused_not_read` (the read-path quarantine assertion that was missing, revert-probed against `is not False`).

## Withholding a poisoned input also withholds the rules that never read it (#2436, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: quarantining a wrong-company thesis meant not populating `details[iid]["thesis"]` in `app/services/portfolio.py`. `_evaluate_exit` opens with `if thesis is None: return False, ""` — so the change would have silently disabled the **severe-risk-event** exit as well, a rule that reads no thesis field at all. Measured on the dev corpus: 5 `EXIT` recommendations across the quarantined set, 4 of whose instruments are currently held.
- Root cause: the early return was written as "no thesis, nothing to evaluate" when the module in fact had three exit rules, only two of them thesis-derived. Removing an input through a shared guard inherits every incidental dependency that guard already carried.
- ⚠ **An exit that stops firing leaves no row.** There is no artefact to notice, no failing test, and no operator-visible count that moves — the regression is only visible by reading the control flow of every rule downstream of the guard.
- Prevention: before withholding a shared input, enumerate the rules downstream of the guard and check which of them actually READ the withheld fields. Rules that do not must keep firing, and each needs a test asserting it still does under the withheld state. Same family as `docs/settled-decisions.md`'s severe-risk-event independence and the #2050 finding that gated the same exit on memo formatting — this is the second time this specific exit has been disabled by an unrelated condition.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/portfolio.py::_evaluate_exit` (the `quarantined` fall-through and its comment); `tests/test_thesis_subject_identity_quarantine.py::TestPortfolioQuarantine::test_quarantined_thesis_still_fires_the_severe_risk_exit` (revert-probed).

## Count a population from the AUDIT ledger, not from the artefact table (#2600, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: reconstructing criterion 6's trial count for S-1..S-4, the obvious source was `strategy_results_store` — it is the table the results live in and it is what every consumer reads. It yields 55 hold-out evaluations. `strategy_holdout_accesses`, the ledger built to AUDIT those reads, records **224 accesses**, of which 4 are `read` eyeballs that wrote no result row at all. A count taken from the artefact table would have silently omitted every look that produced no artefact — which is exactly the population criterion 6 names (*"manual eyeballing"*).
- Root cause: an artefact table answers "what did we keep", an audit ledger answers "what did we do". They differ precisely on the abandoned, discarded and inspected-only cases, and those are the cases a multiple-testing correction exists to count.
- ⚠ The direction is the flattering one again: under-counting `M` lowers `SR_0` and RAISES the Deflated Sharpe, so the omission would have made every future promotion claim easier and nothing would have failed.
- Prevention: when a number is a claim about *how many times something happened*, grep for a ledger/audit/access relation before reading the result table, and state in the artefact which one you counted from. In this repo the pairs are `strategy_results_store` ↔ `strategy_holdout_accesses`, and `strategy_signals` ↔ `strategy_signal_observations`. Verify the two agree where they should: here the 220 `evaluate` accesses match the 220 hold-out result rows exactly, which is what makes the 4 extra `read` rows legible as a real difference rather than a bookkeeping gap.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/trial_register.py` (the S-1..S-4 entries' comment block names the ledger and the arithmetic); `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-12-trial-register-reconstruction.md` §"S-1 to S-4"; `tests/test_trial_register.py::TestExactness::test_each_reconstructed_family_carries_its_derived_count` (revert-probed).

## "Be conservative" is not a licence to invent a number (#2600, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: the viability plan's Gate D-0.1 says to *"declare a bounded conservative per-family floor"* and *"prefers a visible overcount to false precision"*. The first draft of the reconstruction read that as permission to pad. It declared the ETF intraday family at **6** (the preregistered arm set) when only **4** arms are evidenced as executed; residual confluence at **+4** discarded runs when the page evidences *"discarded diagnostic runs"* — at least one, bounded above by nothing; and the sizing A/B at **+4** for one stopped pass. Three numbers, none of which any artefact supports. Caught at Codex checkpoint 1, not by any gate.
- Root cause: "conservative" was being applied to the *direction of the bias* and then silently extended to the *provenance of the figure*. An unevidenced padding number is not conservative — it is indistinguishable from an entry invented to make a statistic look harder-won, which is the exact failure the register's mandatory `evidence` field exists to prevent. It also breaks the flag's own definition: a floor that overcounts is not a lower bound.
- ⚠ Note this is the OPPOSITE error from the one the codebase usually makes, and it wears the same clothes. The habitual failure is under-counting in the flattering direction; the correction to it is not "count high", it is "count what you can evidence and label the remainder".
- Prevention: when declaring a floor, admit only arms the evidence shows actually ran; where the evidence bounds a range, take the SMALLEST count consistent with it; and where a design was preregistered but not executed, count zero — a design is not a search. Say in the same sentence what the floor does NOT cover, so the gap is visible instead of papered over by a bigger number. Test: if you cannot name the sentence or table that evidences arm *n*, arm *n* is not in the floor.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/trial_register.py::TrialExactness.FLOOR` docstring; `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-12-trial-register-reconstruction.md` §"Exactness flag" and §"What this reconstruction still does not reach".

## A declaration passed as an ARGUMENT cannot prove it was made before the look (#2599, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: #2599's first spec put the preregistration declaration in a frozen `PreregDeclaration` dataclass and passed it into `require_outcome_access(conn, declaration, access)`. Every rule in it was correct and every test would have passed. Codex checkpoint 1 killed it in one sentence: *"a caller can construct a favourable declaration after seeing/reading outcomes"*. The gate enforced the CONTENT of a claim while proving nothing about WHEN the claim was made — and "before the look" was the entire property the ticket existed to establish.
- Root cause: a value object is evidence of what a caller believes at call time, never of what it believed earlier. The check read as a gate because it refused things, but the thing it refused was a self-report supplied by the party being gated.
- ⚠ The tell is a temporal word in the requirement — "preregistered", "declared up front", "frozen at", "before". If the requirement contains one and the implementation is a parameter, the implementation does not meet it. What does: a persisted row, with its own timestamp and a digest over its bytes, loaded by identity at enforcement time.
- ⚠ Digest and coherence are SEPARATE checks and both are needed. A second Codex pass (checkpoint 2) found the live-gate path validating `declaration_refusals` but not `digest_intact`, while the outcome-access path validated both — so a declaration edited around the immutability trigger stayed perfectly coherent while carrying a different floor. Coherence says the claim hangs together; the digest says it is the same claim.
- Prevention: before writing a check for "X was declared before Y", ask what artefact would still exist if the process were replayed from the database alone. If the answer is "none", the check is a convention and not a gate. Enforce at the relation that every existing path already funnels through rather than adding a new helper future callers must remember — `record_holdout_access` was that chokepoint here, which is why no door needed a convention.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/333_strategy_preregistration_declarations.sql` (header, and the `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger — DELETE is barred because "unfreeze, look, re-freeze" is the same fabrication with an extra step); `app/services/result_ledger.py::_refuse_incoherent_declaration` + `require_outcome_access`; `app/services/strategy_live_gate.py::register_live_gate_policy` (digest check) and `live_gate_refusals` (`declaration_digest_mismatch`); `tests/test_prereg_declaration_gate.py` and `tests/test_strategy_holdout_namespace.py` (both revert-probed).

## A PARENT table is invisible to the derived test-teardown plan too (#2599, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `sql/333` added `strategy_preregistration_declarations` and pointed `strategy_live_gate_policies.declaration_id` at it. Two new DB tests then failed with `DID NOT RAISE` and a `UniqueViolation` on a declaration a *previous* test had frozen. The table was leaking across tests.
- Root cause: `_build_cleanup_plan` derives the wipe set by walking INBOUND FKs down from the roots in `_PLANNER_TABLES`. That covers new CHILDREN automatically — which is what the #1568 update to the entry above promises — but a new table that an existing entry REFERENCES is upstream of every root, so the closure never reaches it. The existing wording ("no inbound-FK path from an existing entry") does cover this case, but it is written around standalone tables and reads as though a table with an FK is safe. It is safe only if the FK points the right way.
- Prevention: when a migration adds a table, ask which DIRECTION its FKs point. A table that references something already listed is derived; a table that something already listed references is not, and must be appended to `_PLANNER_TABLES` in the same PR — after its own child, so the fallback TRUNCATE order stays child-to-parent. Test: `grep REFERENCES` the new migration; if the new table's name appears on the RIGHT of a `REFERENCES`, list it.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/fixtures/ebull_test_db.py::_PLANNER_TABLES` (the `strategy_preregistration_declarations` entry states the direction and the measurement that caught it).

## A revert-probe inside a rolled-back transaction can prove nothing (#2599, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: a dev-DB probe for `sql/333` froze a declaration, asserted the re-freeze raised `UniqueViolation`, called `conn.rollback()` to recover, then asserted `UPDATE`/`DELETE` were blocked by the immutability trigger. Both printed **"MUTATION ALLOWED <-- BAD"**. The trigger was fine; the rollback had discarded the INSERT, so the statements matched **zero rows** and no `BEFORE ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger fired.
- Root cause: the existing rule — *"a probe that silently matches nothing proves nothing"* — was being read as being about string replacement (`assert s.count(old) == 1`). It is about the probe's TARGET, and a row is a target as much as a source line is. Recovering from an expected error by rolling back the whole transaction deletes the fixture the remaining assertions stand on.
- ⚠ The failure direction is the dangerous one: a row-level guard that never fires reports as "not enforced", so the natural next move is to go and "fix" working code.
- Prevention: isolate each sub-assertion in its own savepoint (`with conn.transaction():` nested inside an outer `force_rollback=True`), never a bare `conn.rollback()`. And assert the fixture still exists between steps — one `SELECT count(*)` line — so a probe that has lost its target says so instead of reporting the guard as absent.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_strategy_holdout_namespace.py::test_a_frozen_declaration_cannot_be_edited_or_deleted` (nested savepoints, and the multi-command note — psycopg prepares every query, so `ALTER; UPDATE; ALTER` in one string fails with `SyntaxError: cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement`).

## A chokepoint closes the doors that EXIST — enumerate them before claiming it closes all of them (#2614, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: #2599's gate was placed at `record_holdout_access` on the verified observation that all three hold-out doors funnel through it, and its docstring added *"which is every path we have written"*. One day later, `grep -ln result_ledger scripts/evaluate_*.py scripts/*_outcomes.py` found **three** sealed outcome openers that touch no ledger function — including C-4, the exact trial #2599 was written for, complete and runnable at `55c75dce`. `select count(*) from strategy_preregistration_declarations` was 0.
- Root cause: the chokepoint reasoning was sound and the SCOPE claim was not. Every path that **writes a result row** goes through the ledger; a sealed study that computes its own statistics from raw price windows and emits a signed artifact writes no row, so there is nothing to intercept. The premise "opening an outcome always goes through the ledger" was never stated, so it was never checked.
- ⚠ The tell is a universal quantifier about the codebase in a docstring — "every path", "all callers", "the only way". That is a **measurement**, and the same rule that binds "most"/"usually"/"every" about source data binds it: run the grep or delete the quantifier. It is more dangerous in a docstring than in prose, because the next reader inherits it as an established property of the system.
- ⚠ Second-order: the ONE action that made C-4 runnable — adding its trial-register entry, which its own gate requires — was also the action that would open the ungated path. A latent hole whose unlocking step is a ticket's own scope item must be closed in the SAME change, or the fix opens the defect.
- Prevention: when placing a gate at a chokepoint, write down the class of caller it covers (here: "writes a result row"), then grep for members of the plausible class that do NOT match it. Encode the result as a TEST over the file glob, not a convention — "remember to call the helper" is what failed five consecutive times before #2599 existed. Make the test assert the name is **CALLED** (AST walk for a `Call` node), because a substring search passes on a comment, an unused import or a dead branch, and a lexical allowlist must carry a reason per entry so an exemption is visible rather than silent.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_sealed_outcome_scripts_are_gated.py` (AST-based, allowlist with per-entry reasons, revert-probed); `app/services/result_ledger.py::require_outcome_access` docstring and `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-12-preregistration-declaration-gate.md` §4 (both corrected to "every path that writes a result row").

## A returned id is not a check — reload the row, or the value object is the whole gate (#2614, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: #2614's first design had `require_outcome_gate` record the access and return `OutcomeGate(..., declaration_id, access_id)`, and the price-window chokepoint re-validated the DECLARATION by identity. Codex checkpoint 1: *"A constructed `OutcomeGate` containing a real declaration ID can bypass `require_outcome_access` and open prices without any access row."* Correct — `OutcomeGate` is a plain frozen dataclass, so the gate object proves only that a caller can copy three constants out of the module.
- Root cause: this is the #2599 value-object defect one frame further out. #2599 learned "load the declaration from the table, never accept one as an argument" and the fix loaded the declaration — but the ACCESS row, the thing that records that a look happened, was still trusted as an integer carried in a struct. Verifying half the provenance leaves the other half a self-report.
- ⚠ Reloading the access row by id also buys the property nobody wrote a check for: a rolled-back INSERT leaves **no visible row**, so the same lookup proves the access COMMITTED. And `frozen_at < accessed_at` must be ASSERTED, not assumed — "the declaration predates the look" is the entire property, and an invariant nobody asserts is one nobody notices breaking.
- ⚠ `now()` IS TRANSACTION-START TIME IN POSTGRES, so a test that freezes and accesses in ONE transaction gets `frozen_at == accessed_at` to the microsecond and a strict `<` refuses. The correct fix is separate transactions in the test (which is what the real flow does — the freeze script is a separate process run earlier), NOT relaxing the comparison to `<=`. Weakening a temporal invariant to make a same-transaction test pass would delete the property.
- ⚠⚠ **AND THEN STATE WHAT THE FIX DOES NOT DO.** Codex checkpoint 3 caught the newest-`read` rule being written up as stopping "look after look". It does not: holding the NEWEST `access_id` still authorises repeat evaluations until some other read is recorded, and the check is relative to the caller's `REPEATABLE READ` snapshot, so two concurrent gates can both pass. It rules out a STALE id — the careless case — and nothing more. Real single-use needs consumable state, which an append-only audit log deliberately does not have. **Writing the stronger claim in the docstring of the ticket whose whole subject is an overstated enforcement is the failure reproducing itself one layer up.**
- Prevention: for every id a gate hands back, ask what a caller who fabricated it could do. If the answer is "everything the gate protects", the id must be re-loaded from its relation at the point of use and bound to the identity it claims. A gate that returns evidence and never re-reads it has moved the trust boundary to its own caller. Then write the residual limit next to the check, in the same commit — a partial mitigation described as a total one is worse than no mitigation, because the next reader stops looking.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/result_ledger.py::verify_outcome_access_provenance` (checks declaration AND access row, including `frozen_at < accessed_at`); `tests/test_c4_declaration_gate_db.py` (8 tests, all revert-probed, including the two-transaction note).

## A forward-shadow floor is derivable from a frozen power calculation — a measured rate is not a chosen number (#2614, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `sql/333` CHECKs both forward-shadow floors `> 0` and `prereg_contract.ForwardShadowFloor` forbids a default, on the grounds that *"picking a central default would be the #2600 padded-floor defect verbatim — a floor no artefact evidences"*. C-4 needed two numbers and neither existed anywhere.
- Root cause: "no default" was read as "somebody has to decide it", which is the *"wants an operator call"* label on an unstarted research step. Both inputs were already frozen or measurable: the contract's own power calculation (785 effective events = `round(7.84888 x (10.0/1.0)^2)`, asserted by `verify_2582_schedule13d_preregistration.py`) and an **outcome-free** full-population arrival rate (963 clean 13D events over 331 distinct public filing dates spanning 547 days — source events and filing dates only, no price bar).
- ⚠ State the DIRECTION of the bound in the artefact, not in a commit message. The contract's 785 is an *effective* sample size and effective <= raw, so 785 raw events is the smallest raw count that could satisfy it: both derived floors are LOWER bounds and clustering raises the requirement. A floor whose direction is unstated gets read as exact by the next reader.
- Prevention: before declaring a threshold operator-gated, check whether the candidate's own frozen contract already contains the power calculation — a preregistration usually does. Then derive by construction, keep the arithmetic in a pure test that recomputes it from the named inputs, and put the reproducing command next to the frozen literals so a stale rate fails loudly instead of shipping.
- Enforced in: this log; `scripts/freeze_2582_schedule13d_declaration.py` (module constants carry the reproducing command; `_FORWARD_SHADOW_DERIVATION` names both inputs and the bound direction); `tests/test_c4_declaration_gate.py::test_the_forward_shadow_floor_is_derived_not_chosen` (revert-probed).

## A recorded input that nothing generates from is a provenance claim with no provenance (#2601, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `run_cohort(..., root_seed=...)` took a seed, stored it on the result row as §9's *"with the seed recorded"*, and drew every one of the 1,000 members from `random_entry_cohort.member_seed(index)` — which is keyed on the module constant `COHORT_ROOT_SEED` and on nothing else. Passing any other value produced a row whose recorded seed reproduced the bootstrap interval and **not the cohort it sat beside**. Caught by Codex at checkpoint 2; every gate (ruff, pyright, 16 tests, 7 revert probes) was green, because the parameter was used — just not for the thing its name claims.
- Root cause: the parameter was added for symmetry with `evaluate_control`'s own `root_seed`, which really does drive the bootstrap. Two consumers of one name, one of which ignores it. The module docstring already said *"NO SECOND ROOT IS MINTED PER RUN"*, so the code and its own header disagreed — the same shape as #2240 5e-5b's interpolated percentile, where `cohort_threshold`'s docstring declared an order statistic and the code took NumPy's default.
- ⚠ The tell is a **declared input that is stored but never read on the generating path**. Grep the parameter name inside the function body: if every hit is in the return value or a log line, it documents the caller's intention rather than the computation. That is strictly worse than no parameter, because the stored number now *looks* like reproduction evidence.
- ⚠ A test asserting "the stored seed is `COHORT_ROOT_SEED`" passes on the defect, because the default is that constant. The test that catches it either passes a DIFFERENT seed and requires the members to move, or asserts the override does not exist.
- Prevention: for every declared input a result row records, name the function that consumes it and check the consumption is on the path that produced the recorded numbers. When a constant is deliberately global — as here, so two runs of one strategy draw the same null — do not offer an override at all; delete the parameter and let the constant be the single source. `inspect.signature(...).parameters` is a one-line regression test for "the override stayed deleted".
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/synthetic_control_run.py::run_cohort` (no `root_seed` parameter, with the reason in situ); `tests/test_synthetic_control_run.py::TestTheMatchIsExact` (the root is the declared constant, the run reproduces, and the signature carries no override).

## Two archives can disagree about what `close` MEANS — measure the basis before the coverage (#2597, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `research_price_series.adjustment_basis` is a per-series column with a CHECK, precisely so a reader can tell an adjusted level from a raw one. #2398 stamped `icyDenev/Intrader` as `split_adjusted` and stored the archive's **raw** OHLC under it, and that stood for four months. Measured on the same mirror the script itself reads: AAPL 2020-08-27 close is `500.04` there — the traded level four days before a 4:1 split — against `125.01` for the same bar in the HF archive, and the 1980-12-12 IPO bar reads `28.75` against Yahoo's split-adjusted `0.1283`. The split AND dividend adjustment live in the ninth CSV column, which the script was already storing separately as `adj_close`.
- Root cause: the basis was written from the vendor's *family* ("it's a Yahoo derivative, and the HF Yahoo derivative is split-adjusted") rather than from the vendor's own numbers. Two redistributions of one upstream can still differ on adjustment, because the adjustment is applied by whoever did the scraping, not by the upstream. The docstring of the same script already said `close` was "the vendor's OHLC close" and `adjclose` carried the dividends — **the code and its own header disagreed, and the header was right**.
- ⚠ The tell is a provenance constant that no test pins to an observation. `ADJUSTMENT_BASIS = "split_adjusted"` is a claim about data, so it is a measurement, and the same rule that binds "most"/"every" about source data binds it. The check is one bar: pick a name with a known split inside the archive's span and compare the pre-split close against the post-split-adjusted one. sql/251 already did exactly this for the HF archive and recorded the arithmetic in its header; nobody re-ran it for the second vendor.
- ⚠ Second-order, and this is what makes it expensive rather than cosmetic: a *downstream* acceptance check inherits the wrong basis silently. #2398's `--verify` asserts `adj_close / close <= 1` across the whole vendor, which is true for a dividend payer and **false for every reverse split**, where the back-adjusted close is legitimately above the raw one. That check only ever passed because the vendor held 16 hand-picked ETFs; the first bulk load of the same vendor would have failed it, and the natural reading of that failure is "the new data is bad" rather than "the old assert was scoped to a panel".
- ⚠ The same pass falsified two more inherited notes about these archives, both from a spot-check rather than a sweep: the freeze date (`2024-09-27` measured as `max(last_bar)`, not the recorded 2023-11-29) and the relative coverage ("+11 on the AMEX residual" — it is 259/260 against the other archive's 247/260, i.e. very nearly the superset). **A capture date is `max(last_bar)` over the vendor and nothing else** — a repo's last commit is not it, since `Stonks/tickers`' HEAD is a 2024-03-27 README edit sitting on data that stops 2023-10-10.
- Prevention: when adding a SECOND vendor to a table whose columns carry semantics (`adjustment_basis`, `upstream_source`, units), put the provenance in one frozen record per archive and assert the two records DISAGREE where they actually disagree — a shared module constant is what let one script's stamp contradict its own parser. Verify the basis on a split boundary before measuring any coverage figure, because coverage computed under the wrong basis is arithmetic on the wrong column. And scope every vendor-wide acceptance assert to the population it was written for, or the next load inherits a gate that was only ever true of a panel.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/research_corpus_ingest.py::ArchiveProvenance` / `HF_ARCHIVE` / `INTRADER_ARCHIVE` (one record per archive, each carrying its measured evidence); `scripts/ingest_2398_benchmark_series.py` (imports the shared record instead of restating it; `verify` scoped to `BENCHMARKS`); `tests/test_research_corpus_ingest.py::test_the_two_archives_disagree_about_their_adjustment_basis` (revert-probed).

## Resolving a filing symbol to a price archive is a SOURCE RULE, and exact-match precedence is the whole rule (#2597, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `link_form25_delistings` joined the Form 25 cohort to the corpus on `c.symbol = s.vendor_symbol`. A Chapter 11 issuer moves to OTC under a `Q`-suffixed ticker and the Form 25 that removes the security carries that POST-bankruptcy symbol, while the price archive is keyed on whatever the scraper saw — the pre-bankruptcy one. So the exact join drops precisely the **bankruptcies** and keeps the acquisitions: bias along the exact axis a survivorship-free corpus exists to protect. Measured on the 15 `Q`-suffixed symbols in `sec_form25_register`, the strip takes one archive from 13/15 to 15/15 and the other from 1/15 to 14/15.
- Root cause: the rule was written down in `.claude/skills/data-sources/research-price-corpus.md` ("a symbol rule, not a lookup trick") and never reached the code, because the linkage looked like plumbing rather than a data-treatment decision. Mapping one identifier space onto another IS resolution, and "source-rule before design" fires before the join is written.
- ⚠ A blind strip is NOT the fix and would be a second defect: `NHIQ` is a real archive symbol under its own name, so stripping unconditionally rebinds it to a different security. Exact match must outrank the strip, and that precedence is the part worth testing — a `set` of candidate spellings loses it silently.
- ⚠ Third-order: once two spellings can resolve to one series, the aggregation has to move. Grouping the filings by `resolved_symbol` in SQL *before* resolving hides the case where `RVLP` and `RVLPQ` both land on `RVLP` — two delisting events against one price history — and lets the second filing's date silently overwrite the first's. Aggregate AFTER resolution and let the existing conflict classifier refuse to write.
- Prevention: express a symbol-resolution ladder as a pure function returning candidates **in priority order**, never as join SQL — the precedence is a correlated `NOT EXISTS` in SQL and untestable in practice, and this is the rule whose failure mode is invisible in aggregate (coverage barely moves; the composition of what is lost moves entirely). Table-test the precedence case explicitly, and re-check the grouping key of anything downstream of the resolution.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/research_corpus_ingest.py::archive_symbol_candidates` / `resolve_archive_symbol` (priority-ordered, with the measured 15-symbol split in the docstring) and `link_form25_delistings` (aggregates after resolution); `tests/test_research_corpus_ingest.py` (5 tests incl. `test_exact_match_outranks_the_q_strip`, all revert-probed).

## "The hook already exists" is a claim about the AUTHORISING path, not about the function that computes the right refusal (#2605, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: #2605 asked me to *"verify [the validated-universe check] already binds and cite it, extend only if it does not"*. `check_promotable` does refuse `instrument_outside_validated_universe`, `run_backtest` does feed it the real `load_validated_universe` output, and the run even cross-checks the refusal set against a separately predicted one and raises when they disagree. I wrote "enforced, not conventional" into a settled-decisions entry on that evidence. Codex checkpoint 1 pointed one function further down the path: `promote_strategy` — the thing that actually moves a strategy to `historical_validated` — never calls `check_promotable`, and `grep -n check_promotable app/services/strategy_control_plane.py` returns nothing.
- Root cause: I traced the refusal FORWARD from the check that computes it and stopped when it looked correct, instead of tracing BACKWARD from the decision that needed it. The refusal is returned in `WrittenRow.refusals` and never persisted — and `strategy_results_store` carries `evaluated_instrument_count` but not the ids, so the transition cannot re-derive it even in principle. A correct check whose output is discarded before the authorising step is not a gate; it is a report.
- ⚠ This is distinct from #2614's "a chokepoint closes the doors that EXIST". There the second path bypassed the check. Here there is one path, the check runs on it, and its verdict is dropped between the producer and the consumer. Both end at "the gate does not bind", so both are invisible to a grep for the refusal name — which returns hits either way.
- ⚠ The tell is a refusal, verdict or score that no table stores. Ask: *at the moment of the decision, what row does the deciding function read?* If the answer does not include the check's output, the check is upstream advice. Persisting a count where the check needs a set (`evaluated_instrument_count` vs the ids) is the same defect in miniature — a summary cannot be re-checked.
- ⚠ It was not fail-open today only because one writer happens to feed the right set, which is precisely the state #2505 recorded before closing the sibling gap: *"it would have become fail-open as soon as a future candidate was registered."* "No candidate has been registered yet" is a fact about the calendar, not about the gate.
- Prevention: before writing that a rule is enforced, name the function that AUTHORISES the outcome the rule is about, and read its body for the check. Cite that call site, not the definition site. If the authorising function cannot reach the check's inputs, say so in the same sentence and file the gap — a settled-decisions entry claiming enforcement that does not exist is worse than no entry, because it is what the next session will cite instead of re-checking.
- Enforced in: this log; `docs/settled-decisions.md` → "v1 strategy capital universe is US-only" (splits "result production — enforced" from "the promotion transition — NOT enforced"); `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-12-promotion-edge-evidence-contract.md` → "Validated universe scope"; #2621 owns closing the gap.

## Revert-probing on an UNCOMMITTED branch restores origin/main, not your work — commit first, every time (#2616, 2026-08-12; repeat of #2621, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: probe 1 of #2616's gate work injected a defect into `scripts/verify_2476_pead_outcomes.py`, confirmed the guarding test failed, then restored with `git checkout -- <file>`. The branch had no commit yet, so "restore" meant origin/main: the entire gate wiring silently vanished and the follow-up "restored" test run failed for the opposite reason. The identical sequence ate #2621's edits earlier the SAME DAY, and the memory one-liner recording it did not fire, because at probe time the salient thought is "undo my injection", not "what is this file's last committed state".
- Root cause: `git checkout -- <path>` restores the INDEX/HEAD version, and on a branch with no commits that is the base branch. A probe harness needs a known-good restore point; an uncommitted working tree does not have one.
- ⚠ The failure is silent in the dangerous direction: the probe printed "injected" and the restore printed nothing, so the only tell was the next test run failing — and a probe sequence that ends "restored exit=1" reads as a flaky test, not as vanished work.
- Prevention: **commit the work-in-progress BEFORE the first probe** — the commit is the restore point, and `git checkout -- <file>` then means what it looks like it means. Sequence: gates green → commit → probe/restore per invariant → follow-up fixes as further commits. This composes with the existing probe rules above (never `git add` mid-probe; restore in `finally`): commit-first is what makes their restores safe at all.
- Enforced in: this log. Not mechanically enforceable — the tell to watch for is any `git checkout --` in a session where `git log` shows no commit on the branch.

## A migration that is WAITING for a lock is not passive — it blocks every reader behind it (#2363, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: `sql/335` adds a column to `strategy_results_store`. `scripts/migrate.py` sat for ten minutes having burned 0.31s of CPU. It was not slow, it was blocked: `pg_blocking_pids` named pid 31499, `ebull-job-body:strategy_backtest_run`, which holds `AccessShareLock` on that relation for the LIFE of its transaction — a job then 2h32m into a run at series 2225/10436 of the first of 8 candidates.
- Root cause, and the part that makes it urgent rather than merely annoying: a PENDING `AccessExclusiveLock` queues **ahead of new readers**. So an `ALTER TABLE` that is merely waiting stops every subsequent `SELECT` on that relation from starting. My migration was not waiting its turn politely; it was stalling the operator's running dev stack for as long as I let it sit. Cancelling my own backend was the fix, not waiting harder.
