- ⚠ `strategy_backtest_run` holds ONE transaction open across a multi-hour run, so any DDL on the strategy tables is blocked whenever it runs. Assume that window is the normal state, not an unlucky collision. Measured 2026-08-12 with `select status, started_at, finished_at - started_at as duration from job_runs where job_name = 'strategy_backtest_run' order by started_at desc limit 4`: the three completed runs took **4h47m, 15m56s and 2h56m**, all `failure`, and the run holding the lock during this ticket was 3h48m in and still going.
- ⚠⚠ **The first draft of this entry said those runs "failed after ~17h each". That number was `now() - started_at` — the AGE of the row, not its DURATION.** Both columns are intervals, both look like a runtime, and the wrong one is the one a `select *` puts in front of you. It is the hardcoded-statistic trap landing in the prevention log itself, which is the worst place for it: the next reader budgets a 17-hour lock window and concludes the migration is simply unappliable. Subtract the two timestamps explicitly and name the column `duration`; never read an unlabelled interval as elapsed runtime.
- ⚠ Second trap, self-inflicted: the retry loop was gated on `migrate.py` exiting 0, and it duly reported "APPLIED" — because a *concurrent* control run of mine had moved `sql/335` aside for thirty seconds, so migrate saw nothing pending and exited 0 truthfully. **Gate a retry loop on the OBSERVABLE EFFECT (`information_schema.columns`), never on the exit code of the thing that might have skipped its work.** And do not mutate the working tree while a background loop is reading it.
- Prevention: put `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s';` at the top of any migration taking `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` on a hot relation. It converts an unbounded stall-everything wait into a clean, retryable `LockNotAvailable`, bounding the reader impact of each attempt to five seconds. Then apply in a quiet window rather than fighting for the lock. ⚠ Note the consequence at app boot: the FastAPI lifespan runs migrations, so a locked-out migration now fails the boot loudly instead of hanging it — which is the better of the two, and is why the smoke tier can fail for purely environmental reasons. Establish that by control (withhold only the migration file and re-run smoke) before blaming the diff.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/335_strategy_result_fx_unmodelled.sql` (the `lock_timeout` and the rationale above it).

## A revert-probe run under the wrong interpreter "fails" for every injection — a probe needs a CONTROL, not just a match count (#2363, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: four probes on the #2363 invariants all reported "FAILS (good)". Every one was worthless. The harness was launched with a `python3 - <<PY` heredoc, so `sys.executable` was **system** python3, which has no pytest — every subprocess returned non-zero on `ModuleNotFoundError`, whether the defect was injected or not. `.venv/bin/python -c "import pytest"` succeeds; `python3 -c "import pytest"` raises. The verdict column was measuring the interpreter.
- Root cause: the existing rule in this log is `assert s.count(old) == 1` — guard against a probe that matches NOTHING. That closes one half. This is the other half: a probe that matches, injects correctly, and whose failure signal is not attributable to the injection.
- Prevention: every probe runs **three** commands and asserts the shape of all three — control (unmodified, must exit 0), probed (must exit non-zero), restored (must exit 0 again). A control that already fails makes the verdict unattributable and the probe must be skipped and reported as skipped, not silently counted. Pin the interpreter explicitly (`.venv/bin/python -m pytest`); never rely on `sys.executable` inheriting from a heredoc. Print the `FAILED` test name from the probed run — a probe that fails in a DIFFERENT test than the one guarding the invariant is also not evidence.
- Enforced in: this log. The #2363 probe harness in the PR body records control/probed/restored per invariant, and the named failing test for each.

## An invariant between two constants that currently hold the same value is UNOBSERVABLE — parameterise it or it is not guarded (#2363, 2026-08-12)

- Symptom: #2363's whole purpose was de-coupling `CARRY_UNMODELLED` from FX — it had been `CARRY_BPS is None or FX_BPS is None` and became `CARRY_BPS is None`. The revert-probe that re-coupled it **passed every test**. Both amounts are `None` today, so the coupled and uncoupled expressions are indistinguishable, and the one change the ticket existed to make was the one change nothing guarded.
- Root cause: the invariant was expressed as a module-level expression over two constants. A test can only observe the value, and the value is identical under both rules until one amount is measured — which is a quarter away and is exactly when the silent re-coupling would bite.
- Prevention: when a change de-couples two things whose current values coincide, move the rule into a function TAKING BOTH as arguments and table-test all four combinations. The mixed rows are the test; the matching rows prove nothing. General form: **if a probe of the defect the ticket is about does not fail, the invariant is not where the test can see it** — treat a passing probe as a design signal, not as a reason to skip the test.
- ⚠⚠ **SECOND INSTANCE, ONE FUNCTION OVER, AND PARAMETERISING THE WRONG SIDE PROVED NOTHING.** `result_ledger._refuse_declared_stamp_substitution` compares four booleans — declared vs actual, for carry and for FX. The shipped test moved all three stamps together, so every *declared* value was `True`; re-pointing the FX comparison at `declared.declared_carry_unmodelled` passed the whole module. The first replacement test varied the two **actual** stamps and the probe *still* passed, because the cross-wire is on the **declared** side. Only when the two DECLARED values were made to differ did both cross-wire probes fail.
- Prevention, sharpened: **the operand that has to differ is the one being substituted.** Before writing the table, name the exact wrong-operand edit you are guarding against, then check that your rows give that operand two different values — a row where the substituted operand happens to equal its neighbour is a matching row wearing a mixed row's costume. For an N-way comparison, vary each side independently; "I parameterised it" is not the claim, "the probe fails" is.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/cost_model.py::unmodelled_markers` (takes both amounts, docstring records the failed probe); `tests/test_cost_model.py::test_each_marker_reads_only_its_own_amount` (four states, re-probed and now failing correctly); `tests/test_strategy_holdout_namespace.py::test_each_cost_stamp_is_compared_against_its_own_declaration` (declared carry ≠ declared FX in both rows; both cross-wire directions probed and failing).

## A boundary validator that checks a NUMERIC's SCALE but not its PRECISION still lets a raw driver error through (#2603, 2026-08-13)

- Symptom: `strategy_core_mandate.validate_core_mandate` rejected `min_rebalance_amount` values finer than the column's scale — the silent-rounding half — and promised every rejection as a named `CoreMandateError`. `Decimal(10) ** 12` passed validation and then failed inside Postgres. Found by Codex at checkpoint 2, not by any test I had written.
- Root cause: `NUMERIC(p,s)` constrains two independent things, and a scale check only covers one. The integer capacity is `p - s` digits. Measured on the real server rather than reasoned about: `INSERT INTO t (a NUMERIC(18,6)) VALUES (999999999999.999999)` succeeds, and `1000000000000` raises `numeric field overflow / DETAIL: A field with precision 18, scale 6 must round to an absolute value less than 10^12`.
- ⚠ The direction of the failure is what makes it worth an entry: a validator whose documented contract is "every rejection is a named error" is *more* dangerous when it is nearly complete, because callers stop defending against the driver's exception classes. The gap only opens at an input magnitude no fixture happens to use.
- Prevention: when a boundary validator guards a `NUMERIC(p,s)` column, assert BOTH halves — representability at scale `s` (not the exponent: `Decimal("60.00000")` is exact at four places and must pass) and `abs(value) < 10 ** (p - s)`. Test the largest storable value as well as the first unstorable one, so the bound cannot drift a digit in either direction; a one-sided test passes with the bound off by one.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_core_mandate.py::_require_storable` (both halves, docstring records why); `tests/test_2603_core_mandate.py::test_an_amount_too_large_for_the_column_is_a_named_error` and `::test_the_largest_storable_amount_is_accepted` (both probed — bound removed, bound +1 digit, bound -1 digit all fail the guarding test).

## An irreversible write's `--dry-run` must print what the digest hashes, not a hand-picked subset (#2631, 2026-08-13)

- Symptom: `scripts/freeze_2582_schedule13d_declaration.py --dry-run` and `scripts/freeze_2616_precutoff_declarations.py --dry-run` each built their summary as a hand-listed dict of 6-7 keys out of the declaration's 13 digest inputs. Absent from both: `structural_refusal_policy_version` — the single field that decides whether the freeze is still valid tomorrow. `sql/333` bars UPDATE and DELETE and holds `UNIQUE (strategy_id, strategy_version)`, and `prereg_contract.declaration_refusals` voids the row the moment `STRUCTURAL_REFUSAL_POLICY_VERSION` moves, so a mistimed freeze is unrecoverable and the operator's only pre-commit view of it did not mention the coupling. Main moved v1 → v2 on 2026-08-12 with C-4's freeze one command away.
- Root cause: the dry-run's field list and the digest's field list were two independent copies of "what this declaration is". Nothing made the review surface track the thing being committed to, so the omission was invisible in both directions — no test failed, and the operator could not tell a subset from the whole.
- Prevention: for any irreversible write with a canonical digest, expose the hashed payload as a property (`PreregDeclaration.digest_payload`) and have the dry-run print **that**, so the review surface is a consequence of the digest rather than a second list. ⚠ The property alone is NOT self-enforcing — a field added to the dataclass and forgotten in the payload goes missing from the digest and the dry-run together, silently — so pair it with a test asserting one payload key per declared field (count, expanded across the nested dataclass) plus a per-field probe that the digest actually moves. State the recovery cost in the same place as the warning: for this table it is a new `strategy_version`, which changes trial identity, strands the old trial forever, and charges the shared trial register a second time.
- ⚠⚠ **The ticket's own proposed guard was unsound, and only measuring showed it.** #2631 scope item 2 said "refuse to freeze when the tree's policy version differs from the one recorded on any existing declaration row". `select count(*) from strategy_preregistration_declarations` returns **0**, so it compares against nothing today; and because a bump supersedes *every* pre-existing row, the predicate becomes permanently true after the first one and would refuse every future freeze. The wider variant — scan every git ref not merged into `origin/main` for a differing constant — measured **31** such refs, 4 carrying the constant and **2 differing**, both stale branches whose work is already squash-merged: it fires on day one and never stops. Shipped instead: refuse when this tree's constant is not the one on `origin/main`, fail closed on unknown, override recorded in the output. **A guard proposed in a ticket is a premise like any other — run its predicate against the live population before implementing it, including the state it will be in after the event it guards.**
- ⚠⚠ **A check against `origin/main` is a check against a LOCAL SNAPSHOT until you fetch.** The first version of the guard compared the tree's constant to `git show origin/main:…` and called that "the merged policy version". `refs/remotes/origin/main` is only whatever the last fetch left behind, so a checkout that had not fetched since the policy moved would compare v1 against a stale v1, report a match, and permit exactly the freeze being guarded against — the guard would fail in the same direction as the defect. Found by Codex at checkpoint 2. Fixed by fetching first and refusing when the fetch fails (an unrefreshed ref is not weaker evidence, it is *no* evidence). ⚠ That `git fetch origin main` advances `refs/remotes/origin/main` and not merely `FETCH_HEAD` was **measured** on git 2.54.0 — ref artificially staled with `git update-ref`, fetch watched to restore it — not taken from memory. General form: **any comparison against a remote-tracking ref must establish that ref's freshness in the same breath, or it is comparing the repository to itself.**
- ⚠ And state what it does not do: this guard cannot see the case that actually occurred — a policy bump on an *unpushed* branch in another worktree — because no check that reads this repository can see a commit that is not in it. There the printed version and the docstring are the whole control.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/prereg_contract.py::PreregDeclaration.digest_payload`; `scripts/_prereg_freeze_guard.py` (both rejected designs recorded with their measurements); `tests/test_2631_freeze_policy_guard.py` (7 revert-probes, control/probed/restored each).

## A source-level "does every script call the guard" test is satisfied by the IMPORT line (#2631, 2026-08-13)

- Symptom: `test_every_freeze_script_calls_the_guard` asserted `"assert_policy_version_merged" in source` for each `scripts/freeze_*.py`. The revert probe replaced the actual call with `policy_version_report()` — removing the guard entirely — and the test **passed**, because `from scripts._prereg_freeze_guard import assert_policy_version_merged, policy_version_report` still contains the name.
- Root cause: a bare substring check over source cannot distinguish a call from any other mention, and the import is guaranteed to be one. The same shape catches a name in a docstring, a comment, or an `__all__`.
- Prevention: a convention test over source matches the **call form** — `re.search(r"name\s*\(", source)` — never the bare name. And it is found by probing, not by review: the injection that removes the behaviour is the only thing that shows the assertion was measuring the import. Record the test's real limits next to it (it proves the call is written, not that it runs before the write, and it only covers files matching the glob).
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_2631_freeze_policy_guard.py::test_every_freeze_script_calls_the_guard` (call-form regex, comment records the probe that found it).

## Uniqueness constraints forbid branching, NOT cycles — and a cycle is the same wedge in the other direction (#2634, 2026-08-13)

- Symptom: #2634's first design made a preregistration declaration's revisions an append-only chain and claimed "exactly one current declaration per trial" followed from three declarative constraints: `UNIQUE (supersedes_declaration_id)` (no branching), a partial `UNIQUE (strategy_id, strategy_version) WHERE supersedes_declaration_id IS NULL` (one root), and a composite FK (same trial). Codex checkpoint 1: none of them forbids a **cycle**. Rows inserted with explicit ids, or a multi-row INSERT forming a closed loop, satisfy every uniqueness rule and leave the trial with **zero** current declarations — a permanent wedge indistinguishable from the one the ticket exists to remove.
- Root cause: uniqueness is a constraint on *in-degree*. "Exactly one row nothing points at" is a *reachability* property, and no combination of uniqueness constraints implies it. The same pass also found the composite FK unusable as written: `REFERENCES t(declaration_id, strategy_id, strategy_version)` needs a UNIQUE on exactly those three columns, and a PRIMARY KEY on `declaration_id` alone does not satisfy one.
- Prevention: when a chain/DAG invariant is claimed from constraints, name the property (acyclicity, reachability, single sink) and find the **single-row** predicate that implies it. Here `CHECK (supersedes_declaration_id IS NULL OR supersedes_declaration_id < declaration_id)` does it: `BIGSERIAL` is monotonic and a predecessor is always inserted first, so every real edge points at a smaller id and a cycle needs one that does not. One row-local CHECK proves a global graph property with no recursion, no depth bound and no cycle-detection code. Assert the invariant in the loader too (`_current_of_chain` raises when it finds zero or two) — the constraints are the proof, the assertion is what notices the proof failing.
- ⚠ **A constraint test that does not name the constraint can pass on a bystander.** The cycle probe first tried `UPDATE … SET supersedes_declaration_id = declaration_id`; it raised, the test went green, and the CHECK under test **never ran** — sql/333's immutability trigger fired first. Fixed by inserting a self-referencing row with an explicit id (a non-deferred FK is satisfied by a self-reference, so the CHECK is the only thing left to refuse it) and by asserting `exc.value.diag.constraint_name` in all five constraint tests. **Test: if a DB-constraint test only asserts the exception CLASS, it is asserting that something refused, not that your constraint did.**
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/337_preregistration_supersession.sql` (header records why the CHECK is load-bearing); `app/services/result_ledger.py::_current_of_chain`; `tests/test_2634_prereg_supersession_db.py` (five constraint tests, each asserting `diag.constraint_name`).

## Widening an identity rule in one place leaves the OTHER comparison of the same identity behind (#2634, 2026-08-13)

- Symptom: #2634 made a trial's declaration a chain of revisions, so "the declaration that authorised this access" stopped being "the trial's only declaration". `_SELECT_ACCESS_PROVENANCE`'s join was correctly moved onto `a.declaration_id`, and `verify_outcome_access_provenance`'s docstring was rewritten to say the function deliberately accepts a historical revision because provenance means *"was current when the access happened"*. Twenty lines below, `elif frozen.declaration_id != declaration_id: refusals.append("declaration_identity_mismatch")` still demanded the CURRENT id. Every signed artifact naming a predecessor would have been refused — the exact wedge the ticket exists to remove, rebuilt inside the fix for it. Found by Codex at checkpoint 2; every gate was green on it.
- Root cause: the identity was compared in two places — once in SQL, once in Python — and only the SQL one was in the diff's line of sight. The docstring was updated with the design, so it described the intended behaviour while the code beside it enforced the old one, and no test could fail because the paved path cannot reach the state (supersession refuses a trial that has any access row, so a predecessor never legitimately carries one).
- Prevention: when a cardinality changes from one-to-one to one-to-many, **grep for every comparison of the changed key**, not only the one you are editing — `declaration_id` appeared in a JOIN, an equality guard, a live-gate identity test and three scripts' persisted artifacts. ⚠ And treat a state the paved path cannot reach as *needing a constructed test*, not as *not needing one*: build it by direct INSERT and say in the test why the paved path cannot. A docstring that promises behaviour no test exercises is the most confident wrong thing in the file.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/result_ledger.py::verify_outcome_access_provenance` (chain membership, with the comment naming the checkpoint that caught it); `tests/test_2634_prereg_supersession_db.py::test_provenance_accepts_the_revision_the_access_row_names` (revert-probed).

### A gate that asks "is this value SUPPORTED?" where it should ask "does it match THIS ROW?" is a partial lift waiting for the set to widen

- First seen in: #2603 item 4 (2026-08-13), Codex checkpoint 1 on the spec. Not caught by any gate, and not by the spec author.
- Symptom: a single-valued domain (currency, unit, venue, base asset) is being lifted from a scattered literal into one declared constant, and every comparison against the literal is mechanically rewritten to membership of the new set. Behaviour is identical while the set has one member, so all tests stay green and the diff reads as a pure refactor. The spec here proposed exactly that for `strategy_paper_executor.py:555` (broker eligibility response currency) and `:593` (each cost component's currency). But those two sites are not asking *"is this a currency we support?"* — they are asking *"did the broker answer in the currency THIS deployment trades in?"*. Widen the set to `{"USD","GBP"}` and a GBP-quoted response satisfies membership against a USD deployment; `_costs` then runs `total += component.amount` across a USD component and a GBP one and returns a single number with no FX applied — the arithmetic #2363 created `fx_unmodelled` specifically to refuse. The widening commit would look like a one-line constant change and would pass every test.
- Root cause: "one source of truth for constants" (global CLAUDE.md, *Code quality defaults*) is read as "every literal becomes the constant", which erases a distinction the literal was silently carrying. When one value is the only legal value, *the set of supported values* and *this row's declared value* are the same string, so the two comparison kinds are indistinguishable in the code being replaced. Only widening separates them, and by then the site has shipped.
- Prevention: before rewriting a literal comparison to a membership test, ask **whose value is on each side**. Membership is right where the left side IS the declaration (`strategy_deployments.currency` — is the stored deployment currency one we support?). Equality against the row's own declared value is right where the left side is a THIRD PARTY's answer about that row (a broker response, a provider payload, a counterparty's quote) — and equality also ties several such answers to each other transitively, which membership never does. Tell: the site sits upstream of arithmetic that combines values (`+=`, `sum`, a weighted mean). Anything summed must be equal-denominated, not merely individually admissible.
- ⚠ **A test written against the one-member set cannot tell the two apart, so do not claim it does.** `eligibility_currency="GBP"` is refused under equality AND under membership of `{"USD"}`; that test pins behaviour-preservation only. The discriminating test monkeypatches the set WIDER while leaving the row's declared value alone, and asserts the third-party value is still refused — it passes under equality and fails under membership. Write that one, or the invariant is undefended.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_paper_executor.py::_eligibility_reason` + `::_costs` (equality against `intent.currency`, with the comment naming why); `app/services/strategy_base_currency.py` (the site list distinguishes the two kinds); `tests/test_strategy_paper_executor.py::test_widening_the_supported_set_does_not_widen_what_the_broker_may_quote` (revert-probed: swapping equality for membership turns it red).

### Deriving the set from the scalar makes "these two constants agree" untestable — and the test that appears to check it is green for every possible value

- First seen in: #2603 item 4 (2026-08-13), caught by revert-probing, not by review.
- Symptom: Codex asked for the invariant "the default value is a member of the supported set", which is the standard two-constants-must-agree pairing `docs/review-prevention-log.md:2081` calls for. It was implemented as `SUPPORTED_DEPLOYMENT_CURRENCIES = frozenset({DEPLOYMENT_CURRENCY})` plus `assert DEPLOYMENT_CURRENCY in SUPPORTED_DEPLOYMENT_CURRENCIES`. The revert-probe — set the scalar to `"EUR"` — left the test **green**, because the set is built from the scalar and the assertion holds for every possible value of either.
- Root cause: the same shape as "a reference that IMPORTS the constant it validates is a tautology" (#2240 phase 5c), arriving from the opposite direction. There the verifier imported the value; here the *thing under test* was constructed from it. Deriving one constant from the other is genuinely the better design — it makes disagreement unrepresentable — but it also dissolves the invariant the test was written to defend, and the test is not deleted along with it.
- Prevention: when a pairing rule ("two constants that must agree get an invariant test") meets a design where one is derived from the other, **the derivation discharges the rule and the test must be deleted or repointed at something falsifiable** — here, the literal value the default call path persists (`DEPLOYMENT_CURRENCY == "USD"`), which a probe does turn red. General test: for any assertion of the form `A <op> f(A)`, ask what value of `A` makes it fail. If there is none, it is documentation wearing an `assert`. **Revert-probing is what surfaces this class; a passing test and a plausible docstring never will.**
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_strategy_base_currency.py::test_the_declared_currency_is_the_one_the_default_call_path_uses` (docstring records the probe and why the membership form was dropped).

### A test module is `db`-marked by SUBSTRING over its SOURCE TEXT — so naming the fixture in a DOCSTRING silently drops every pure test in the file out of the push gate

- First seen in: #2612 (2026-08-13), found by an exit code, not by review or by a failing assertion.
- Symptom: a new module held nine pure-logic tests (a stage-machine coupling guard plus a refusal table) and four DB tests. `uv run pytest <file> -m "not db"` exited **5** — pytest's "no tests collected" — so all nine pure tests were silently absent from the fast pre-push gate. Splitting the DB half into a `_db.py` sibling did not fix it: the pure module still collected zero, because the docstring explaining the split *named the connection fixture in order to document this very rule*. The literal string in prose marked the module exactly as a real fixture would.
- Root cause: `tests/conftest.py::_module_source_touches_db` is `functools.cache`d over `pathlib.Path(path).read_text()` and returns `any(marker in source for marker in _DB_SOURCE_MARKERS)`. It does not parse — no AST, no import analysis, no distinction between a fixture parameter, an import, a comment and a docstring. It is the same bare-substring shape already logged for `test_every_freeze_script_calls_the_guard` (a name satisfied by the `import` line), reappearing in the collection hook rather than in a convention test. The failure direction is the dangerous one: over-marking is invisible, because a deselected test and a passing test both leave the gate green.
- Prevention: a test module that must run on the fast tier contains **no DB token anywhere in its source, prose included** — refer to the connection fixture by description, never by spelling it. Put DB tests in a `_db.py` sibling (the existing `test_outcome_ledger.py` / `test_outcome_ledger_db.py` convention). ⚠ **Verify by exit code, never by "the tests passed":** run `pytest <file> -m "not db" --collect-only -q` and read the count off the first line. Exit 5 means zero collected; `-q` prints `path: N`. A pure test that never runs on the gate is worth less than no test, because it is claimed as coverage in the PR description.
- ⚠ The general form, worth carrying beyond this hook: **any rule implemented as a substring scan over source text is satisfied by a mention and cannot be satisfied by intent.** Whenever such a scan gates something, the honest verification is to run the selector and count, not to inspect the file and reason about what it should match.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_2612_forward_window_single_entry.py` (module docstring carries the rule and the incident, and deliberately describes the fixture without naming it); `tests/test_2612_forward_window_single_entry_db.py` (header records why the split is load-bearing rather than cosmetic).
- ⚠⚠ **RECURRED THE SAME DAY, in #2611, with this entry already written.** A new pure-logic module named the settings database-URL attribute in a class docstring — in a sentence whose entire purpose was to say *that attribute is the wrong source for the audit DSN* — and all eight tests dropped out of the fast tier. **The recurrence is the point:** knowing the rule did not prevent it, because the mention was semantically a warning against the very thing it tripped, which is exactly the case intent-reading skips over. It was caught only by running `pytest <file> -m "not db"` and reading **exit 5**. So the prevention above is not "remember the rule" — it is **run the selector after writing any new pure-logic module, unconditionally**, the way `ruff` is run rather than recalled. Note the marker list is wider than the fixture name: the settings URL attribute, `TestClient`, `run_migrations(` and the test-DB helpers all mark a module, and any of them can appear in prose.

### A window anchored on `max(...)` encodes a splice policy that only the STAGE MACHINE makes correct — and nothing in the reading module can see it

- First seen in: #2612 (2026-08-13). The ticket reported the splice as a live bug; the premise was false, and the real defect was the undocumented coupling underneath it.
- Symptom: `assess_live_gate` derives the forward-evidence window from `max(promoted_at) FILTER (WHERE to_stage='forward_observation')` and the paper window likewise. Read locally that is a splice: promote twice and the window restarts, discarding the first observation period. #2612 asked which semantics were intended, splice or accumulate. Neither: `strategy_control_plane._NEXT_STAGE` is a DAG with no back-edge (`paused` → `retired` → nothing), only `historical_validated` has an edge into `forward_observation`, and the partial UNIQUE index `idx_strategy_promotions_one_successor` on `(strategy_id, strategy_version, from_stage)` lets each stage be departed exactly once. `max` therefore aggregates over **at most one row** and the choice does not exist.
- Root cause: correctness lived in a different module from the code relying on it, with no comment, no test and no runtime check joining them. `strategy_live_gate` cannot import or inspect `_NEXT_STAGE`, so a future re-entry edge — `paused` → `forward_observation` is the plausible one, and "a strategy re-enters forward observation after a pause" is a reasonable feature request — would make `max` re-anchor **silently**, restarting exactly the `forward_days` and `forward_decision_dates` that #2599's contract-frozen floor reads. No test would fail, because every existing test promotes once.
- Prevention: when an aggregate (`max`, `min`, `DISTINCT ON`, `LIMIT 1`) is correct only because an invariant elsewhere bounds the row count, do all three — **state** the invariant and its enforcement points where the aggregate is read; **carry the count as a fact** and refuse on it, so a relaxation fails closed instead of re-anchoring quietly; and **pin the coupling with a pure test over the machine that provides it**, whose failure message names the module that must be revisited. ⚠ The runtime refusal is not dead code for an impossible state: it is the only thing standing between a future one-line edit in another file and a silently corrupted evidence window. Cost here was one `count(*) FILTER` in a scan already being run.
- ⚠ Also: "exactly one predecessor" does **not** imply single entry — a cycle satisfies it. Assert the DAG property directly (rank the stages, assert every edge increases the rank), the same single-row-predicate move #2634 used against uniqueness-does-not-forbid-cycles.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_live_gate.py::LiveGateFacts` (field comment names both enforcement points) + `::live_gate_refusals` (`forward_window_ambiguous` / `paper_window_ambiguous`); `tests/test_2612_forward_window_single_entry.py` (coupling guard + DAG rank test, both revert-probed by injecting a `paused` → `forward_observation` back-edge).

### A boundary test written with decimal-looking floats is VACUOUS — `abs(0.6 - 0.4)` never reaches `0.2`, so `>` and `>=` both pass

- First seen in: #2625 (2026-08-13), caught by revert-probing, not by review or by the test suite.
- Symptom: `ambiguity_verdict` implements §3.4's *"differ by MORE than the threshold"*, so the strictness of one comparison is the rule. The guarding test asserted `ambiguity_verdict(_arms(0.6, 0.4, 0.2)) is False` — visibly "a gap of 0.2 against a threshold of 0.2". The revert-probe flipping `>` to `>=` left it **green**. `abs(0.6 - 0.4)` is `0.19999999999999996`, so the gap is below the threshold under either operator and the assertion never visits the boundary it is named after.
- Root cause: the values were chosen to *read* as the boundary rather than to *be* it. Every one of 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2 is inexact in binary, and the subtraction compounds it. This is invisible on inspection precisely because the literals look exact — the defect is in the arithmetic, not in the assertion, so reading the test carefully cannot find it.
- Prevention: a test that pins the strictness of a comparison MUST use binary-exact values — dyadic rationals (halves, quarters, eighths: 0.5, 0.25, 0.125) — and should **assert the exactness inline** (`assert abs(0.5 - 0.25) == 0.25`) so the test fails loudly if someone later "tidies" the literals back to decimal-looking ones. ⚠ The general form: **whenever a test's whole purpose is `<` versus `<=`, the probe is not optional** — a boundary assertion that never lands on the boundary is indistinguishable from one that does, in every way except the probe. Integer or `Decimal` arithmetic sidesteps the class entirely where the domain allows it.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_strategy_result_ambiguity.py::TestVerdict::test_the_comparison_is_strict_at_the_boundary` (docstring records the incident and carries the inline exactness assertion).

### Postgres defines `'NaN'::float8 = 'NaN'::float8` as TRUE — so the obvious "is it a real number" CHECK silently ADMITS NaN

- First seen in: #2625 (2026-08-13), caught by probing the constraint against the real database before writing it, per "verify before asserting".
- Symptom: `strategy_result_ambiguity` stores two Sharpes whose difference is compared against a threshold. A NaN Sharpe compares false against everything, so a NaN pair reads as "the arms differ" while carrying no information — it must be refused at the boundary. The reflexive guard is a self-equality test (`CHECK (x = x)`), which is the IEEE-754 idiom for "not NaN" and is **wrong in Postgres**: Postgres orders NaN as greater than every other float8 so that `float8` has a total order for indexing, and `NaN = NaN` is TRUE.
- Root cause: an assumption imported from IEEE-754 / C / Python semantics into a database that deliberately diverges from them. Nothing about the SQL reads as unusual, and the constraint would have been green in every test that did not specifically insert a NaN.
- Prevention: refuse non-finite floats with the RANGE form — `CHECK (x IS NULL OR (x > '-Infinity'::float8 AND x < 'Infinity'::float8))` — which rejects NaN (`NaN < Infinity` is false), `+Infinity` and `-Infinity` in one predicate, and admits every finite value. Measured on this database before the migration was written: `NaN > -Infinity` → **t**, `NaN < Infinity` → **f**, `NaN = NaN` → **t**, `Infinity < Infinity` → **f**. ⚠ Mirror the constraint in the Python dataclass with `math.isfinite` rather than trusting the table: the same object is also built from in-memory measurements at write time, where no constraint has run yet.
- ⚠ Corollary, and the reason this is not just a SQL trivia note: **a float ordering assumption is exactly the kind of thing that is "obviously true" and version/engine-specific.** Probe it against the real engine; do not port the idiom.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/339_strategy_result_ambiguity.sql` (`strategy_result_ambiguity_sharpes_finite`, whose comment records the measured values); `app/services/strategy_result_ambiguity.py::AmbiguityRecord.__post_init__`.

### A guard keyed on a MANY-TO-MANY PROJECTION of what it guards is evadable — classify the inputs, not the output codes

- First seen in: #2625 (2026-08-13), killed at Codex checkpoint 1, before the guard was written.
- Symptom: #2625 declares which of `check_promotable`'s inputs the promotion transition replays FROZEN, which against TODAY, and which not at all. The point of the policy is that a *new* gate input cannot be added without a decision, so it needs a coupling guard. The first design asserted that every **refusal code** `check_promotable` can emit is classified in the policy. That is satisfiable while an input goes unclassified: one input emits several codes (`promotion_evidence` emits a dozen), several inputs emit one, and a new input can simply reuse an existing code — `no_instruments_evaluated` is already shared. The guard would have been permanently green and proved nothing about coverage.
- Root cause: the codes are what the gate *returns*; the inputs are what it *reads*. The guard was keyed on the observable rather than on the thing whose growth it exists to detect, and the two are related by a many-to-many map, so neither direction of the assertion constrains the other.
- Prevention: when writing a coupling guard, name the edit you want it to fail on, then key it on the **structural artefact that edit necessarily produces**. Here a new gate input necessarily arrives as a new `PromotionCandidate` field, so the guard reads `dataclasses.fields(...)` and asserts the policy classifies all of them — and asserts the reverse inclusion too, so a stale entry for a deleted field cannot keep it green. ⚠ General test: **ask what the guard's assertion would look like if the defect were present.** If the answer is "identical", the key is a projection and not an index.
- ⚠ Same session, adjacent variant worth carrying: **"persisted" is not "replayed".** #2625's inventory listed several gate inputs as "✅ on the result row", which reads as covered; `grep -n "universe_basis\|carry_unmodelled\|fx_unmodelled" app/services/strategy_control_plane.py` returned **nothing**, so the promotion transition never read any of them. When a table says an input is available, grep the CONSUMER for the column name before believing it is used — the M9 pattern ("the control sits on a path the decision does not take") one layer down, in the data rather than the call.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_promotion_replay.py` (module docstring states the field-keying rule and why); `tests/test_strategy_promotion_replay.py::TestEveryGateInputIsClassified` (both inclusion directions, revert-probed by dropping a policy entry).

### `bool(None)` is `False`, and for a `*_unmodelled` flag `False` is the PERMISSIVE value — so coercing a NULL stamp fails OPEN

- First seen in: #2625 (2026-08-13), caught by the review bot, not by a test — and no test could have caught it.
- Symptom: `promote_strategy` began replaying the row's structural stamps, reading them as `(None if row[3] is None else str(row[3]), bool(row[4]), bool(row[5]))`. The text column defensively preserved `None`; the two booleans did not. `carry_unmodelled` / `fx_unmodelled` are named so that **`True` is the restrictive value** — `True` means "this cost is NOT modelled" and refuses — so `bool(None) is False` silently converts an unset stamp into *"the cost IS modelled"*, a PASS on one of the Tier 1 refusals.
- Root cause: the polarity of the flag inverts the usual intuition. For a flag named `is_valid` or `passed`, `bool(None) → False` fails closed and is harmless. For a flag named `*_unmodelled`, `*_missing`, `*_stale` or `*_suppressed`, the safe default is `True`, and the language's coercion gives the opposite. The inconsistency was visible in one expression — one element preserved `None`, two discarded it — which is what the reviewer spotted; nothing else would have, because both columns are `NOT NULL` today and no fixture can produce the NULL.
- Prevention: never `bool(x)` a nullable flag read from SQL. Write the fail-closed direction explicitly — `True if x is None else bool(x)` — and let the polarity of the NAME decide which direction that is. ⚠ **Read the flag's name before choosing the default: for a negatively-named flag the safe default is `True`, and it is the opposite of what every coercion helper will give you.** Prefer `NOT NULL` in the schema so the question cannot arise; where the column is already `NOT NULL`, the explicit form is defence in depth and **must be documented as untestable rather than claimed as covered** — no fixture can reach the branch, and a revert-probe cannot turn any test red.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_control_plane.py::promote_strategy` (the `stamps_by_result` comprehension carries the rule and records that both columns are `NOT NULL` as measured).

### A CHECK constraint cannot hold a subquery, and the scalar rewrite has a NULL hole that ACCEPTS

- First seen in: #2611 (2026-08-13), caught by probing the DDL against a real cluster before writing the migration, not by review.
- Symptom: `sql/340` needed "this refusal names at least one non-blank code". The readable spelling — `cardinality(refusals) > 0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(refusals) AS code WHERE code IS NULL OR btrim(code) = '')` — is rejected outright by Postgres at `CREATE TABLE` time with `FeatureNotSupported: cannot use subquery in check constraint`. That failure is loud and harmless. The rewrite is where the defect lives: `cardinality(refusals) > 0 AND '' <> ALL(refusals)` looks complete and **accepts `{NULL}`**, because `'' <> ALL(ARRAY[NULL])` evaluates to NULL and a CHECK that evaluates to NULL passes.
- Root cause: three-valued logic at the constraint boundary, in the direction nobody checks. A CHECK is refused only when it evaluates to FALSE; UNKNOWN is a pass. Every intuition about `ALL` / `ANY` over an array carries an implicit "and there are no NULLs in it", and the array-typed column is exactly where that assumption is unstated. The same shape as the NULL-comparison entry already in `sql-correctness.md`, arriving through an array operator rather than through a `WHERE` clause.
- Prevention: validate an array inside a CHECK with **two** scalar predicates, not one — `array_position(col, NULL) IS NULL` for the NULL element and `'' <> ALL(col)` for the blank one — plus `cardinality(col) > 0`. ⚠ **Probe the DDL against a real cluster before shipping it**, with a `CREATE TEMP TABLE` and one INSERT per case; measured here as `{}`, `{NULL}`, `{""}`, `{"a",""}` all refused and `{"a"}` accepted. Reasoning about a constraint cannot distinguish "refuses" from "evaluates to NULL and passes", and the wrong one of those is invisible until a bad row is already stored.
- ⚠ Wants extracting into `.claude/skills/engineering/sql-correctness.md` next to its "NULL in comparisons" section — the edit was blocked by a tool permission prompt in the authoring session (headless), so it lives here until an interactive session moves it.
- ⚠⚠ **RECURRED THE SAME DAY (#2602, 2026-08-13, `sql/341`), in the plainest possible form — so the array framing above is too narrow to trigger on.** The trap is not about arrays: it is about **making an existing column NULLable and leaving an `=` comparison on it inside a CHECK**. `sql/341` drops `NOT NULL` from `broker_account_equity_snapshots.currency` and its new constraint read `WHEN account_currency_id = 1 THEN currency = 'USD'`. That admits `(1, NULL)` — an account measured as USD whose code is missing — which is the single combination the constraint exists to reject. Caught by the constraint test, not by review or by reasoning. Fix: `currency IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 'USD'`. **Generalised trigger: any migration containing `DROP NOT NULL` must re-read every CHECK, index predicate and generated column that mentions that column, because each one silently changed meaning from "enforced" to "enforced except on NULL".** Grep the column name across `sql/` after writing the `DROP NOT NULL`, and write one constraint test per NULL-bearing combination — a test asserting only the happy path cannot see this.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/340_holdout_access_refusals.sql` (`strategy_holdout_access_refusals_names_a_reason` carries the rule and the measured cases); `tests/test_2611_refused_access_audit_db.py::test_the_relation_refuses_a_refusal_that_names_no_reason` (asserts `diag.constraint_name`, so a bystander constraint firing cannot pass it); `sql/341_account_equity_observed_currency.sql` (`broker_account_equity_snapshots_currency_observed`, with the reason written next to the predicate); `tests/test_account_equity_evidence.py::test_currency_and_reported_id_cannot_disagree_at_rest` (three parametrised NULL-bearing combinations, asserting `diag.constraint_name`).

### A long job's FIRST statement decides which locks it holds for the whole run — and a *waiting* `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` blocks new readers, so the stall is not confined to the migration

- First seen in: #2628 (filed 2026-08-12 while applying `sql/335` for #2363, fixed 2026-08-13). Found by `pg_blocking_pids`, not by review or by any test.
- Symptom: `scripts/migrate.py` sat for ten minutes having burned 0.31s of CPU. The blocker was `strategy_backtest_run`, `idle in transaction` for 26 minutes with an `AccessShareLock` on `strategy_results_store`, cycling statements the whole time — working, inside ONE transaction it held for the entire multi-hour run. Polling every 0.3s for ~40 minutes found **zero** moments when no session held a lock on that relation.
- Root cause: a `psycopg` connection with `autocommit=False` opens its transaction at the **first statement** and holds every lock that statement took until commit or rollback. §10's pre-flight `SELECT` on `strategy_results_store` runs in the first seconds; the corpus pass that follows takes hours and never touches that relation again. Nothing in the code says "hold this lock for four hours" — the transaction boundary was simply never stated, so it defaulted to the widest one available.
- ⚠ The second half is what makes it more than a slow migration: **a pending `AccessExclusiveLock` queues AHEAD of new readers.** A migration that is merely *waiting* stops every subsequent `SELECT` on that relation from starting, so a waiting `ALTER TABLE` stalls the running dev stack rather than politely taking its turn. The FastAPI lifespan runs migrations at boot, so `tests/smoke/test_app_boots.py` — and therefore the pre-push hook — fails for purely environmental reasons while the job runs. Verified by control: withholding only the migration file makes smoke exit 0.
- Prevention: for any job whose body runs for minutes or more, **state the transaction boundary rather than inheriting it**. Ask which relations the first statements lock and whether the long phase needs them; if not, end the read transaction before the long phase begins. Measure it, do not reason about it — `SELECT c.relname FROM pg_locks l JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = l.relation WHERE l.pid = <backend_pid>` from a SECOND connection, at each phase, is the whole technique. ⚠ **A service function that takes a caller's `Connection` must not `commit`/`rollback` it** (the entry above on `load_credential_for_provider_use`), so the release belongs behind an **opt-in flag whose guard refuses a connection that is already in a transaction** — that is what makes the exception safe instead of merely documented. ⚠⚠ **And check what the release does to the transactions BELOW it**: once the connection is idle, a nested `with conn.transaction():` stops being a savepoint and becomes top-level, so a write phase that was invocation-atomic silently becomes commit-per-unit. Here that would have left a partially written pinned evidence window behind, which `_recent_evidence_completion` refuses as needing operator repair — a resumable failure turned into one that needs a human. Wrap the write phase explicitly so the grain is stated on both paths.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/backtest_run.py::_end_read_phase` + `run_backtest`'s `release_read_locks` docstring (carries the measurement and the reason the default is off); `tests/test_backtest_run_lock_scope.py` (reads `pg_locks` from a second session at the evaluation boundary, and pins the write phase's transaction status).

### A settings patch scoped to ONE module, handed a REACHABLE url, fails open — and writes to the dev DB

- First seen in: #1887 (2026-07-02), recurred #2629 (2026-08-13). The #1887 entry above ("A mocked-module rename after a connection-helper migration…") recorded the mechanism and fixed the two files it had bitten. It recurred anyway, in a third file, through a *different* wrapper — so the per-case patch was not the fix.
- Symptom: `tests/workers/test_scheduler_error_category.py` drove `_tracked_job` under `patch("app.workers.scheduler.settings")` with `mock_settings.database_url = _test_database_url()`. `_tracked_job` opens no connection of its own: every `job_runs` write goes through `app.db.background_write.background_write_connection`, whose raw fallback reads `settings` from ITS own module namespace. The patched name was never consulted, so all four tests read an empty per-worker test DB and asserted `row is not None` — while the rows landed in the operator's dev `ebull`. Measured 2026-08-13: **40** `test_tracked_%` rows in dev `job_runs`, accumulating since 2026-08-10; a controlled probe (restore the old patch, run the file) moved that count **36 → 40**, four rows for four tests.
- Root cause — and the reason the #1887 framing did not catch it: patching a module-local alias pins the dependency's **location**, not the dependency. Every refactor that moves a connection site to another module silently un-patches it, and the test keeps passing its *setup*. But the amplifier is the **url's reachability**, which #1887 never named. The other 29 `*.database_url = …` assignments in `tests/` all assign a bogus literal (`"postgresql://test"`, `"postgresql://stub/"`): when production code does consult one of those the connection FAILS LOUDLY, which is correct by construction. Only a real, reachable url turns "the patch stopped working" into a silent dev-DB write. Neither existing defence sees it — the static guard greps for `connect(settings.database_url` in *test* source, and the dev-DB size tripwire is 1 MB-granular AND warn-only while the jobs daemon holds the lock, so four small rows are invisible twice over.
- Prevention: **never assign a reachable url onto a mocked `settings` alias.** Either assign a bogus string literal — a leak then fails loudly instead of writing — or redirect the SHARED object with `monkeypatch.setattr(settings, "database_url", test_database_url())` / `patch.object(settings, "database_url", …)`, which keeps every consumer in step however many modules the write path crosses. That is already the established pattern: six `settings_use_test_db` fixtures in `tests/` do exactly this. ⚠ The generalisation beyond DB urls: when a test patches a module-scoped name to isolate a side effect, the isolation is only as good as the assumption that production still reads THAT name — so make the failure mode loud, because you will not be told when the assumption expires.
- ⚠ Also note what the db tier's absence from the push gate costs here. This was not a subtle bug; it was four tests failing on every run since 2026-08-10, seen by nobody because `-m db` is off the gate (#2224) and CI runs no pytest. **A test suite nothing runs is not a defence, and it is worse than none when its failure mode writes.**
- ⚠ Wants extracting into `.claude/skills/engineering/test-quality.md` §85 ("Mock the name the code actually calls"), whose current text is the #1887 per-case framing this entry supersedes. The edit was blocked by a tool permission prompt in the authoring session (headless), the same way the #2611 entry above was — it lives here until an interactive session moves it.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/smoke/test_no_settings_url_in_destructive_paths.py::test_no_reachable_url_assigned_onto_a_mocked_settings_alias` (regex guard, **0 offenders tree-wide** at #2629 — and it lives in `tests/smoke`, which IS on the push gate, unlike the tier that hid the original); `tests/workers/test_scheduler_error_category.py::_run_tracked` (docstring names the failure mode and why the object, not the alias, is patched).

### `date.today()` is the RUNNER's clock; a value written by SQL `CURRENT_DATE` is the SERVER's — asserting equality between them fails for one hour a day

- First seen in: #2629 (2026-08-13). Filed as a deterministic failure; it is deterministic only inside a window, which is why it "passed earlier in the same session".
- Symptom: `tests/test_instrument_history.py::test_rename_closes_prior_and_opens_new` asserted `chain[0][2] == date.today()` against an `effective_to` that `app/services/instrument_history.py` closes with SQL `CURRENT_DATE`. Measured: the dev and test clusters run `TimeZone = Etc/UTC`; the operator's box runs BST (UTC+1). The two dates therefore disagree for 23:00–00:00 UTC every day, and the ticket caught it inside that hour (`date(2026,8,12) != date(2026,8,13)`).
- Root cause: two clocks, one comparison, and the divergence window is small enough that the test is green almost all the time — so it reads as flaky when it is fully determined by the run's wall time and the runner's zone. Nothing in the assertion says which clock it means.
- Prevention: **compare a server-written date against the server's clock.** Read `SELECT CURRENT_DATE` on the same connection (`_db_today(conn)`) rather than calling `date.today()`. ⚠ **And probe it with a skewed zone, not by waiting for the window** — `TZ=Pacific/Midway` (UTC−11) puts the runner a day behind the server on demand: the old assertion reproduces the exact ticket signature, the new one passes under both `TZ=Pacific/Midway` and `TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati` (UTC+14). A probe that only bites during one real hour is a probe you will never run. Measured full-population at #2629: exactly **1** occurrence of `assert … == date.today()` in `tests/` — the other 122 `date.today()` uses seed relative dates and are tolerant of the skew.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_instrument_history.py::_db_today` (+ the why-comment on the assertion it serves).

### A timing assertion cannot be made deterministic by tuning its margin — and the arm producing the timings may never run the code under test

- First seen in: #1769 (2026-06-28), recurred #2610 (2026-08-13). The #1769 fix replaced an absolute wall-clock constant with a *measured ratio* against an in-process sequential baseline, on the reasoning that both arms dilate together under load. They do not dilate together enough: the same assertion false-failed again 46 days later, in the same file, on the same gate.
- Symptom: `tests/test_concurrent_fetch.py::test_concurrent_total_time_smaller_than_sequential` asserted `concurrent < sequential * 0.85`. On PR #2609 it failed the pre-push gate on **3 of 4 attempts** and passed standalone every time, with a sibling headless autonomy loop holding the box's load average at 2.68–3.59. It sits on the fast tier (`-m "not db"`), i.e. the per-push path, so each false failure costs a full fast tier plus pyright plus the chokepoint lints — and per #2224 a gate that fails randomly trains `--no-verify`, which is strictly worse than no gate. A sibling loop on this machine is a **normal** operating condition (see the parallel-session section of `.claude/CLAUDE.md`), so there was no margin that made this arrangement sound.
- ⚠⚠ The second defect is the one the two rewrites did not see. The test's worker was a **test-local `fire()`** that called `rc._throttle_and_stamp()` and then slept the simulated RTT itself. `ResilientClient._request` was never invoked. The "the HTTP round trip happens outside the throttle lock" ordering being asserted was therefore the ordering *the test had written*, not the one at `app/providers/resilient_client.py:186-195` — moving the real `self._client.send` inside the real lock could not have moved either arm's number. **A test that reimplements the sequence it claims to guard measures its own fixture, and it will stay green through the exact regression it is named for.** Both rewrites tuned the threshold; neither asked what the threshold was measuring.
- Root cause: a stopwatch answers "how long did this take on this box just now", which is a different question from "does the code have this structural property". Every timing assertion therefore needs a margin, the margin is a guess about the host, and the host is shared. The two failures compound: a test observing the wrong code will *never* fail for the right reason, so all its observed failures are host noise — which is precisely the evidence that leads you to widen the margin again.
- Prevention: **replace the stopwatch with a rendezvous, and drive the shipped entry point.** Concurrency questions of the form "did N operations overlap?" are decided exactly by `threading.Barrier(N)` placed at the point that can only be reached past the property under test — here, an `httpx.MockTransport` handler, reachable only after `_throttle_and_stamp` has returned. If the property is broken, occupancy caps at 1, the barrier cannot form, `BrokenBarrierError` fires, and the test fails on every run and every box; host load moves only how long a pass takes. ⚠ Drive the real public call (`rc.get(...)`) rather than a hand-rolled worker, so the ordering under test is the shipped one. ⚠ Revert-probe it: injecting `with self._throttle_lock:` around `response = self._client.send(request)` in `_request` failed **exactly one** test in the file, with its own message — a probe that also topples neighbours has not isolated anything. Assert `s.count(old) == 1` before the string replace, or the probe may match nothing and prove nothing.
- ⚠ Generalised trigger, since this class recurs under other names: **if an assertion's pass/fail depends on a duration, a rate, or a ratio of two measured durations, it is a host measurement and it does not belong on the push gate.** Ask what discrete, decidable event the timing was standing in for — a barrier forming, a lock grant ordering, a counter's final value — and assert that instead. Compare the sibling entry on pacers (#2648): no *emission-side* observation can falsify a pacer either, because oversleeping only ever delays.
- Enforced in: this log; `tests/test_concurrent_fetch.py::TestResponseTimeIsSpentOutsideTheThrottleLock` (its docstring carries the #2610 evidence, the wrong-code finding, and why the assertion is a barrier); `tests/test_concurrent_fetch.py::TestRateLimitSafetyUnderConcurrency::test_throttle_lock_serialises_request_stamping` (still pins the other half of the design — that stamping *is* serialised at `1 / min_interval` — so dropping the throughput arm leaves no gap).

### A documented safety layer that does not exist is worse than documenting none — it makes readers stop looking for the one that matters

- First seen in: #2645 (2026-08-13), noticed because #2644 exercised the path the documentation said was closed.
- Symptom: `.autonomy/loop_prompt.md` told every unattended run that "the loop is also run with **NO broker credentials configured**, so the order client fails closed — see setup.md; this rule is the second layer", and #2604's `loop-ineligible` list skipped "anything needing broker credentials" on the same premise. Both were false, and the second one had already cost something concrete: #2598 was classified unreachable-by-the-loop and left unworked, when #2644 later completed its live informational preflight decode from that worktree without breaking any rule.
- Root cause: the premise was checked on the filesystem and nowhere else. `ls /Users/lukebradford/Dev/.ebull-autonomy/.env` is genuinely absent — but **neither half of the credential path is in `.env`**. Measured 2026-08-13 from the loop worktree: the database-URL setting defaults to `postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/ebull` (`app/config.py`), i.e. the shared dev cluster every worktree points at, which holds 2 `etoro` rows in `broker_credentials` (both `environment = 'demo'`, both `health_state = 'valid'`, zero `real` rows); and the decryption root secret resolves through `platformdirs.user_data_dir("eBull")` to `~/Library/Application Support/eBull/root_secret.bin` (present, 32 bytes, mode 0600) — a machine-wide OS data directory, not a repo path (`app/security/master_key.py::root_secret_path`). Absence of a repo-local file says nothing about a secret held in the OS data dir and a ciphertext held in a shared database.
- ⚠ The generalisable half is not about credentials. **A safety claim of the form "X cannot happen because Y is absent" is a measurement of Y's full resolution order, not of one location.** Read the resolver, not the directory: `resolve_data_dir()` has three fallbacks and `Settings` has a default, so two independent lookups both succeed with no `.env` at all.
- ⚠⚠ And the reason it survived several readings: nothing failed when it stopped being true. Every other protection here is rule-shaped (a prohibition plus discipline), and a rule that is never exercised never reports. Whoever read "credentials are absent" was satisfied and stopped looking for the enforcement that actually holds.
- ⚠⚠ **A push-time gate is not an execution-time control, and the first fix here confused the two.** My initial answer was a static AST scan asserting no file under `scripts/` calls a state-mutating `BrokerProvider` method (measured: **192 scripts, 0 offenders**), on the reasoning that the real risk is accident rather than a determined agent, and accident is what a gate catches. Codex checkpoint 1 killed it in one line: **the scan runs at push time, and #2644's probe ran long before anything was pushed — so the proposed control could not have stopped the very near-miss that motivated it.** The shipped answer is a runtime refusal (`app/security/unattended_guard.py`) raised before any network I/O, keyed on the git worktree layout itself: a linked worktree's `.git` is a FILE holding a `gitdir:` pointer, the main checkout's is a DIRECTORY. That needs no environment variable anyone must remember to set and no cooperation from the separate autonomy-engine repo. **Test: ask when your control runs relative to when the harm happens. If the answer is "later", it is drift detection, not protection.**
- ⚠ **But do not accept the reviewer's placement either.** Codex proposed centralising the refusal on the provider's write transport, `_http_write`. Measured: `_http_write` also carries `check_instrument_eligibility` and `get_what_if_costs` — informational POSTs to `_v2_info_prefix`. Guarding the transport would have blocked exactly the preflight decode #2644 completed correctly, i.e. re-imposed the *other* half of the error this ticket exists to correct. The refusal is therefore per-method on the five mutating methods, with a scan asserting the informational ones do NOT call it. A seam that looks like a chokepoint is worth measuring before you put policy on it — "write client" named a transport, not an intent.
- ⚠ **A suite-wide disarm needs a re-arming test, or it is a fail-open default.** Wiring the guard turned ~25 existing broker tests red *in a worktree only* — they drive `place_order`/`close_position` against a mocked transport, and worktrees are where long-running work is supposed to happen. A result that depends on which checkout you ran in is worse than a flaky test: deterministic per-environment, inconsistent across them. The fix is an autouse fixture pinning the detection FALSE, plus one test that re-arms it and drives the shipped `EtoroBrokerProvider.place_order` with `_http_write` replaced by an object that fails on any attribute access — proving both that the refusal fires and that it precedes all network I/O. Without that second half the fixture would silently void the whole guard (compare #2647's fail-closed default disarming an absence-asserting test).
- ⚠ Pair any hand-written list of forbidden symbols with a partition assertion over the live interface — `_MUTATING | _INFORMATIONAL == BrokerProvider`'s public surface — or the guard silently stays as wide as the day it was written; that is the #2614 "a chokepoint closes the doors that EXIST" entry above, in its list-shaped form.
- Prevention: when a document claims a *mechanical* layer, either point at the code that fails closed or delete the claim and name the real first layer. If the layer is worth having, **build it as something that fails, at the moment the harm would occur.**
- Enforced in: this log; `app/security/unattended_guard.py`; `tests/test_unattended_broker_mutation_guard.py` (runtime refusal, end-to-end armed test, and three static scans — guard-present-on-mutating, guard-absent-on-informational, no-script-reaches-mutating — each revert-probed); `tests/conftest.py::_disarm_unattended_broker_guard`; `.autonomy/loop_prompt.md` (hard-safety section now lists the four layers in order and marks the credential state as safety by absence).

### A pure-logic test can be exiled from the push gate by prose in its own docstring — the `db` auto-marker is a substring scan

- First seen in: #2645 (2026-08-13), caught only because the new guard was explicitly checked for fast-tier membership rather than just "does it pass".
- Symptom: `tests/test_unattended_broker_mutation_guard.py` touches no database — it parses files with `ast` and reads one class's method names. `uv run pytest tests/... -q` exited 0, so it looked done. `uv run pytest -m "not db" --collect-only -q tests/...` exited **5** (no tests collected): it had been auto-marked `db`, which is exactly the tier `.githooks/pre-push` does not run (#2224). A guard against unattended trading would have shipped off the gate it exists to stand on.
- Root cause: `tests/conftest.py::_module_source_touches_db` is `any(marker in source for marker in _DB_SOURCE_MARKERS)` — a **substring** match over the whole module source, docstrings and comments included. The file's module docstring explained the bug it guards by naming `settings.database_url`, which is one of the markers. The heuristic is deliberately conservative and correct to be; the collision is with *prose*, and it is silent in the direction that matters — over-marking removes a test from the gate without removing it from the run, so nothing is ever red.
- Prevention: **after adding any test that should be on the push gate, assert its tier, not just its result** — `uv run pytest -m "not db" --collect-only -q <file>` and check the collected count, because exit 5 and exit 0 both look like success next to a green run. When a pure-logic test needs to *discuss* a DB symbol, paraphrase it ("the database-URL setting") rather than quoting the literal; the markers to avoid are listed at `tests/conftest.py::_DB_SOURCE_MARKERS`. Do not widen the marker list to allow the prose — the conservative direction is the safe one for the other 200-odd files.
- Enforced in: this log; the module docstring of `tests/test_unattended_broker_mutation_guard.py` (paraphrases rather than quoting).

### An "independent" cross-check that traces to the same venue decodes the UNIT and cannot validate the LEVEL

- First seen in: #2598 (2026-08-13), while running the band-stratified preflight census the ticket asked for.
- Symptom: the decode of eToro's undocumented what-if `value` field rests on comparing `value / ticket_amount` against `quotes.spread_pct`, described in the skill as *"an independent same-quantity measurement"* because `quotes` *"is written by a feed path that never reads a what-if response, so this is not circular"*. That is true about the code path and misleading about the evidence: `quotes` is written by `market_data._upsert_quote` **from eToro**. Two endpoints of one venue.
- Root cause: "independent" was applied to the *producing code path* when the property that matters is the *upstream observer*. For a UNIT question (is this field monetary or a rate?) the code-path independence is sufficient — a rate would miss by four orders of magnitude whatever the source. For a LEVEL question (is this spread real / is our band table calibrated?) it is worth nothing: both sides inherit the same book, the same staleness and the same venue-specific markup.
- ⚠ The distinction had already been half-noticed and half-lost. The skill's *"do NOT upgrade this to `marketSpread == the quoted spread`"* caution is exactly the right instinct, but it is justified by per-observation noise on four names — which invites the reading that a bigger sample would license the upgrade. It would not. The 60-instrument census measured a population median of **0.995x**, and the identity still cannot be read as validation, because the wider sample makes the correlation tighter without making the sources any more independent.
- ⚠⚠ Generalises past this endpoint: **before writing "independent" about a cross-check, name the two OBSERVERS, not the two code paths.** If the answer is one observer twice, the check can settle representation (unit, scale, encoding) and never magnitude.
- Prevention: state, next to any cross-source claim, which upstream produced each side. Where only one upstream exists, say what the comparison can and cannot license, in that sentence rather than in a caveat further down.
- Enforced in: this log; `scripts/verify_2598_preflight_quote_crosscheck.py` (the census arm's docstring); the #2598 comment carrying the census results.

### A p75 is not a bound, and neither is the maximum of a snapshot the market can exceed

- First seen in: #2598 (2026-08-13), scope 5 asked for the banded static cost model to become *"the declared execution-side conservative bound"*.
- Symptom: `static-p75-insession-v2+split-adjusted-max` was proposed as that bound. **A 75th percentile is exceeded by a quarter of its population by construction** — a property of the statistic, not of the sample — so the fix looked like "recalibrate at p95 or the max". Measured, that fails too: the `>=$100` band's p95 is 87.1 bps and its whole in-session sample max is 245.9 bps, while a single broker preflight for ETR came back at **381.5 bps**, 1.55x the largest spread anywhere in that band's calibration snapshot.
- Root cause: two different jobs were being asked of one artefact. The banded model exists for the BACKTEST, where no quote exists and a per-band figure is the only thing available. Execution has the broker's own number at entry time and needs no model at all. Once that is separated, the bound question dissolves for execution and stays honest for the backtest — where the right disclosure is the measured exceedance, not the word "conservative".
- ⚠ **The exceedance RATE is not the finding; the worst multiple is.** On the census the `>=$100` band's rate (4 of 15 over the p75) reads unremarkable and its worst observation is 11.85x. A rate near 25% says only that a p75 is behaving like a p75. Any report of a bound's adequacy that prints a rate without a tail is reporting the half that cannot fail.
- ⚠ Second-order, and the reason a "conservative" label was plausible for so long: the frozen table was calibrated from a snapshot concentrated in the CLOSING hour (1,149 of 1,159 captures at 15:00-15:59 ET) and re-measured against one concentrated in the OPENING hour (1,517 of 1,569 at 10:00-10:59 ET). Same one-hour-of-the-day defect, opposite direction of bias, and it moved every band from "conservative" to "optimistic" without anything about the model changing. **A percentile inherits the sampling hour; two snapshots of one statistic can disagree in direction for a reason that is not drift.**
- Prevention: before declaring any statistic a bound, ask what fraction of its own population exceeds it. If the answer is not ~0, it is a central estimate with a disclosure attached. And check whether the consumer already holds the true value — a modelled bound in front of a live measurement is the wrong artefact however well it is calibrated.
- Enforced in: this log; `scripts/verify_2240_cost_model.py::_report_bounding_statistics` (prints p95/max with the freeze-ready quantisation and the sample caveat); `scripts/verify_2598_preflight_quote_crosscheck.py::_census_statistics` (`worst_over_p75` is a field beside the rate); `sql/342_strategy_entry_preflight_cost_basis.sql` (declines to mint a `static_band_bound` vocabulary member on this evidence).

### A magnitude guard that bounds an AGGREGATE can be escaped by an overflow in the aggregation itself

- First seen in: #2603 item 3 (PR for `app/services/strategy_core_allocator.py`), Codex
  checkpoint 2, by probe rather than by reading.
- Symptom: `_state_refusal` checked each component finite and non-negative, then bounded the
  **sum** (`core_market_value + cash_balance >= _MAX_AMOUNT`) — reasoning, correctly as far as
  it went, that two non-negative components under a bounded sum are each under it too, so a
  per-component check was redundant. It is not redundant, because the guard has to *compute*
  the sum to test it: two finite components near `Decimal`'s `Emax` raise `decimal.Overflow`
  **on the addition**, before the comparison the refusal depends on ever runs.
  `Decimal("9e999999") + Decimal("9e999999")` raises; `Decimal("1e999999") + Decimal("1e999999")`
  does not — so the failure is reachable only in part of the input space, which is why reading
  the code did not surface it and executing it did.
- The general shape: **the guard's own arithmetic is unguarded.** Any refusal of the form
  "combine these inputs, then check the combination" runs the combination on inputs nothing has
  bounded yet. Same class as the ordering rule already logged for `Decimal("NaN") < 0` raising
  rather than returning False — a validator whose steps are in the wrong order does not fail
  loudly, it fails *past* its own refusal.
- Prevention: when a validator bounds a derived quantity (a sum, product, ratio or difference),
  bound **each input first**, then the derived quantity. Both checks stay: the per-input one
  exists to make the derivation safe to perform, the derived one to enforce the contract, and
  neither implies the other (two inputs at 60% of a bound each pass individually and sum past
  it). Self-review prompt: for every comparison in a validator, ask what would happen if the
  expression on the left *raised* — if the answer is "the caller gets an exception instead of
  the named refusal", the operands need bounding above it.
- Enforced in: `app/services/strategy_core_allocator.py::_state_refusal` (per-component check
  documented as overflow-safety, not as a shortcut); `tests/test_2603_core_allocator.py`
  parametrises `9e999999 + 9e999999` and a pair that clears the component bound but sums past it.

### An IN-RANGE bound is not a REACHABLE bound — a non-strict CHECK can leave a strict downstream comparator dead

- First seen in: #2670 (`sql/336_strategy_core_mandate.sql`), found at #2603 item 3's Codex
  checkpoint 1 while reviewing the allocator that consumes the constraint.
- Symptom: two schema CHECKs written to keep a rebalance band's triggers "inside `[0,100]`"
  each admitted the value at which one trigger can never fire. `core_target_pct -
  rebalance_band_pct >= 0` permits `lower == 0`, and the allocator's trigger is
  `core_pct < lower` — unreachable for a non-negative sleeve, *including* by the core going to
  zero, which the CHECK's own comment named as the surviving case (`0` is not `< 0`). The
  comment described a guarantee the comparator did not provide, and nothing failed: the
  allocator computed correctly on such a mandate, one side simply never triggered.
- The general shape: **a write-time bound and a read-time comparator are two different
  inequalities, and the boundary value is where they disagree.** A constraint keeping a
  derived quantity in a *closed* range is compatible with a consumer testing it with a
  *strict* comparator, which makes the range's endpoint a value the consumer can never act on.
  Nothing downstream can tell such a row apart from a genuinely one-sided intent, so it is a
  write-time authority defect rather than a computation bug — which is exactly why no test
  caught it.
- Prevention: when adding a CHECK on a quantity some other module compares against, write down
  the consumer's comparator and solve for reachability, not for range. Concretely: for a strict
  `x < L` the bound is `L > min(x)`, not `L >= min(x)`. Then state in the migration what the
  constraint forbids that was previously storable — an empty answer means the CHECK is
  redundant, and a surprising one means it is not the constraint you thought.
- Enforced in: `sql/344_core_mandate_trigger_reachability.sql` (both bounds strict, header
  derives reachability from the consumer's comparators);
  `app/services/strategy_core_mandate.py::validate_core_mandate`;
  `tests/test_2603_core_mandate.py::test_a_band_whose_trigger_can_never_fire_is_refused` plus
  `::test_the_narrowest_mandates_with_both_triggers_live_are_accepted`, which pins the
  tightening at exactly one `NUMERIC(8,4)` quantum so a later over-correction fails.

### "0 stored rows" does not excuse a version bump — a version denotes a RULE SET, not a row population

- First seen in: #2670, at Codex checkpoint 1, against a spec amendment that had argued the
  opposite at length.
- Symptom: tightening `strategy_core_mandate_events`' invariants over an empty table, I argued
  `CORE_MANDATE_POLICY_VERSION` need not move because no row was written under the old
  arithmetic, so nothing could be silently reinterpreted — and cited `sql/342`'s refusal to
  mint a vocabulary member nothing could produce as support. Both halves are wrong. `sql/342`
  declined a state nothing could *produce*; here every future mandate is produced under the new
  rules, so `v2` denotes a live rule set, not an empty one. And persistence is not the only
  carrier: `CoreMandate` is a public frozen dataclass and `validate_core_mandate` a public
  function, so a `v1` mandate can exist in a test, a cached input or a retried command without
  ever having been stored — and goes from valid to `core_mandate_invalid` across the change.
  One version string, two arithmetics, which is the exact silent reinterpretation the stamp
  exists to prevent.
- The general shape: **the question a version stamp answers is "under which rules was this
  object judged", and objects outnumber rows.** Reaching for the row count is reaching for the
  easiest measurement rather than the governing one, and it reads as evidence because it *is* a
  real number — it just answers a different question.
- Prevention: when a change alters what a validator accepts, bump the version regardless of row
  count, and justify any exception by naming every carrier of the old rules (stored rows,
  constructible objects, fixtures, cached requests) rather than by counting one of them. If the
  governing spec states the rule unconditionally, follow it — proposing a carve-out at the
  moment it first costs something is the weakest possible time to weaken a rule.
- Enforced in: `app/services/strategy_core_mandate.py` (`core-mandate-v2`, with the reasoning on
  the constant); `sql/344_core_mandate_trigger_reachability.sql` (re-issued `policy_version`
  CHECK + `COMMENT ON`); `tests/test_2603_core_mandate.py::test_the_policy_version_records_which_arithmetic_wrote_the_row`;
