  `tests/test_2603_core_mandate_db.py` parametrises a `v1` row as a rejected raw INSERT.

### An output whose EMPTINESS is a legitimate outcome cannot be aged — age the artefact that records the ATTEMPT

- First seen in: #2624 scope 3, whose own ticket text proposed the unbuildable version.
- Symptom: the ticket asked for an alert on *"current version has no **signal** newer than N
  days"*. Measured on dev: `s2-cross-sectional-momentum` has **zero** `strategy_signals` rows
  under any version, while carrying a current-version watermark at `2026-08-11` written the
  day before. It scans successfully and fires nothing — and the scan job's own docstring says
  so (*"`row_count` is signals WRITTEN, and zero is a legitimate success"*). A signal-aged
  check would have alerted on s2 permanently, with no input that could ever clear it: the
  exact false-positive class the ticket's own text ruled out, one table over from where it
  looked.
- The general shape: **a freshness check needs a record of the attempt, not of the result.**
  Results are allowed to be empty; attempts are not. Where a pipeline writes both — a
  watermark and a payload, a run row and its rows, a scan and its hits — the payload is a
  measure of what the world contained and only the attempt is a measure of whether the system
  ran. Ageing the payload conflates "nothing happened" with "nothing was found".
- Prevention: before ageing a table, ask what a **healthy empty** looks like in it. If a
  legitimate run can leave zero rows, that table cannot carry the freshness signal — find the
  one the run writes unconditionally. Test it with the real empty case, not a synthetic one:
  s2 exists and would have failed any check written against the ticket as stated.
- Enforced in: `app/services/strategy_scan_freshness.py` (keyed on
  `strategy_scan_watermark`, with the s2 measurement in the module docstring);
  `tests/test_2624_strategy_scan_freshness.py::test_a_strategy_that_emits_no_signals_is_still_healthy`.

### A conjunct on an existing health signal inherits that signal's SEMANTICS, not its name

- First seen in: #2624 scope 3, at Codex checkpoint 1.
- Symptom: the ticket's condition was *"… while prices are fresh"*, and the obvious build is
  `and check_layer_staleness(conn, "prices").status == "ok"`. Measured on a healthy system at
  2026-08-13 19:10 UTC: **that layer reads `stale`**. `_LAYER_QUERIES["prices"]` is
  `MAX(price_date)::timestamptz` — *midnight of the last trading date* — aged against a
  **4-hour** threshold, so it is stale from ~04:00 UTC every day and for every weekend. The
  conjunct would have suppressed the new check essentially always: a control that cannot fire,
  shipped green, with a plausible-sounding reason in its own docstring.
- The general shape: **a named health signal is a threshold over a specific column, and the
  name is a summary of the intent rather than of the semantics.** Reusing it as a term in a
  new predicate imports the column, the cast and the threshold — which were chosen for a
  different question. "prices are fresh" and "`prices` layer is ok" are not the same
  proposition and were never meant to be.
- Prevention: before ANDing an existing check into a new one, **evaluate it against live data
  and read its actual distribution**, not its name — one call. If it is not `ok` in normal
  operation, the conjunct is a suppressor. Then ask whether the guard is needed at all: here
  it was not, because measuring the lag in *trading days against `price_daily` itself* makes
  the check self-suppressing by construction — a corpus that stops advancing cannot grow the
  lag. **A structural suppression beats a conditional one, and removes the term rather than
  fixing it.**
- Enforced in: `app/services/strategy_scan_freshness.py` (module docstring records the
  measurement and the absence of the conjunct);
  `docs/proposals/ops/2026-08-13-strategy-scan-freshness.md`.

### An index is not automatically the fix for a seq scan — `Unique` over an index still walks every row of each distinct value

- First seen in: #2624 scope 3, Codex checkpoint 2 (which flagged the seq scan correctly and
  proposed the index).
- Symptom: `SELECT DISTINCT price_date … ORDER BY price_date DESC LIMIT 30` on a polled health
  endpoint seq-scanned all 6,755,721 `price_daily` rows (70,183 buffers, 279 ms). Adding the
  obvious `price_date` index turned it into `Limit -> Unique -> Index Scan Backward`, which
  **stops after the 30th distinct date and still reads every row of each of them** — ~3,400
  instruments per date: 93,734 buffers, 57 ms warm and 523 ms cold. It traded a cost that
  grows with the corpus for one that grows with rows-per-key, which is the same regression a
  season later. A loose index scan (recursive `max()` walk, one probe per distinct value) is
  130 buffers and 1.0 ms.
- The general shape: **an index changes how rows are FOUND, not how many are READ.** For a
  low-cardinality leading column, `DISTINCT`/`Unique` is O(rows), not O(distinct values),
  whichever access path serves it.
- Prevention: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` the remedy, not just the defect, and compare
  **buffers** rather than milliseconds — a warm cache hides the read volume that a cold one
  will not. When the query wants distinct values of a low-cardinality column, reach for the
  loose index scan; the counter in its recursive term is load-bearing, since an outer `LIMIT`
  cannot stop a recursive CTE.
- Enforced in: `sql/345_price_daily_price_date_index.sql` (header carries all three
  measurements and states that the index alone is insufficient);
  `app/services/strategy_scan_freshness.py::_RECENT_TRADING_DATES`.

### A `try/except` around a DB call contains the exception, not the transaction

- First seen in: #2624 scope 3 (Codex checkpoint 2, in new code), then #2674 (the same defect
  already shipped in `check_all_layers`, `_stalled_job_names`, `_jobs_process_down` and
  `_build_credential_health_summary`).
- Symptom: `check_all_layers`' docstring promised "the rest of the report still renders" and
  it did not. `get_conn` hands out a **non-autocommit** pooled connection, so a failed query
  leaves Postgres' transaction ABORTED; catching the Python exception does not clear that, and
  every later statement on the same connection raises `InFailedSqlTransaction`. Measured on
  dev: `caught: UndefinedTable` → `subsequent query RAISES: InFailedSqlTransaction`; the same
  failure inside `conn.transaction()` → `after savepoint: OK`. So ONE broken layer failed all
  eight — seven of them for a reason unrelated to their own health, which also hides which
  layer started it — and then took out `_build_credential_health_summary`, which runs outside
  the handler's 503 guard, turning a per-layer `error` row into an HTTP **500** on the page
  whose entire job is to stay readable when something is broken.
- The general shape: **containment on a transactional connection is `with conn.transaction():`
  (a savepoint), not `try/except`.** The bare catch reads as correct at the call site precisely
  because the damage lands on an unrelated later statement.
- Prevention: any `try/except` whose justification is "best-effort, must not fail the caller"
  around a DB call on a **caller-supplied** connection needs the savepoint. Grep the handler
  for every probe that shares one connection and check each — the fault propagates forward, so
  the LAST reader is where it surfaces and the FIRST is where it starts. ⚠ A test asserting the
  returned `error` row PASSES against the broken version (`check_all_layers`' pre-existing
  `test_single_layer_failure_does_not_abort_others` did); the post-condition that distinguishes
  contained from poisoned is a **subsequent statement on the same connection**.
- Enforced in: `app/services/ops_monitor.py::check_all_layers`;
  `app/api/system.py::_stalled_job_names` / `_jobs_process_down` /
  `_build_credential_health_summary`; `app/services/strategy_scan_freshness.py::check_scan_freshness`;
  `tests/test_2674_status_probe_containment.py`;
  `tests/test_ops_monitor.py::TestCheckAllLayers::test_a_failed_layer_leaves_the_connection_usable`.

### A CHECK constraint passes on NULL, so `col = 'x'` does not require `col = 'x'`

- First seen in: #2603 item 2 (`sql/346_core_eligibility_proofs.sql`), caught by the module's
  own DB test before review.
- Symptom: `CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (verdict <> 'underlying' OR (settlement_type = 'real' AND ...))`
  was written to refuse a row that *looks* like a pass and is not one — a stored eligibility
  proof asserting `underlying` while carrying no matched arm. It admitted exactly that row.
  Postgres CHECKs are satisfied unless the expression evaluates to **FALSE**, and
  `NULL = 'real'` is NULL, not FALSE. Two of the six parametrised cases
  (`settlement_type=None`, `direction=None`) went straight through the constraint whose entire
  purpose was to stop them.
- The general shape: **a completeness constraint on nullable columns must use NULL-safe
  comparison.** `settlement_type IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 'real'` returns FALSE on NULL and is the
  fix; `col IS NOT NULL AND col = 'x'` is equivalent and noisier. `col IS TRUE` is already
  NULL-safe (unlike a bare `col`), and `1 = ANY(arr)` needs an explicit `arr IS NOT NULL`
  conjunct for the same reason.
- ⚠ The trap is specific to the constraint direction that matters. On a `verdict <> 'x' OR
  (...)` shape the NULL leaks through the arm that is supposed to be strict, so the constraint
  keeps refusing every case you thought to test *except* the omission it exists to catch —
  which is the case a writer bug actually produces.
- Prevention: for any CHECK of the form "when this row claims X, these columns must be
  populated and equal to Y", parametrise a test over **each column set to NULL individually**,
  not just over wrong values. A wrong value is refused by plain equality; only the NULL case
  discriminates. If every column in the implication is `NOT NULL`, say so in a comment so the
  next reader does not have to re-derive that the trap does not apply.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/346_core_eligibility_proofs.sql`
  (`core_eligibility_underlying_is_complete`, with the reasoning inline);
  `tests/test_2603_core_eligibility_db.py::test_an_underlying_row_cannot_be_incomplete`
  (revert-probed: swapping `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` back to `=` turns the two NULL cases red).

### One enum explaining several nullable values is lossy the moment two of them can be null independently

- First seen in: #2623 gap 2 (2026-08-14, PR #2681), review bot on the first push.
- Symptom: a field named `rate_unavailable_reason` explained why *either* of two derived
  values was null. The bot found a reachable state it could not express — a version scanned
  over several days on which every bar was `not_evaluable` has a perfectly good date axis, so
  its weekly rate is a real `0.00`, while its share-of-evaluable is genuinely unknowable. The
  reason field read `None` (correct for the rate) and the null share shipped with nothing
  saying why, breaking the API's own stated "null is not zero, and the API says which"
  contract.
- Root cause: the two nulls have **independent causes**. One enum can only ever describe the
  value it was named after; the other borrows it and is silently wrong whenever they differ.
  Adding a third member to the single enum does not fix it — it mislabels the row as though
  the *rate* were the unavailable thing.
- The tell, and it is visible without running anything: **the reason field is named after ONE
  of the values it serves.** `rate_unavailable_reason` sitting beside both
  `fired_share_of_evaluable` and `entries_per_calendar_week` is the smell.
- Prevention: when one enum explains several nullable values, ask whether any two of them can
  be null **independently**. If they can, split the enum — one reason per nullable value — and
  assert the correspondence in **both** directions over a parametrised set of states: a value
  is `None` if and only if its reason is not. A test asserting only "this value is null here"
  passes while the reason is missing, which is exactly how the gap survived the first review.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/strategy_monitoring.py` (`share_unavailable_reason` /
  `weekly_rate_unavailable_reason`, with the independence argument on `derive_fire_rate`);
  `tests/test_strategy_fire_rate.py::TestEveryNullNamesItsReason`.

### Three positional lists that must agree, edited separately — the INSERT column list, its placeholders, and the reader's unpack tuple

- First seen in: #2623 gap 1 (2026-08-14). Adding three columns to `strategy_results_store`.
- Symptom: values landed in the **wrong columns**. `median_hold_days` was written into the
  DSR block, because the three column names were appended to `_RESULT_COLUMNS` after
  `trial_register_version` while the three placeholders were inserted after
  `%(bootstrap_model_id)s` — a different position in the same statement. Then the same
  mistake again, mirrored: the reader's unpack tuple got them at the END while
  `_RESULT_COLUMNS` (which is shared by the INSERT *and* the SELECT) had them in the middle,
  so the round trip reconstructed a metric set with no holding period.
- Why it is easy: nothing types these. The column list, the placeholder list and the unpack
  tuple are three separately-edited sequences whose only contract is positional, they are
  tens of lines apart, and both a name and a `%(name)s` read as self-describing at the point
  of edit. `psycopg` binds placeholders BY NAME, which makes it feel order-independent — the
  ORDER that matters is the one against the column list, not against the params dict.
- What caught it, and what did not: types and lint were clean. The write-side misalignment was
  caught by an unrelated pre-existing `CHECK` (`strategy_results_dsr_all_or_nothing`) firing
  on a row whose DSR block had been half-filled by the shifted values; the read-side one by a
  round-trip test. **A schema without all-or-nothing CHECKs would have stored the shifted row
  silently.**
- Prevention: after adding a column to a wide INSERT, **count the entries in the column list
  and the placeholder list and confirm the new names occupy the same ordinal in each**, then
  do the same against the reader's unpack. Where a constant is shared between the INSERT and a
  SELECT (`_RESULT_COLUMNS` is), the unpack tuple must match THAT constant, not read
  naturally. Always land a round-trip test — write then read then compare — for any new stored
  field; a write-only test passes on a misaligned read.
- Enforced in: this log; `app/services/result_ledger.py` (a comment on the unpack stating that
  its order is `_RESULT_COLUMNS`' and not a natural one);
  `tests/test_strategy_holdout_namespace.py`'s existing round-trip tests, which is what went
  red.

### A column shaped to the VALID domain cannot store the observation that was refused for leaving it

- First seen in: #2603 item 3 step 1 (2026-08-14), `sql/348_core_rebalance_intents.sql`.
  Twice in one diff, on two different column types — which is why this is filed as its own
  entry rather than as an instance of an overflow gotcha.
- Symptom: `strategy_core_rebalance_intents` stores one row per rebalance evaluation,
  **including refusals**, because a verdict is evidence. But `_state_refusal` refuses
  `sleeve_valuation_invalid` on a component that is non-finite or `>= 10^12`, and
  `sleeve_currency_mismatch` on a blank or over-long currency. Storing those observations
  into `NUMERIC(18,6) NOT NULL` and `TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (btrim(currency) <> '')`
  respectively makes the INSERT raise — so the evidence for an unrepresentable observation
  is exactly the row that cannot be written. #2437's standing pattern: *the control cannot
  express a state the system can reach.*
- Why it is easy, and why catching it once is not enough: the numeric case reads as an
  overflow bug and gets fixed as one. The **text** case is the same defect and does not look
  like it — a non-blank CHECK feels like hygiene, not like a domain restriction. The first
  draft here shaped the two valuation columns correctly for this exact reason and then wrote
  `currency TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (btrim(currency) <> '')` twenty lines later. The trigger is
  not "could this number overflow"; it is **"is this column shaped to the values I accept,
  on a table that also stores the ones I reject".**
- What caught it, and what did not: the numeric half was caught by writing the spec's
  refusal-storage section — i.e. by thinking about it in advance. The currency half survived
  that, survived self-review, survived `ruff`/`pyright`, and survived a 48-case constraint
  test suite that included `("blank_currency", {"currency": ""})` as a **rejection** case —
  the test asserted the CHECK worked, which it did; nobody asked whether the writer could
  reach it. Codex checkpoint 2 found it. **A constraint test that only asserts a bad value
  is refused cannot see that a legitimate writer path produces that value.**
- Prevention: for any table that stores refusals/rejections alongside accepted rows, list the
  refusal reason codes and, for each, ask which observed column the refusal is ABOUT. Every
  such column must be able to hold the value that triggered its own refusal — in practice
  nullable, with `NULL` meaning "no representation in this column's shape; the reason code
  says what was wrong" and an enforceable `NULL ⟹ refused` CHECK. Store observations
  **unnormalised**; normalising on the way in hides the difference the refusal was about.
  ⚠ Distinguish the writer's OWN fields (`recorded_by`, a policy version) — those stay
  `NOT NULL` and non-blank unconditionally, because a blank one is a bug in us rather than
  evidence about the caller.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/348_core_rebalance_intents.sql` (three nullable observation
  columns with the reason stated at each, plus
  `core_rebalance_intent_null_observation_implies_refused`);
  `app/services/strategy_core_rebalance_intent.py::_storable_or_none` and
  `_storable_currency_or_none`; `tests/test_2603_core_rebalance_intent_db.py`
  (`test_an_unstorable_valuation_is_recorded_rather_than_lost`,
  `test_a_nan_valuation_is_recorded_rather_than_raising`,
  `test_an_unstorable_currency_is_recorded_rather_than_lost` — all three drive the REAL
  writer, which is what the rejection-only cases could not do).

### `now()` in a DEFAULT is transaction start time, and a freshness CHECK against it rejects fresh data

- First seen in: #2603 item 3 step 1 (2026-08-14), `sql/348`, found by Codex checkpoint 2.
- Symptom: `evaluated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()` alongside
  `CHECK (state_as_of <= evaluated_at)`. A writer called inside a transaction that opened
  before the sleeve snapshot was taken stamps the evaluation at the **transaction's** start,
  which is earlier than the observation it just evaluated — so the constraint rejects a
  perfectly current snapshot for no reason but the caller's transaction boundary. The longer
  the enclosing unit of work, the wider the window.
- Why it is easy: `now()` reads as "the current time" and is the repo's habitual default. It
  is only wrong where the value is compared against something the caller measured *during*
  the same transaction — which is precisely what an as-of / observed-at column is.
- Prevention: when a `DEFAULT now()` column is compared in a CHECK against a caller-supplied
  timestamp, use `clock_timestamp()` (wall clock at insert) or `statement_timestamp()`.
  Keep it a DEFAULT and never a parameter regardless — a caller supplying its own stamp can
  backdate the record at will (`sql/346`'s rule). Test it by opening the transaction,
  `SELECT pg_sleep(...)`, and inserting a row whose as-of falls between `now()` and
  `clock_timestamp()`; assert `now() < clock_timestamp()` first so the test cannot go inert.
- Enforced in: this log; `sql/348_core_rebalance_intents.sql`;
  `tests/test_2603_core_rebalance_intent_db.py::test_a_snapshot_taken_after_the_transaction_opened_is_not_future_dated`.

### A "N/N CAUGHT" probe result is a measurement with a date, not a standing property — the anchor decays as the source moves (#2357, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2357 step 3 (2026-08-14). Re-running the seven phase-5a/4a revert-probe harnesses, the position-builder probe for "an unbookable hold left open forever instead of ending at its ceiling" reported `*** BAD ANCHOR ***`: `anchor occurs 0 times, expected exactly 1`. Its anchor was a verbatim copy of `open_until = ceiling if open_reason == "close_bar_unfillable" else None`. A later `series_break` arm turned that into a three-way conditional and the formatter split it across six lines, so the anchor stopped matching. The 5a claim of "28 revert probes, all CAUGHT" had been **27** for however long, and that invariant was unprobed.
- Why it is invisible: the uniqueness guard is correct and it fired the moment it was asked. Nothing asks. A probe script is not a test, CI does not collect it (by design — it mutates tracked source on disk), and the pre-push hook does not run it. So its output exists only on the day a human runs it, while the *claim* derived from that output is written into a PR description, a spec acceptance section or this log and read forever after as a property of the code.
- ⚠ The decay is one-directional and silent in the safe-looking direction. A stale anchor cannot make a probe report a false `CAUGHT` — the guard prevents that — but it removes the probe from the count without removing the sentence that cites the count.
- Prevention: never write "N/N CAUGHT" without the **SHA of the source file the probes mutate** beside it, and re-run before citing the figure again. When you touch a file that a `scripts/probe_*.py` names in its `SRC`, re-run that harness in the same PR — `grep -l "SRC = Path(\"app/services/<file>.py\")" scripts/probe_*.py` finds it in one call. Reformatting counts: an anchor is a verbatim source copy, so `ruff format` alone can break one. Prefer anchors on the smallest span that still identifies the rule (one arm of a conditional, not the whole expression) — they survive unrelated edits to the sibling arms and keep the mutation scoped to the invariant the probe names.
- Caught by: the harness's own BAD ANCHOR report, on a re-run that only happened because #2357 required one. No gate would have.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/probe_2240_position_builder.py` (re-anchored on the `close_bar_unfillable` arm, with the decay recorded inline).

### A cross-script import breaks the invocation the script's own docstring documents, and neither ruff nor pyright can see it (#2357, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2357 (2026-08-14). Seven probe harnesses gained `from scripts.probe_2240_cost_model import PYTEST_PASSED, PYTEST_TEST_FAILED` so the exit-code gate would live once. Lint, format and pyright were all clean. Every one of the seven then died at import with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scripts'` under the command its own docstring gives (`uv run python scripts/probe_2240_s3_mean_reversion.py`) — and under `docs/review-prevention-log.md:3073`, which names the s2 form as the reproduction for a merged finding.
- Cause: `python path/to/x.py` puts the **script's directory** on `sys.path[0]`; `python -m pkg.x` and `python -c` put the **CWD** there. So a repo-absolute import works under `-m` and fails under a path, and the two forms are not interchangeable however much they look it.
- Why no tool catches it: ruff and pyright resolve imports from the project root regardless of how the file would be invoked. They are answering a different question, and they answer it correctly. The only detector is running the documented command.
- Prevention: a script that imports `scripts.*` or `app.*` must either be documented as `-m scripts.<name>`, or carry `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))` above the import with `# noqa: E402` (`scripts/verify_2354_nonpositive_open.py:65`). Prefer the bootstrap: it is CWD-independent, leaves both forms working, and needs no edit to the docstrings or to any doc that already cites the path form. ⚠ The `sys.path.insert(0, ".")` variant also in the tree only works from the repo root. Whenever you add a cross-script import to an existing file, **run the docstring's own command once** — the import worked before precisely because there was nothing to resolve.
- Caught by: running the seven probes. Not by lint, format, pyright, or the review that approved the gate change.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; the seven `scripts/probe_2240_*.py` harnesses changed in #2357.

### A check reaches its subject differently from the way production does, and the difference is what it cannot see (#2695, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2695 (2026-08-14). `scripts/audit_probe_anchors.py` verifies every revert-probe anchor still matches its source exactly once. It reaches each harness through `importlib.import_module("scripts.<harness>")`, which requires — and therefore supplies — the repo root on `sys.path`. Four of the sixteen harnesses (`block_bootstrap`, `deflated_sharpe`, `result_model`, `statistics`) could not be started **at all** under the command their own docstrings print: `uv run python scripts/probe_2240_result_model.py` raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scripts'`. The audit reported all 27 of `result_model`'s anchors OK. 92 probes, structurally invisible to the thing auditing them.
- Cause: the audit and the operator do not reach the file the same way. `import_module` resolves from the root; `python path/to/x.py` puts `scripts/` on `sys.path[0]` and the root nowhere. Every claim the audit makes is true *of its own access path*, and it never says so.
- ⚠ It compounds the #2357 entry above rather than repeating it. #2357 fixed the seven harnesses it happened to touch; the remaining eight were never swept, and nothing could tell — a harness that cannot start fails LOUDLY, which is exactly why it survived: nobody had started it.
- ⚠⚠ The fix shipped proving nothing, twice over, and only a revert probe separated the two. `_launch_failure` first reproduced the path (`scripts/` first, root removed) but not the STATE: the sweep `import_module`s each harness before the check, caching `scripts.probe_2240_cost_model`, so the sibling import inside `runpy.run_path` was answered from `sys.modules` and never consulted `sys.path`. Deleting `result_model`'s `sys.path.insert` and re-running the audit still exited 0. **Manipulating `sys.path` without purging `sys.modules` is a half-emulation.**
- Prevention: when you write a checker, state the access path it uses and ask what that path SUPPLIES that the real caller does not — `sys.path`, an env var, a warm cache, an open transaction, a credential. Then reproduce the real one. And revert-probe the checker itself: inject the defect it exists to find and confirm it exits 1. A checker is code with no test above it, so "it reads correctly" is the only evidence it otherwise has, and that was true of both broken versions here.
- Caught by: revert-probing the check. Not by lint, pyright, review, or the audit's own clean run.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/audit_probe_anchors.py::_launch_failure` (path + `sys.modules` purge, with the two-stage failure recorded inline); the eight `scripts/probe_2240_*.py` harnesses that now carry the root bootstrap.

### zsh aborts a command whose glob matches nothing, so `rm -f <glob> && <the real work>` silently skips the work and reports success (#2695, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2695 (2026-08-14). A ~55-minute probe sweep was launched as `rm -f /tmp/probe_sweep_*.txt && for h in …; done; echo SWEEP DONE >> status`. It returned in under a second with **exit 0**. No harness ran.
- Cause: zsh's default `nomatch` makes an unmatched glob a hard error — `zsh: no matches found: /tmp/probe_sweep_*.txt` — and `-f` does not help, because `rm` is never reached. bash passes the pattern through, which is why the idiom looks safe. The `&&` then skipped the entire loop, and the trailing `;`-separated `echo` still wrote the file that made it look finished.
- ⚠ Same family as `cmd | tail` hiding the exit code, and the same direction of failure: the harness reports success for work that did not happen. Here it was worse than a pipe, because the artefact ("SWEEP DONE") was written by the surviving half.
- Prevention: never glob in a cleanup step that gates real work. Write to a fresh directory, or use `rm -f a.txt b.txt` with literal names, or separate with `;` so a cleanup failure cannot cancel the work. For any long background job, make the FIRST thing it writes a start marker with a timestamp, and check that marker exists before believing a fast exit — the absence of per-item output is the tell.
- Caught by: reading the status file, which held only the trailing line. The task notification said exit 0.
- Enforced in: this prevention log.

### `git add -A` while a probe sweep is running can commit INJECTED source (#2695, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2695 (2026-08-14), avoided rather than suffered. A revert-probe harness mutates the file it probes for the duration of one pytest run and restores it in a `finally`. A ~90-minute sweep therefore spends most of its wall clock with a tracked `app/services/*.py` holding a **deliberately broken** version of an invariant, and `git status` looks clean only in the gaps between probes.
- Why it is easy: the sweep is backgrounded precisely so other work can continue, and committing unrelated files is the most natural thing to do while waiting. `git add -A` does not know which of its paths the harness owns.
- ⚠ It is the mirror image of the existing "commit BEFORE revert-probing" entry, which covers losing your work to `git checkout --`. This one is the opposite direction: gaining someone else's injected defect. That direction is worse, because the restore in `finally` makes it invisible the moment the sweep ends — the diff is committed and the file on disk is correct.
- Prevention: while any `scripts/probe_*.py` is running, stage EXPLICIT paths only (`git add docs/... scripts/check_x.sh`), never `-A` and never `.`. Before any commit during a sweep, `pgrep -f probe_2240` and confirm the staged set contains no file a live harness names in its `SOURCES`/`SRC`. The same window makes `scripts/check_probe_anchors.sh` report false dead anchors, for the same reason.
- Caught by: noticing the hazard before staging. No gate exists for it.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/check_probe_anchors.sh` (the concurrency warning in its header).

### A predicate answers a different question than its name, and every field agrees (#2603, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2603 step 3a (2026-08-14), twice in one slice, at two levels.
  - **The data.** The core sleeve observer needs one instrument's net long **market value**. The obvious source is `BrokerAccountRiskSnapshot.instrument_investments`, whose `amount` is *committed capital* (`app/providers/broker.py:364-368`; derived at `app/providers/implementations/etoro_broker.py:1237-1279`). Feed cost basis to a weight computation and on a holding up 30% the core weight is understated — so the allocator computes a **buy** for an already-overweight sleeve, with every field internally consistent and no refusal reachable. The same figure also folds in copy-trader mirrors (`:1246-1257`) and pending orders (`:1261-1279`). Filed as #2704.
  - **The predicate.** A first draft of the in-flight rule classified each `strategy_trades.status` as "reflected in the broker snapshot" or not, and derived the blocking set from that. That is inference from lifecycle **names**, and it was wrong in both directions: `failed` is written both after a definitively rejected submission (`strategy_paper_executor.py:1272`) and on the resume path (`:998`); `open`/`closed` are local transitions carrying no claim about when a snapshot catches up.
- Cause: a field's name and its docstring describe the thing it *is*; a predicate needs the thing it *means for this decision*. Nothing malformed appears when the two diverge, so there is no defect for a review, a CHECK or a test to find — only a coherent answer to a question nobody asked.
- ⚠ It is the fail-mode complement of the #2437 R4 family. Those are controls that never run. This is a control that runs, passes, and computes the wrong quantity.
- Prevention: when a predicate needs **"has this happened yet"**, find the table whose PURPOSE is recording that, before deriving it from a vocabulary named for something else. Here `sql/285` already had it — the backlog index is `WHERE state NOT IN ('resolved','rejected')` and the `strategy_order_reconciliation_resolved_shape` CHECK ties exactly those two to a non-NULL `reconciled_at`. The sourced predicate is shorter than the inferred one. ⚠ Then BIND the constant to its source in a test rather than copying it (`test_the_reconciliation_terminal_set_matches_the_backlog_index_it_was_copied_from` parses the migration), because a constant and its source in two files with nothing between them is two constants. For a money figure, ask **cost or value** out loud before using it in a ratio — the two are equal exactly when the position is flat, which is the state every fixture is in.
- Caught by: reading the derivation, prompted by writing the spec's source-rule section. Not by any gate; the first version type-checked and passed every test.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_core_submission_gate.py` (`_RECONCILIATION_TERMINAL_STATES`, sourced with the reason inline); `tests/test_2603_core_submission_gate.py`; #2704.

### A `pg_locks` assertion without `objsubid` proves a coincidence, and a missing state row is not "not blocking" (#2603, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2603 step 3a (2026-08-14). The submission gate asserts its serialising advisory lock is held rather than documenting the precondition — a docstring precondition is the #2437 R4 pattern by construction. Two defects in the first version of that assertion, one found by reading and one by Codex checkpoint 2.
- **`objsubid` omitted.** Postgres records a two-`int4` advisory key as `classid`/`objid` with `objsubid = 2`, and a one-`int8` key as the high/low halves of the bigint with `objsubid = 1`. Matching on `classid`/`objid` alone lets an unrelated `pg_advisory_lock(bigint)` whose halves collide satisfy the check — the gate then confirms a critical section that is open somewhere else entirely. ⚠ Also: `classid`/`objid` are OID-width **unsigned** while `pg_advisory_lock(int, int)` takes signed `int4`, so a negative key component never compares equal to its literal and the assertion would fail permanently-closed. Both keys in use are positive; a future negative one breaks this silently.
- **A missing row read as a passing one.** The in-flight predicate blocked on `recon.state IS NOT NULL AND state <> ALL (terminal)`. Nothing in the schema requires a linked order to have a `strategy_order_reconciliation_state` row, so an order with none satisfied **neither** arm — not blocking by state (NULL), not blocking by absence (the order exists). That admits a second rebalance while the first order's broker effect is entirely unknown, which is the one outcome the predicate exists to prevent. Same family as "a CHECK passes on NULL", on the other side of the join.
- Prevention: state what a lock assertion actually proves and no more — `pg_locks` has no reference count, so the honest claim is *"this backend currently holds a matching lock"*, never that this call acquired it or that no reentrant acquisition is outstanding. For any `LEFT JOIN` to a state table, write the three cases explicitly (terminal / non-terminal / **absent**) and decide the third deliberately; a `WHERE state <> ...` alone silently answers "absent" as "fine". Revert-probe both: re-inject the old predicate and confirm exactly one test fails.
- Caught by: `objsubid` on reading the catalogue definition; the missing-row fail-open by `codex exec review --base origin/main` at checkpoint 2, after lint, format, pyright, the fast tier and 24 passing DB tests were all green.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_core_submission_gate.py` (`_lock_held`, and the in-flight LATERAL's three-case filter with the fail-open recorded inline); `tests/test_2603_core_submission_gate.py::test_the_lock_assertion_pins_the_two_int4_advisory_encoding`; `tests/test_2603_core_submission_gate_db.py::test_a_linked_order_with_no_reconciliation_row_blocks`.

### A "verification" that recomputes the proposed formula proves its arithmetic, not its meaning (#2704, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2704 (2026-08-14), caught by Codex checkpoint 1 on the spec. The spec had to establish that a broker payload's `amount + unrealizedPnL.pnL` is a position's **market value**. It argued by decomposition — eToro publishes `Equity = Available Cash + Total Invested + Unrealized PnL` and names `positions[i].amount` and `positions[i].unrealizedPnL.pnL` as the per-position terms, so one position's contribution to the identity is their sum — and then presented a live table showing that sum differs from `amount` by -27.42% to +26.66% across the account, headed "full-population verification".
- Cause: both halves are weaker than they read. **Restricting a documented aggregate to one of its terms does not establish what that term MEANS** — it is still a first-principles inference, and the "source rule" citation makes it look sourced. And the table computed the proposed formula, named the result "market value", and compared it to a *different* field: it can only ever confirm its own arithmetic. Neither step involves any quantity measured independently of the claim.
- ⚠ The tell is that the evidence cannot come out negative. If a table's every column is derived from the formula under test, no possible data falsifies it. A "verification" with no failing outcome is a restatement.
- Prevention: to settle what a source field MEANS, measure the same quantity with a path that has never read it. The repo's own technique is `scripts/verify_2598_preflight_quote_crosscheck.py`, which decided eToro's undocumented what-if `value` by dividing it by ticket size and landing the ratio on our separately observed quoted spread. Applied here: `(amount + pnL) / units` must land on `quotes.last` if it is a market value — measured **-0.00% on four of seven live positions**, the two residuals tracking 47- and 21-minute quote staleness — and `amount / units` must land on the independently reported `openRate` if `amount` is cost basis — **±0.005% on 7/7**. The clincher was structural rather than statistical: two lots of one instrument opened at 22.59 and 22.66 imply the *same* current price, 18.5000, which only a genuine per-unit mark does.
- ⚠ Also fix the label. "Full-population verification" of one demo account at one instant is the full population **of that account's rows**, not of accounts, products, directions or payload states. Name what the run could not see — here shorts (7/7 were `isBuy: true`) and pending orders (both arrays empty) — in the spec, next to the claim, not only in a session note.
- Caught by: `codex exec` checkpoint 1 on the spec ("Circular verification … identifies no independent market-value source"). No gate exists for it; the spec type-checked nothing and the implementation would have passed every test.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-14-core-sleeve-observer.md` ("Arm 1 — independent cross-check of the semantics", and the "Not settled by this run" section); `app/providers/broker.py::BrokerInstrumentInvestment`.

### "Does X exist" cannot be carried by a sum of X's values (#2704, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2704 (2026-08-14), caught by Codex checkpoint 1. The core sleeve is a long holding, so the observer must REFUSE when a direct short exists on the core instrument — folding a short in misstates the value and dropping it misstates it the other way. The first design carried `direct_short_market_value: Decimal` and would have refused on it being non-zero.
- Cause: the predicate is existential and the carrier is additive. `direct_short_market_value == 0` is ambiguous three ways — no short at all, two short lots whose contributions offset, or a single short sitting at `amount + pnL == 0` — and only the first is "no short". Every comparison a reviewer would reach for (`> 0`, `!= 0`, `< 0`) mishandles at least one of the others, and `> 0` specifically admits the *most distressed* shorts, whose contribution has gone negative.
- ⚠ Same shape one level down on the long side: a zero market value cannot distinguish "no direct holding" from "a holding wiped out to zero". On the live demo account **33 of 38 reported instruments had no direct position at all**, so that is the common case, not an edge one.
- ⚠ This is the #2623 family — *the control cannot express a state the system can reach* — arriving through a field's TYPE rather than through its logic. A `Decimal` domain includes a zero reachable by more than one route; a count's zero is reachable by exactly one.
- Prevention: when a refusal turns on **whether something exists**, carry a count (or the rows), never a monetary or otherwise-signed total. Test: can the carrier take its "absent" value while the thing is present? For any sum over signed terms the answer is yes. State the same question of any nullable/zero sentinel before using it as a presence flag.
- Caught by: `codex exec` checkpoint 1 on the spec. No test would have failed — the fixture that exposes it (two offsetting short lots) is one nobody writes unless they already know.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/providers/broker.py::BrokerInstrumentInvestment` (`direct_long_positions` / `direct_short_positions`, counts with the reason inline); `app/services/strategy_core_sleeve.py::observe_core_sleeve`; `tests/test_broker_provider.py::test_direct_long_lots_net_and_shorts_are_counted_not_valued` (a short summing to exactly zero); `tests/test_2704_core_sleeve_observer.py::test_a_short_is_refused_even_when_the_long_leg_looks_ordinary`.

### A gate's refusal is only transient if some PRODUCER covers the population it reads (#2603, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2603 step 3b-1 (2026-08-14), caught by Codex checkpoint 1 on the spec. The core submission preflight refuses `core_quote_missing` when the mandate's instrument has no `quotes` row. That reads as a transient state — the quote job runs hourly, so wait an hour. It is not. `quotes_refresh`'s scope is `held ∪ (tradable ∧ coverage_tier IN (1,2)) ∪ (tradable ∧ symbol ∈ BENCHMARK_SYMBOLS)`, and **the first core buy is by definition not yet held**. Measured on dev across six plausible core ETFs, three — `IVV`, `VTI`, `SPY.RTH` — are Tier 3, unheld and non-benchmark, so a mandate naming any of them would refuse **for ever**, with every field internally consistent and no error anywhere.
- Cause: the gate and the producer were designed against different populations, and nothing in either states the overlap. A consumer's "the row is missing" and a producer's "that instrument is out of scope" are the same fact viewed from two modules, and neither module names the other.
- ⚠ The failure mode is the expensive one: a **permanent refusal that looks transient**. An operator waits, retries, re-reads the gate's code — which is correct — and never looks at a scheduled job's `WHERE` clause. Distinct from a fail-open, and harder to notice than one, because nothing is wrong.
- Prevention: for any gate predicate of the form "row X exists", identify the PRODUCER of X and read its scope query before calling the refusal transient. Then either prove the gate's population is a subset of the producer's, or extend the producer in the SAME change — shipping the check without the arm ships a control that cannot pass. ⚠ Say which in the module: `core_quote_missing`'s comment names the scope arm as the thing to check if it is ever seen persistently. Self-review prompt: **"what makes this refusal go away, and who runs it?"** If the answer is a scheduled job, open that job's scope query.
- ⚠ A producer-scope change is a JOBS change: the daemon must be restarted onto the merged commit or the new arm never runs, and the symptom is identical to not having made the change.
- Caught by: `codex exec` checkpoint 1 on the spec, then confirmed by measurement against the dev DB (`1539 → 1540` with an enabled mandate naming `IVV`, back to `1539` when disabled — run inside a transaction and rolled back). No test would have failed: every test seeds its own quote.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/workers/scheduler.py` (`quotes_refresh`'s fourth scope arm, with the `IVV`/`VTI`/`SPY.RTH` measurement inline); `app/services/strategy_core_preflight.py` (`core_quote_missing`'s comment); `tests/test_2603_core_preflight_db.py::test_an_enabled_mandate_puts_its_core_instrument_in_the_quote_scope`.
- ⚠⚠ **RECURRED 2026-08-22 (#2833), as a CYCLE — and this is the variant to look for, because the first fix makes it invisible.** Arm 4 put the ADOPTED state's instrument in scope. Nothing put the EVALUATION state's instrument in scope, so the sleeve's own pass bar — a spread percentile over ~5 trading days of stored `quotes` — could not be measured until a mandate naming the candidate was already enabled. `select count(*) from quotes where instrument_id in (3417, 3434, 3075)` returned 0 for all three proved candidates. The only exit was adopting the sleeve before evaluating whether to adopt it, i.e. the exact shortcut the gate exists to prevent.
- ⚠ **Generalised prevention: extending a producer to cover the state a gate ADMITS is only half of it. Also ask what population the DECISION TO ENTER that state reads.** A gate answers "may I proceed"; a pass bar answers "should I", and the second is measured strictly earlier. A producer scoped to the first leaves the second unsatisfiable — and unlike the original bug this one does not look like a permanent refusal. It looks like a ticket that is merely *blocked on wall-clock*, so it gets parked and re-read rather than diagnosed. Self-review prompt, extending the original: **"what makes this refusal go away, who runs it — and is anything required to DECIDE to reach this state produced by the same job?"**
- ⚠ Don't gate candidate membership on the proof's freshness ceiling. `CORE_ELIGIBILITY_MAX_AGE` is 24h and governs *configuring* a mandate (an act that commits capital). Applying it to quote scope re-creates the cycle at a smaller radius: a five-day measurement whose subject drops out of scope on day two. Pinned by `tests/test_2603_core_preflight_db.py::test_a_stale_passing_proof_still_holds_a_candidate_in_the_quote_scope`.
- Enforced in (#2833): `app/workers/scheduler.py` (`QUOTES_REFRESH_SCOPE_SQL`, arm 5); `tests/test_2603_core_preflight_db.py` section 3.

### A threshold flag whose formula can go NEGATIVE fails open on the inverted case (#2603, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2603 step 3b-1 (2026-08-14), caught by Codex checkpoint 1. The preflight's first draft trusted `quotes.spread_flag` to mean "this quote is not tradable-quality". It cannot detect a **crossed** book. `compute_spread_pct` (`app/services/market_data.py`) is `(ask - bid) / mid * 100`, and the flag is set by `spread_pct > max_spread_pct` — so `bid > ask` yields a NEGATIVE spread, which cannot exceed a positive threshold, and the flag stays `FALSE`. The one quote shape that most clearly means "do not trade on this" is the one shape the wide-spread flag reports as fine.
- Cause: a one-sided comparison against a quantity whose domain is two-sided. The formula was written for the "too wide" direction and the flag's NAME records only that direction, so every later reader inherits "spread is checked" and stops.
- ⚠ Generalises past spreads: any `derived > threshold` flag where `derived` can go negative (or wrap, or be NULL) is silent on the inverted case. `spread_pct` is additionally nullable — `compute_spread_pct` returns `None` when `mid <= 0` — and `None > threshold` never fires either, so a zero-or-negative mid is also unflagged.
- Prevention: before consuming someone else's boolean flag as a safety property, read the FORMULA that sets it and ask what values of its inputs leave it `False`. Enumerate the inputs' full domain, not the expected range. Where the flag is one-sided, check the other side yourself at the point of use rather than widening the producer's flag — the producer's threshold has other consumers with other tolerances. ⚠ And validate BOTH sides of a two-sided quantity even when only one is consumed: corruption of the untraded side is evidence the whole quote is incoherent, and sizing off the other half is not safer for being arithmetically possible.
- Caught by: `codex exec` checkpoint 1 on the spec. No gate: the flag was being read exactly as documented, and every fixture had a healthy book.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_core_preflight.py` (`core_quote_crossed`, with the `spread_flag` derivation quoted inline, and both sides validated); `tests/test_2603_core_preflight.py::test_a_crossed_quote_refuses_even_though_spread_flag_is_false` and `::test_the_untraded_side_is_validated_too`.

### An inherited formula carries its DOMAIN, and the domain is the thing that goes stale (#2603, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2603 step 3b-2 item 1 (2026-08-14). The allocator spec's Q3 derived two cost corrections for a rebalance and stated its domain explicitly: *"the one cost shape the algebra covers — a fee deducted from cash, not embedded in the execution price"*. Step 3b-1's close-out then listed the follow-up as a one-line scope item — *"the order sizing re-solved against the cost actually quoted (`strategy_core_allocator.py:334-339` — a cash-deducted fee leaves a sell above `upper`)"* — and the domain caveat did not travel with it. #2598 had meanwhile decoded the cost we are actually quoted: `marketSpread`, which is **embedded in the execution price**, the one shape Q3 says it does not cover. Implementing the inherited line would have shipped a correction in the wrong direction: a cash fee makes a buy SMALLER and a sell LARGER, a price-embedded one makes **both larger**, by different multipliers.
- Cause: a derivation and its domain live in the same paragraph; a scope item quotes the derivation. Each hand-off is lossy in the same direction, because the formula is the actionable part and the domain is the hedge. Note the original author did nothing wrong — Q3 named its domain in bold and even named the implicit-equation risk.
- ⚠ This is step 3c ("an INHERITED root-cause is a premise too") pointed at a FORMULA rather than a root cause, and the tell is different: there is no discriminator to re-run, so nothing feels unverified. The question is not "is this true?" but **"is this still in domain?"**
- Prevention: before implementing an inherited formula, re-read the source it came from and check its stated domain against the CURRENT inputs — especially where another ticket has since measured those inputs. Cheap test: **if the formula's source names a precondition, the scope item that quotes the formula must quote the precondition too, or it is not a scope item, it is a trap.** Corollary for writing them: when a close-out defers an obligation, carry the *constraint* into the deferral, not just the task.
- Caught by: reading #2598's close-out while researching the sizing item, before writing code. No gate could have — the inherited line was internally coherent and pointed at real line numbers.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_core_sizing.py` (module docstring opens on the superseded derivation and why); `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-14-core-rebalance-cost-sizing.md` §"Why the inherited derivation does not apply".

### A per-row rounding quantum bounds PER ROW — one allowance for the whole response under-states it (#2603, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2603 step 3b-2 item 1 (2026-08-14), caught by Codex checkpoint 2. eToro rounds every what-if cost component to 0.01, so a component that rounds away is `< 0.01` — which the decoder used to bound an omitted row rather than coercing it to zero (the skill's "never coerce a missing key to zero"). The bug was applying **one** quantum to the summed response. Rounding happens per row, independently: three components each reported as `0` can each stand for a real cost just under 0.01, so the realised total approaches 0.03 while the bound reads 0.01. The fix is `0.01 × max(rows, |documented vocabulary|)` — the vocabulary count, not the row count, because an OMITTED component is exactly the one that rounded away and contributes no row to count.
- Cause: "the quantum" reads like a property of the response because it is quoted as one number in the source. It is a property of each *measurement*, and a sum of N measurements carries N of them.
- ⚠ Direction is everything here and it is worth stating separately: the value is consumed as an **upper bound**, and every downstream guarantee has the form `realised ≤ bound`. An over-statement costs a fractionally larger trade; an under-statement silently voids the guarantee. When a decoded figure is a bound rather than an estimate, every rounding, defaulting and absence rule must be checked for which way it leans, and the safe lean is not the accurate one.
- Prevention: when bounding a SUM of independently rounded/quantised figures, multiply the quantum by the number of terms — and count the terms the source COULD return, not the ones it did, whenever an absent term is itself a possible rounding outcome. Self-review prompt: **"is this quantum a property of the response, or of each row in it?"**
- Caught by: `codex exec review --base origin/main` (checkpoint 2). The same pass caught a sibling: `Decimal("9e999999").is_finite()` is `True`, so a finite-but-enormous provider value reached the addition and raised `decimal.Overflow` — which is **not** an `InvalidOperation`, so the promised refusal was escaped by a crash. `DecimalException` is the parent of both; catching the guessed subclass is how that gap opened.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_core_sizing.py::decode_quoted_trade_cost` (`_DOCUMENTED_COST_COMPONENTS`, and `except DecimalException`); `tests/test_2603_core_sizing.py::test_rounding_slack_is_PER_COMPONENT_not_per_response` and `::test_a_huge_but_finite_component_refuses_instead_of_raising`.

### One arm of a two-arm endpoint is not evidence about the other (#2712, 2026-08-14)

- First seen in: #2712 (2026-08-14). #2598 decoded eToro's what-if cost response over a 60-instrument census and wrote the result up as *the* cost contract — components returned, monetary unit, the `marketSpread ≈ full quoted spread` identity, the rounding quantum. Every one of those observations came from `action: "open"`, because `EtoroBrokerProvider.get_what_if_costs` hardcodes it and nobody noticed the field was an enum. The close arm turns out to exist, and its number is different: over every held demo position (5 instruments, both arms decodable on all 5, same $1,000 ticket seconds apart) the close was **dearer on 4 of the 5 — 5.7x, 8.5x, 13.0x, 18.5x — and cheaper on the fifth at 0.5x**. The open arm reproduced our separately observed spread at ~1.0x on all five; the close arm tracked it not at all, and returned two components where the open returns three.
- Cause: a hardcoded request field makes a *choice* look like a *property of the endpoint*. Every subsequent measurement inherits the choice silently, and the write-up describes "the endpoint" while measuring one arm of it. Nothing in the data can reveal the omission, because the omitted arm was never requested.
- ⚠ The near-miss is the substitution: #2603's sizing spec needed a close-side bound, had none, and considered using the open-arm quote. It declined on the grounds that *"an open cannot cost more than a close at the same notional" is plausible and unmeasured*. That reasoning was correct and the measurement now shows it would have under-stated the bound by up to **18.5x** — in the one direction a cost bound cannot be wrong in. **"Plausible and unmeasured" was worth more than it felt like at the time.**
- Prevention: when a request builder hardcodes a field the API documents as an **enum**, treat every finding derived through it as scoped to that value, and say so in the write-up ("measured on `action: open`"). Before reusing a decoded contract for a new direction/side/mode, ask **"which arm was this measured on, and was that a measurement or a default?"** — then measure the new arm rather than arguing about whether it should differ. ⚠ Corollary for bounds specifically: a substitution that is plausible-but-unmeasured is not a conservative fallback, because plausibility says nothing about which SIDE of the true value it lands on.
- ⚠ Also: the portal documented `positionIds` as *"For `close` action; currently rejected"*. It is **required** and it works — 400 without it, 200 with. A doc field-note can be stale in the direction that hides a whole capability, so the skill's protocol step 5 ("verify empirically on demo") applies to a field's *note*, not only to its presence.
- Caught by: a probe, not a gate — `scripts/probe_2712_close_side_cost_quote.py --all-held`, with `action: open` as a control arm so a run of refusals could not be misread as "the close arm does not exist".
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `.claude/skills/data-sources/etoro-api.md` (the close-arm section, with the per-instrument table and the "does NOT bound" rule); `app/providers/broker.py::BrokerWhatIfOrder` (`action` / `position_ids`, validated both directions); `tests/test_broker_provider.py::test_what_if_costs_sends_the_CLOSE_arm_with_its_position_ids` and siblings; `app/services/strategy_core_sizing.py` (module docstring, corrected).

### A "standing" refusal set diverges silently from the constants that stamp the rows (#2721, 2026-08-15)

- First seen in: #2721 step 3 (2026-08-15), caught by the rolled-back survivorship-free smoke run's own preflight cross-check — not by any reviewer or unit test. `STANDING_REFUSALS` still listed `carry_unmodelled` and `fx_unmodelled` as refusals "no invocation can close", but #2720 had closed both STRUCTURALLY the day before (`CARRY_UNMODELLED = FX_UNMODELLED = False` under cost model v3). `build_result` stamps rows from those constants and `check_promotable` re-derives refusals from the stamps, so the ACTUAL refusal list dropped both members while `_expected_refusals` still predicted them — every post-#2720 backtest invocation would have failed its preflight cross-check before the first INSERT. Nothing noticed for a day because no run happened in the gap.
- Cause: a "standing" set is a cached claim about OTHER modules' constants. The modules moved; the cache did not; no test tied the two together, because the pin test asserted the cached set's own contents — a tautology against drift in what it summarises.
- Prevention: a refusal (or any gate verdict) that is a function of a module constant must be PREDICTED from that same constant, never enumerated in a second place. A standing set may contain only members that are standing by construction (e.g. `promotion_evidence_missing` — true of every fresh row whatever the invocation does). Self-review prompt when closing any refusal structurally: **"grep every place that refusal's name appears and ask which of them is a cache of the state you just changed."**
- Caught by: `scripts/verify_2721_survivorship_universe.py --smoke-run` — the write-phase preflight (`_expected_refusals` vs `check_promotable`, the deliberate criterion-8 duplication) doing exactly what it was built for. The duplication is the detector; do not "fix" it by sharing a helper.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/backtest_run.py::STANDING_REFUSALS` (docstring ledger of the three departures) and `_expected_refusals` (carry/fx predicted from `CARRY_UNMODELLED`/`FX_UNMODELLED`); `tests/test_backtest_run.py::test_carry_and_fx_are_predicted_from_the_stamping_constants`.
## Negating a closing keyword does not stop GitHub closing the issue (#2741, 2026-08-15)

- Incident: PR #2740 correctly described a partial #2493 census, but its body said `does not close #2493`. GitHub ignores natural-language negation and treated `close #2493` as a closing reference, so merging the PR falsely closed the unfinished issue.
- Prevention: partial work must use only `Refs #N`, `Part of #N`, or `Umbrella #N`. Never put a closing keyword immediately before an issue number while explaining that work is incomplete. `scripts/check_pr_issue_link.sh` now rejects negated closing-keyword prose before the PR can merge. Its regression tests pin the exact incident and require the negation guard to cover every separator accepted by the positive closing-reference parser, including colon forms.

### A mutation probe proves nothing about the branch its selector's fixture never enters (#2772, 2026-08-19)

- First seen in: #2772 (2026-08-19). The compiled/reference split gave `equity_curve` up to three copies of one rule — `build_equity_curve` dispatches on the STORAGE type (`SharedMarkLegBook` → the `@njit` kernel, `LegBook` → the Python walk), and the Python walk splits again on `all_realised`. `scripts/probe_2240_statistics.py` kept mutating the KERNEL's cash cap and sell-side charge while both selectors built a `LegBook`, so the defect was injected perfectly into code the test never executed. The harness printed `*** NOT CAUGHT ***` — for two real, correctly-injected defects — and five sibling anchors printed `*** BAD ANCHOR ***` because the text had moved. Measured: 2 NOT CAUGHT + 5 BAD ANCHOR out of 12 curve probes, i.e. **58% of the equity-curve harness was proving nothing** while the PR reported "31/31 caught".
- Cause: an anchor is checked for existing exactly once, and a selector is checked for naming at least one test. Neither check ties the two together, so a dispatch split — which moves no anchor and renames no test — voids a probe silently. The harness's own criterion 3 already says the selector is unguarded; what was new is that the selector did not have to change to become wrong.
- ⚠ The two verdicts differ in cost. `BAD ANCHOR` is loud and self-announcing. `NOT CAUGHT` reads as "the codebase has a coverage gap", so the triage order is selector → fixture → code — and a reader who skips to "code" concludes the guard is missing rather than unreached.
- Prevention: when a function grows a second implementation of the same rule (a compiled kernel, a fast path, a storage-shaped branch), every probe over that rule needs **one probe per copy, each with a selector whose fixture provably enters that copy**. Cheapest kill for the duplicate is a differential test — build one adversarial book in both representations and assert byte-exact equality of every field — so any single-copy mutation breaks equality; then point every copy's probe at it. ⚠ The fixture must make each rule LOAD-BEARING: a basket-denominator mutation is invisible unless two legs open on one date, and the probe would report `NOT CAUGHT` for a defect that is really there. Self-review prompt on any dispatch split: **"which book shape does this probe's selector build, and which branch does that reach?"**
- ⚠ `@njit(cache=True)` does not defeat the harness: numba re-keys its on-disk cache on the source file, so rewriting the file recompiles. Verified by the compiled probes reporting `CAUGHT`, which is unreachable if the pre-mutation kernel had been served.
- Caught by: running the harness and reading its output, not by any gate. Ruff, Pyright and the whole fast tier are green on a probe file whose anchors match nothing.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/probe_2240_statistics.py` (module docstring's "THREE IMPLEMENTATIONS" section, and one probe per copy of the cash cap, spread charge, exit/entry order, same-bar split, halted-mark carry and basket denominator); `tests/test_equity_curve.py::TestCompiledSharedWalkEquivalence::test_the_compiled_walk_is_EXACTLY_the_reference_on_an_adversarial_book` and `::TestUnrealisedWalkOrdering::test_an_unrealised_book_keeps_the_exit_split_the_same_bar_split_and_the_halt`.

### A lifetime high-water mark cannot measure a delta — differencing it reads zero (#2775, 2026-08-19)

- First seen in: #2772 / PR #2773 (2026-08-19), caught by `codex exec review` standing in for a review bot that cannot run on a stacked base. The synthetic-control scale gate sized each spawned worker's memory as `member_private_peak = max(pilot_peak_rss - pilot_baseline_rss, 0)`, with `_peak_rss_bytes()` returning `resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss`. That is the process **lifetime** maximum and is monotonic, so the difference answers *"how much did this pilot push the record up"*, not *"what does a member cost"* — and it is **zero** as soon as the process has already been that large. `run_cohort` is called once per ambiguity x quarantine arm against one shared budget (`app/services/backtest_run.py:2033`), so from the second cohort of an invocation onward the per-worker term collapsed and all eight workers were budgeted at the flat 128 MiB base, whatever the member book actually cost. The same collapse hits the *first* cohort in the long-lived jobs daemon, which peaks higher for other jobs.
- Cause: `ru_maxrss` is the only portable memory reading in the stdlib, so it gets used as though it were current usage. Nothing in its name or type says "monotonic", and a subtraction of two readings looks exactly like an interval measurement. The bug is invisible in a fresh short-lived process, which is where such code is written and tested.
- ⚠ The failure direction is the dangerous one: the gate fails **OPEN**, and reports "admitted" with every logged field internally consistent. Contrast the time arm of the same gate, which is correct because `time.monotonic()` differences ARE intervals — the two lines sit next to each other and only one of them is a measurement.
- ⚠ A numeric test cannot see this on a small fixture: the child's unique footprint there is its own interpreter, which is below the floor, so the correct and the collapsed projection land on the same number. The guard has to be STRUCTURAL — assert that a fresh child is consulted at all, and on every cohort rather than only the first.
- Prevention: before differencing any resource reading, establish whether it is a **gauge** (current value, can fall) or a **high-water mark** (monotonic). Only a gauge supports `after - before`. For a per-process figure that a parent cannot observe about its children, measure it **in a freshly spawned child**, whose own mark starts clean — and subtract the shared pages it touched, or unique memory is over-counted once per worker. Self-review prompt: **"if I called this twice in a row, would the second call return zero?"**
- Caught by: `codex exec review --base origin/fix/2697-metric-axis-integrity`, then confirmed by reading `_peak_rss_bytes` and counting `run_cohort` call sites. No test failed and no gate fired; the projection is only consumed by a refusal that did not trigger.
- ⚠⚠ THE FIRST REPAIR FIXED ONE OF TWO COPIES. The projection was written twice — in `_run_members` and in `run_launch_pilot` — and the first fix touched only the former, leaving the function that PRODUCED the published 89.9m/16.4m/4.39 GB pilot figures still differencing lifetime marks. That is the #2772 lesson (one probe per copy of a rule) recommitted within the hour, by the same session that had just written it up. The durable fix is not vigilance: both call sites now go through one `_project_unique_memory_bytes`, so there is one copy to be wrong.
- ⚠⚠ A SECOND, INDEPENDENT UNDER-COUNT in the same projection, caught by the re-review: `_shared_member_inputs` concatenates the per-series arrays into four contiguous temporaries AND allocates equally sized `SharedMemory` blocks to copy them into, keeping the temporaries referenced for the pool's whole lifetime. The parent therefore pays about **twice** `shared_input_bytes` on top of the placements it already holds, and the projection added it once. Near the ceiling that is the difference between admitting and refusing. Fixed by ORDER rather than by a coefficient: read `ru_maxrss` AFTER the child probe has built and released those blocks, so the real cost is measured and there is no multiplier to get wrong. **When a projection needs a coefficient on a cost you could instead arrange to have already paid, arrange to have paid it.**
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/synthetic_control_run.py::_measure_child_member_peak` (the docstring carries the mechanism) and `SYNTHETIC_CONTROL_WORKER_BASE_RSS_BYTES` (now a floor, with a note that it had silently become the whole estimate); `tests/test_synthetic_control_run.py::TestScaleGate::test_the_memory_projection_measures_a_FRESH_CHILD_ON_EVERY_COHORT`; `scripts/probe_2601_synthetic_control.py` (the eighth probe kills a revert to the flat base, the ninth a parent peak read before the shared blocks exist).

### A verification harness can become a tautology through a change to the code it tests, with nobody touching the harness (#2780, 2026-08-20)

- First seen in: #2780 (2026-08-20). `scripts/verify_2437_level_scan.py --equivalence` proved the `LevelScan` hoist by comparing `scan.at(...)` with `levels_at(...)` over real series — 319,668 comparisons, exit non-zero on a single mismatch. That was a real check when written. It is not one now: #2437's own hoist made `levels_at` build a `LevelScan` and call `at`, and the module docstring recorded the collapse approvingly — *"there is exactly one code path and no oracle to keep in agreement"*. From that commit on, both sides of the comparison were the same function. #2780 then rewrote `at` to filter clusters before materialising them, and the arm would have reported 0 mismatches over any rewrite whatsoever, including a wrong one.
- Cause: the harness was never edited, so nothing drew attention to it, and no gate can see it — the comparison still runs, still touches real data, and still prints a large number of successful comparisons. The tell is not in the harness but in the *other* file: a refactor that removes a second implementation silently removes an oracle, and the two facts are usually written up as the same sentence ("one code path now") without the second half being followed through.
- ⚠ This is a distinct member of the family the log already carries. "A reference that IMPORTS the constant it validates" (#2240 phase 5c) and "the thing under test was constructed from the constant" (#2772) are both authored tautologies — someone wrote the coupling. "A probe whose selector's fixture never enters the branch" (#2772) is a mis-aimed probe. This one is **an oracle that was deleted by an unrelated, correct refactor**, and the harness that depended on it kept passing.
- Prevention: when a refactor collapses two implementations into one, grep for every harness that compares them and decide explicitly — either the harness gets a transcribed reference, or it is deleted as spent. Do not leave it running. Self-review prompt when unifying code paths: **"what was comparing these two, and does it still have two things to compare?"** ⚠ The transcribed reference must not be built on the code under test either: `_reference_at` is built on `_cluster`, which `at` no longer calls and which the unit suite pins bit-for-bit against hand-written arithmetic over 1,500 randomised cases — so the chain terminates in something a human wrote out.
- ⚠ Second, independent trap in the same change: **a fixture in which a filter never fires leaves that filter unverified**, and it passes. `at`'s two filters (`MIN_TOUCHES`, `MAX_TOUCH_AGE_BARS`) were hoisted into the vectorised pass; the first fixture built for them produced 0 stale clusters at every bar, so half the hoist was "proved" by a comparison that never exercised it. This is the mirror of the existing "a fixture that refuses everything proves nothing" rule — there the fixture admits nothing, here it rejects nothing, and both read as green. Fixed by probing for parameters rather than guessing: n=900, no drift, atr=1.5 yields built 10,758 / thin 8,330 / stale 1,217 / survive 1,211. **Any test of a filter must assert a non-zero count on BOTH sides of it.**
- ⚠ The same pass falsified the performance premise it was handed. The prior session's note put psycopg `wait` at 13% and named the duplicate per-series quarantine loads as the next target; on the s5 profile that its own verification command uses, `wait` is 6.63s of 128.8s (5.1%) across all 273 queries and `load_arms` is 3.62s (2.8%), so fusing the passes recovers ~1.4%. The measured target was `price_levels.at` at **78.9% cumulative**, discarding 94.1% of the clusters it built (30,756,116 reached `len`/`max`, 1,822,327 survived). **An inherited "next task" carries the author's confidence but not their measurement — re-profile before building on it** (the working-order 3c rule, applied to a performance handoff rather than a root-cause one).
- Caught by: writing the new oracle and noticing the old arm could not fail, not by any gate. Ruff, Pyright and the full fast tier are green on a harness that compares a function with itself.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/verify_2437_level_scan.py::_reference_at` (the docstring carries the mechanism) and its `--equivalence` arm, which now also exits non-zero when no level survived anywhere or when either filter never rejected anything; `app/services/price_levels.py::LevelScan` (the docstring's "THERE ARE NOW TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS AND THAT IS THE POINT" section, replacing the "no oracle to keep in agreement" claim that licensed the collapse); `tests/test_price_level_scan.py::TestAtFiltersBeforeMaterialisingWithoutMovingAVerdict` (`_reference_at` plus `test_both_filters_actually_reject_something_in_the_fixture`).
### Three merge-path mechanisms all key off a PR's BASE, and all three fail silently on a stacked PR (#2783, 2026-08-20)

- First seen in: merging PR #2782 (2026-08-20), which was based on `fix/2697-metric-axis-integrity` rather than `main`. Discovered only because `gh pr merge` was blocked locally and the investigation went looking for the sanctioned path.
- The root is one fact with three consequences. `pull_request: branches: [main]` filters on the PR's **BASE**, not its head. So: (1) the review workflow never runs, and `gh pr checks` reports *"no checks reported"* — which reads identically to "not finished yet"; (2) `.autonomy/config.yaml`'s `merge_gate.strategy: bot_comment` waits for a `github-actions` comment carrying `"Claude Code Review"`, so `safe_merge.sh` reaches `REFUSE -- no review comment from github-actions on #N yet` and stays there **forever**, because the comment it waits on cannot ever exist; (3) GitHub registers `closingIssuesReferences` only for PRs targeting the **default** branch, so a `Closes #N` line is inert and `done_everywhere` — which correctly reads that array rather than a prose regex (#301) — closes nothing and boards nothing.
- ⚠ **The practice had already silently diverged from the tooling.** `#2773`, `#2776`, `#2777` and `#2782` all merged into that same base and **every one was merged by hand**, bypassing `safe_merge.sh`. Nobody recorded that the gate was skipped, so the gate's existence kept implying a guarantee that no stacked PR had actually received. A tool that is always bypassed for a whole class of change is not a gate for that class; it is a belief about one.
- ⚠⚠ Facet 3 is the exact MIRROR of #2741 and the pair is the lesson. There, prose negation (*"does not close #2493"*) closed an issue that had to stay open. Here, a well-formed `Closes #2779` left an issue open that had to close. **Both directions are invisible from the PR body**, and `scripts/check_pr_issue_link.sh` passes in both — it validates the body's grammar, which was never the variable. The variable is the base branch.
- Prevention: **before trusting any merge-path automation, ask what it keys off and whether this PR's base satisfies it.** Concretely, on any PR whose base is not the repo default: expect no bot and no CI *by construction*, treat that as a TERMINAL state rather than a pending one, substitute `codex exec review --base <the actual base>` plus the local pre-push gate, and close the `Closes #N` issues BY HAND after merging. ⚠ `.claude/CLAUDE.md` already says *"Know which one the project's tooling does"* about absent review — this entry is the answer for the stacked-base case, which previously had none.
- ⚠ Also learned at the same chokepoint, from `safe_merge.sh`'s own comment (#72): do **not** use `gh pr merge --delete-branch` in this repo. It runs a post-merge local `git checkout <base>`, which git refuses under a sibling-worktree topology (`fatal: '<base>' is already used by worktree`) — the merge lands, a confusing error prints, and cleanup is skipped. Merge, then detach and delete the ref explicitly.
- Caught by: reading `safe_merge.sh` and `.autonomy/config.yaml` after a blocked merge, then checking `mergedBy` on the three prior PRs into the same base. No gate reported anything — facets 1 and 3 are silent by construction, and facet 2 only speaks if someone runs the tool.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; issue #2783 (the three fix directions and their acceptance).

## A "fail closed" gate is only conservative if it tests the hazard it names — ours tested "is anything stranded", not "does anything move" (#2230, 2026-08-20)

- First seen in: #2230 residual (`_reconcile_insider_control_groups`, deemed-chain tier). The tier fails closed when folding a non-rep member would release that member's other-channel rows into a different pie wedge. It asked `_releases_other_rows` — *does this identity hold any row outside the cluster?* — but the hazard the inline comment describes requires the stranding to change what `_reconcile_owner_once` DECIDES about the identity. That function branches on `present & _INSIDER_SOURCES`: a Section-16 person is classified `insiders` at the MAX of its beneficial restatements and its 13F stays a `dropped_source` (#1640). So a member that strands a `form4` / `form3` / `def14a` row is still a Section-16 person after the fold — same wedge, 13F still suppressed, nothing released. The two propositions differ on exactly the commonest case.
- Symptom: the residual was carried across **three** session summaries as *"gated on revisiting #1652's exact-value-only consumption rule, which is a bigger decision than this ticket"*, and no one measured what the gate refused. Full population (3,108 instruments, `scripts/audit_2230_release_hazard.py` sharded 3 ways): **28** deemed-chain clusters admitted, **21** refused by the release gate, and the refused clusters' stranded rows are `form4` 43 · `form3` 3 · `def14a` 1 · `13d` 4 · `13g` 1 · `13f` **1**. Of the 21 refusals, **18** have no genuinely-releasing member at all. The dominant shape is a venture chain (`ESTC`, `RYTM`, `COUR` — NEA managing members) where each deemed owner also holds a personal Form 4 stake, so its identity keeps its Section-16 classification and the fold is free. The gate that "reversing #1652" was being priced for governed **3** clusters, not 21.
- ⚠ The wider predicate is not merely cautious — a fail-closed gate that fires on a non-hazard is a **silent false refusal**, and it looks identical to a correct refusal from every angle: nothing errors, no count looks odd, the conservative direction is preserved, and the residual double-count it leaves is attributed to the hazard rather than to the gate.
