- Prevention: **when a gate is described as failing closed, write down the mechanism it prevents and check that the predicate tests THAT mechanism, not a proxy for it.** The test is mechanical: name the downstream function whose decision would change, read its branch condition, and confirm the predicate implies that branch flips. Here the branch is one line (`if present & _INSIDER_SOURCES:`) and reading it collapsed a "bigger decision" into a two-line predicate. ⚠ The same self-review question the repo already asks about INFERENCE gates — *"what evidence is this gate standing in for?"* (#2385/#2386) — applies verbatim to SAFETY gates: *what hazard is this gate standing in for, and can it actually occur here?*
- ⚠ Second, narrower lesson: `_INSIDER_SOURCES` (`form4`/`form3`/`def14a`) and `_INSIDER_GROUP_SOURCES` (`form4`/`form3`) are NOT interchangeable, and the one that governs a read-path branch is whichever set the CONSUMER uses. Using the group set in `_releases_into_another_wedge` would silently keep refusing every `def14a`-stranded member; the test that sees it is the `def14a` case alone (probe 8).
- ⚠ Third: instrumenting this needed care about WHICH call site. `_releases_other_rows` has two callers — the fold gate and `_select_control_group_rep` clause 4 — and the first census recorded both, reporting 3 clusters of which 0 were gate-admitted and 3/3 carried a rep from outside their own cluster. That inconsistency is what exposed it; the fix is a re-entrancy flag around the rep selector. Generalises the #2386 lesson (*a census wrapped on the collapser is blind to refusals*) one layer down: **a shared predicate is a bad instrumentation point unless the harness can tell its callers apart.**
- Caught by: writing the census before writing the fix, then reading `_reconcile_owner_once`'s docstring instead of reasoning about what the fold "should" do. ⚠ That docstring also *refuted* the first hypothesis this session formed — that the released 13F row was a correction rather than a regression. It is a regression: 13F is managed/economic exposure, a different concept, and #1640 settled that it never inflates an insider's stake.
- Enforced in: `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_releases_into_another_wedge` (+ the gate comment in `_reconcile_insider_control_groups`); `scripts/audit_2230_release_hazard.py`; `tests/test_insider_deemed_chain_collapse.py` (the "Release hazard" block, 12/12 revert-probed); follow-up #2785 for clause 4, which still uses the wide predicate deliberately.

## ⚠ PENDING SKILL EDIT — `data-engineer/SKILL.md` has no invariant for the Section-16 control-group collapse (#2230, 2026-08-20)

- The I-series covers the institutional family (I16), the 13D/G group (I17) and the DEF 14A demotion (I21), but **nothing states the Rule 16a-1(a)(2) control-group rule** that `_reconcile_insider_control_groups` implements — the one pass in the ownership rollup with two admission routes and a fail-closed release gate. A reader of the skill would not know the pass exists.
- Writes to `.claude/skills/**` were **DENIED on this worktree again** — fifth recorded occurrence, tracked as #2403. Apply on a session that has permission. The edit is one new table row after I21:

> | I24 | A Section-16 **control group** (Rule 16a-1(a)(2) — a fund/trust plus the GPs and managing members deemed to own its block) is ONE owner in the insiders wedge, counted once at the block value. Two independent admission routes, and the difference matters: **value proxies** (#1652) infer membership from an exact non-round block ≥1M across ≥2 distinct CIKs; the **deemed chain** (#2230) READS it off the structured Form 3/4 fields — ≥3 distinct CIKs, every member flagged 10% Owner, and the ownership-form shape (≤1 `direct`, ≥2 `indirect`) — so the magnitude floor and roundness guard do not apply to it, because they exist only to substitute for the evidence it supplies directly. ⚠ `ownership_nature` is OVERLOADED (four writers, three meanings; sec-edgar §2.3), so any branch on it must also check `Holder.nature_from_table_i` (#2385/#2386). ⚠⚠ **The fold's release gate tests `_releases_into_another_wedge`, NOT "are any rows stranded".** Demoting a member only releases something if it changes what `_reconcile_owner_once` decides — that function branches on `present & _INSIDER_SOURCES` (`form4`/`form3`/`def14a`, NOT the narrower `_INSIDER_GROUP_SOURCES`), so a member retaining any insider-source row outside the cluster stays a Section-16 person and its 13F stays a `dropped_source` (I14/#1640). Only a member left with 13F/13D/13G alone can change wedge; that case still fails closed. Consumption is exact-value-only (#1652), so a member's larger genuine 13D block survives for I17. Re-measure with `PYTHONPATH=. uv run python -m scripts.audit_2230_release_hazard --out /tmp/a.jsonl` rather than quoting a remembered count. | `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_reconcile_insider_control_groups` + `_is_deemed_chain` + `_select_control_group_rep` + `_releases_into_another_wedge`; `scripts/audit_2230_release_hazard.py`; `tests/test_insider_deemed_chain_collapse.py`; prevention-log "A 'fail closed' gate is only conservative if it tests the hazard it names"; open #2785 (clause 4 still uses the wide predicate) |


## A gate's narrowing does not transfer to a sibling gate just because the ARGUMENT does — a fold removes, a swap re-parents (#2785, 2026-08-20)

- #2230 narrowed the deemed-chain FOLD gate from `_releases_other_rows` ("does this identity hold any row outside the cluster") to `_releases_into_another_wedge` ("would demoting it change what `_reconcile_owner_once` decides"), because an identity retaining any `_INSIDER_SOURCES` row stays a Section-16 person and its 13F stays a `dropped_source` (#1640). Correct, and it shipped. #2785 was filed to carry the same narrowing to `_select_control_group_rep` clause 4, which still asks the wide predicate. **The argument does transfer. The arithmetic does not, and the arithmetic is what the clause fences.**
- Measured before deciding — `PYTHONPATH=. uv run python -m scripts.audit_2785_rep_swap_gate`, 3,108 instruments, 0 harness errors: 5,283 clusters reach the selector, 203 reach clause 4, **81 declines**, **72 of them would flip** under the narrow predicate; the 9 that stay refused strand only `13d`/`13g`/`13f`. On the census alone the change looks obviously right — 88.9% of refusals are for a hazard that cannot occur, the identical finding #2230 made.
- The paired full-population A/B (control = a worktree at `origin/main`, both arms 3,108 instruments, 0 harness errors) is what refuted it. Net **−385,131,434** shares looks like a clean win, and the net is the trap: **17 instruments GROW, by +82,886,088 in total**, against 26 shrinking. `.claude/skills/engineering/full-population-ab.md` says inspect the gain side; here the gain side IS the verdict.
- Mechanism: while the incumbent is the rep, its stranded rows share an IDENTITY KEY with the block row, so `_reconcile_owner_once` groups them — **additively** for pooled Section-16 forms (#1941), by **MAX** across competing beneficial restatements. Demoting the incumbent breaks that grouping, and which way the pie moves depends on which interaction was in play. Two worked cases, offered as the two ends and explicitly NOT as a population taxonomy: `WBD` is exactly pie-neutral (`Newhouse Steven O` 184,070,739 becomes the partnership's 184,023,290 + his own 47,449 — same total, and the block finally sits on the entity that holds it); `AIRS` grows by **+14,038,819**, exactly the block value.
- ⚠⚠ **Three discriminators for the grow side were tried and all three died on the full population**, and that — not the net figure — is what settles the ticket. `max(stranded) >= block value`: 11 of 17 growers, 14 of 55 non-growers. "the instrument carries more than one collapse" (the `AIRS` shape, which I had written up as the mechanism before measuring it): 14/17 GROW, 25/29 SHRINK, 13/26 NEUTRAL. "the incumbent is the kept rep of a collapse": 17/17, 29/29, 25/26 — a **tautology**, true by construction in the control arm, and it looked like a strong signal until that was noticed. `TTRX` grows by 15,416,260 on an instrument carrying exactly ONE collapse, which is what refutes the `AIRS` story as the general explanation. Repeated failed keys is this repo's own signal to question the MODEL: "neutral-or-better" is a statement about the owner-once GROUPING, and no predicate over one member's stranded rows can decide it.
- ⚠ Route stratification does not rescue it either: flip outcomes are `value_bucket` 20 neutral / 16 shrink / 7 grow and `same_accession` 6 / 13 / 10, so both admission routes grow and the narrowing cannot be scoped to one of them. (Cluster-level attribution of an instrument-level delta; an instrument with two flipped clusters is counted twice.)
- ⚠ **I generalised from two cases and a Codex pass on the FRAMING caught it**, which is the #2282-2c "a descriptive claim is a measurement too" rule landing on a causal claim rather than a prose quantifier. The first draft of this entry asserted the `AIRS` overlapping-cluster topology as the mechanism for the grow side; measuring that topology across all 72 flips falsified it. The claim was weakened to what was measured. **A mechanism inferred from the two cases you happened to inspect is a hypothesis — score it on the population before it goes in a docstring, because a docstring is where the next session will trust it.**
- ⚠ This is a REFUSAL to ship, not a closure of the question. The narrowing does improve representative correctness — `WBD` puts a 184M block on the partnership that holds it instead of on a natural person who won a CIK tie-break. What blocks it is the downstream identity/component arithmetic, so the follow-up is to model the owner-once grouping across connected clusters, not to keep the arbitrary representative forever.
- Prevention: when two gates share a predicate and you are about to align them, ask what each gate's decision DOES, not just what the predicate means. A gate that only removes rows can be argued non-inflating from the predicate alone; a gate that changes which identity survives re-parents every row grouped under it, so it needs its own A/B with the gain side inspected. Enforced in: `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_select_control_group_rep` clause 4 (carries the numbers and the mechanism) + `_releases_other_rows`' docstring (a "do not finish the job" note); `scripts/audit_2785_rep_swap_gate.py`; `scripts/probe_2785_wedge_detail.py`; `tests/test_insider_deemed_chain_collapse.py::test_swap_is_declined_even_when_the_stranded_row_is_an_insider_row`.

## A probe that resolves nothing exits 0 and diffs clean — zsh does not word-split an unquoted parameter (#2785, 2026-08-20)

- `SYMS="HCA WBD SGU"; probe $SYMS` passes ONE argument in zsh, not three (bash splits; zsh does not). Every symbol lookup missed, the probe printed a single `NOT FOUND` line, exited 0, and `diff control treatment` came back **empty** — which reads exactly like "the change moved nothing" on a run whose whole purpose was to show that it moved something. Caught only because the A/B had already said those instruments moved.
- Same family as the archived `cmd | tail` gotcha and the #2386 census trap: **a broken measurement and a clean result must not be the same output.** The pipe version hides an exit code; this one hides an empty input set.
- Prevention: a comparison probe must report how much input it actually resolved and exit non-zero when any of it is missing — `scripts/probe_2785_wedge_detail.py` prints `resolved N/M symbols` to stderr and returns 1 on any unresolved symbol. In zsh, pass list arguments literally or via an array (`syms=(A B C); probe $syms`), never via an unquoted scalar.
- ⚠ Related, same session: **macOS `pgrep` has no `-c` flag.** `pgrep -fc pattern` is a usage error (rc=2, usage text on stderr, nothing on stdout), so `until [ "$(pgrep -fc X || echo 0)" -eq 0 ]` evaluates to `0` immediately and the wait-loop reports the job finished the instant it starts. Use `[ "$(pgrep -f X | wc -l)" -eq 0 ]`. The `|| echo 0` fallback is what converts the error into a false clean signal — the same shape as gating on a pipe's exit status.

## A multi-channel ticket that ships ONE channel leaves the rest unticketed — and the tracker moving is what hides it (#2230/#2229, 2026-08-20)

- #2226 partitioned the ownership-oversubscription cohort and named mechanism **M1** as *"no `_current` table can ever release a position"*, explicitly across all three: `ownership_institutions_current`, `ownership_insiders_current` (which *"holds Form 3 rows dated back to 1987"*) and `ownership_blockholders_current`. It was split out as **#2229**, which shipped **13F-HR supersession only** — `superseded_by_later_13f_hr`, institutions. Grep the read path for the ticket and every hit is institutional (`app/services/ownership_rollup.py:158`, `:991`, `:1149`, `:5005`).
- The insider half was never re-filed, and #2226's own close-out is what buried it: *"#2229 merged. This tracker moves 47.0% → 40.3%."* A tracker percentage that moves reads as progress on the whole mechanism. **The channels that did not ship have no ticket, no owner and no number, so nothing surfaces them again.** Nine days later #2230 — a DIFFERENT axis of the same tracker — was still being worked as though it were the binding one.
- Measured today, full population through the real read path (`PYTHONPATH=. uv run python -m scripts.audit_2230_insider_oversubscription`, 12,739 instruments rendered, 0 harness errors), pricing both axes on ONE cohort with ONE criterion — "would this mechanism, applied perfectly, bring the wedge back under `shares_outstanding`":

  | | |
  | --- | ---: |
  | instruments whose rendered insiders wedge > `shares_outstanding` | **664** |
  | … cleared by folding every surviving equal-value cluster (#2230's mechanism) | **16** (2.4%) |
  | … cleared by bounding insider rows to 2y of the slice's own newest as-of | **452** (68.1%) |

  On the 372 instruments where de-duplication is even arithmetically possible, unfolded equal-value clusters carry **1,603,720,100** of the **14,468,619,737**-share overage — **11.1%**. The other **292** have a SINGLE holder exceeding the denominator (median 2.52×, p90 16.7×), so no additivity treatment of any kind can fix them.
- ⚠ The staleness arm is a **diagnostic, not a design**, and the same run says so: it removes 26,534,264,979 shares against a 14,468,619,737-share overage on that cohort — it over-corrects by 183%, because a long-held stake nobody has had occasion to restate is indistinguishable from an exited one. Quoting it as a proposed rule would be the #2231 mistake (a bound fitted to the symptom rather than derived from the source).
- ⚠⚠ **The insider channel is not the 13F channel and the source rule differs**, which is why #2229's fix does not port mechanically. A 13F exit is reported by OMISSION — that is the premise #2229's supersession rests on. A Section-16 disposal is an affirmative FILING: the sec-edgar skill's §2.3 transaction-code table gives `S` (sale), `D` (transfer back to company), `G` (gift) and `U` (tender) as reported transaction codes, so a sale arrives as a row rather than as silence. A frozen insider row therefore does **not** mean the same thing a frozen 13F row means, and the treatment has to be derived rather than copied. ⚠ What a frozen row DOES mean is unmeasured — do not assume "the holder ceased to be a reporting person" without checking; that is the first question the follow-up ticket has to answer, not a premise it may inherit.
- Cross-source, SEC EDGAR direct (`data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0001731303.json`): `Forge Energy, LLC` has **5 filings in total** — Form 3 `2018-02-20`, Form 4 `2018-06-13`, SC 13G `2018-02-20`, two 13G/A ending `2019-01-30` — and nothing since. We render its Form 3 holding of 46,000,000 shares as a current `CHRD` insider position today, against 54,697,872 shares outstanding.
- Prevention: when a ticket names a mechanism across N channels and the fix ships for one, **file the remaining channels before closing it**, and say in the tracker's close-out which channels moved and which did not. A percentage is not a channel list. Self-review prompt: after merging a fix for a mechanism described as general, grep the read path for the ticket number and check the hits cover every channel the issue named — if they do not, the gap now exists only in your head. Enforced in: this entry; `scripts/audit_2230_insider_oversubscription.py` (reprices both axes on demand); `tests/test_audit_2230_insider_oversubscription.py` (10/10 revert-probed).

## ⚠ PENDING SKILL EDIT — `data-engineer/SKILL.md` states no release mechanism for five of the six `_current` tables (#2230, 2026-08-20)

- The five-axis category table lists every `ownership_*_current` table and its identity key, and says nothing about EXPIRY — so a reader takes "latest observation per holder" at face value. Only `institutions` has a release mechanism (#2229). Writes to `.claude/skills/**` were **DENIED on this worktree again** — sixth recorded occurrence, tracked as #2403. Apply on a session that has permission. The edit is this block, immediately before **Provenance block** (currently `.claude/skills/data-engineer/SKILL.md:163`):

> ⚠⚠ **Only the `institutions` row has a release mechanism. The other five never expire.**
> `refresh_*_current` deletes a `_current` row only `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`, i.e. when the observation itself disappears — so "latest observation per holder" means "forever" unless something supersedes it. #2229 built that something for 13F alone (`superseded_by_later_13f_hr`; grep the ticket in `ownership_rollup.py` and every hit is institutional). `ownership_insiders_current` therefore still carries Form 3/4 rows the filer last restated years ago: full population 2026-08-20, **100,437 of 170,941 rows (58.8%) have a `period_end` older than two years**, holding **320,316,309,513 of 561,235,592,698 shares (57.1%)** —
>
> ```sql
> SELECT source,
>        count(*) FILTER (WHERE period_end >= current_date - interval '2 years') AS within_2y,
>        count(*) FILTER (WHERE period_end <  current_date - interval '2 years') AS older
>   FROM ownership_insiders_current GROUP BY 1;
> -- form4 63,080 / 87,289 · form3 7,424 / 13,148
> ```
>
> It is the largest single axis of the #2226 oversubscription tracker — 452 of the 664 instruments whose rendered insiders wedge exceeds `shares_outstanding` fall back under it when insider rows are bounded to two years, against 16 for the Section-16 deemed-attribution collapse (`scripts/audit_2230_insider_oversubscription.py`, which reprices both). ⚠ That bound is a **diagnostic, not a proposed rule** — it over-removes by 183% of the overage. The source rule differs from 13F's and has to be derived, not copied: a 13F exit is reported by omission, whereas a Section-16 disposal is an affirmative filing (sec-edgar §2.3 transaction codes `S`/`D`/`G`/`U`), so a frozen insider row does not mean what a frozen 13F row means.

## ⚠⚠ A "research-only" ingest override wrote the operator-visible ownership layer — check the WRITE TARGET, not the caller's intent (#2788, 2026-08-20)

- First seen in: #2788, investigating why `ownership_insiders_current` rows freeze. The ticket's framing — "no `_current` table can ever release a position" — described a structural gap. Measured on the full population this run, most of the symptom is **six days old** and has a single cause.
- `sec_insider_dataset_ingest.ingest_insider_dataset_archive` takes a `retention_cutoff_override`, added for #2701 so a RESEARCH run could read past #1233 §4.3's 3-year Form 4 cap. Its comment says the injection exists so "both consumers keep the boundary they need" and that the override "CHANGES NO DEFAULT" for "the operator ALERTING path". Both statements are about the alerting path. **Neither is about the consumer that was actually exposed.** The function's only write target is `ownership_insiders_observations`, which is the sole source of `ownership_insiders_current`, which is the insiders wedge on the ownership rollup. There is one store, not two.
- `scripts/backfill_2701_insider_research_ingest.py` ran it at `RESEARCH_CUTOFF = date(2006, 1, 1)` on 2026-08-14. Measured (`PYTHONPATH=. uv run python -m scripts.audit_2788_insider_retention --census`, which computes every figure below at run time rather than storing it):

  ```
  -- ownership_insiders_current rows beyond form4_retention_cutoff(), by backing
  -- observation's ingest day:
  --   written 2026-08-14 : 76,920 rows / 3,559 instruments / 203,364,662,254 shares
  --   every other day    :  1,123 rows /   719 instruments /   1,992,203,569 shares
  ```

  **98.6% of the beyond-retention rows arrived in that one run**, carrying filings back to `2006-01-03`. Before it, the form4 observation corpus was retention-bounded by construction: pre-2026-08-14 rows split 975,515 within-retention against 19,650 beyond, and the beyond side reached back only to `2023-06-05` — rows that had aged past the rolling boundary, not rows written past it.
- ⚠ **The research goal was not met either.** #2701's own consumer is `insider_transactions` / `insider_filings` (`scripts/verify_2437_insider_forward_returns.py`); the DERA ingest never writes those — its only INSERT target is `ownership_insiders_observations`. Measured after the run:

  ```sql
  SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE period_of_report < date '2017-01-01') AS pre_2017,
         count(*) AS total, count(*) FILTER (WHERE period_of_report IS NULL) AS undated
    FROM insider_filings;
  -- 2,581 | 568,814 | 22,434     (pre-2017 is 0.45% of the corpus)
  ```

  So the run moved ~4.5M rows into the ownership layer and left the research corpus's pre-2017 share where #2701 found it. That is the inverse of its intent, and nothing failed or reported an error.
- Prevention: before widening ANY ingest bound "for research", grep the ingest function for its INSERT targets and then grep those tables for readers. Write the answer in the PR. A parameter that is injected rather than defaulted proves the caller had to ask; it does not prove the callee is isolated, and "changes no default" is a statement about configuration, not about blast radius. The general form: **an ingest's blast radius is its write set's read set, and neither is visible from the call site.** Same family as the repo's standing "a job that no-ops and reports success is invisible to every automated check we have" — here a job that succeeded loudly and wrote 4.5M rows to the wrong layer was equally invisible, because every row it wrote was valid.
- Enforced in: this entry; `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::_INSIDER_BEYOND_RETENTION_SQL` + `_read_beyond_retention_insiders` (read side honours the write chokepoint, with per-row telemetry); `scripts/audit_2788_insider_retention.py --census`; `tests/test_ownership_insider_retention_bound.py` (6 cases, 5/5 revert-probed). Follow-ups filed for the write side and for the equal-value de-fold interaction.

## ⚠⚠ A reporting person's EDGAR submissions JSON is per-FILER, not per-issuer — it manufactures coverage gaps (#2788, 2026-08-20)

- First seen in: #2788 clause 9. Cross-checking whether we were missing Form 4s for `BALLMER STEVEN A` (CIK `0000902015`) on MSFT, where our stored position is dated `2014-08-19`, `data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000902015.json` reports a **latest Section-16 filing of `2025-04-25`**. Read at face value that is an eleven-year ingest gap, and it is the claim I was about to write.
- It is not. `filings.recent` for a reporting person carries every Section-16 form that PERSON filed against ANY issuer, and **has no issuer field at all**. The 2025 filing is a **Form 3 for Stagwell Inc** (`STGW`, issuer CIK `0000876883`, resolved from `…/Archives/edgar/data/902015/000095017025058893/ownership.xml`). His last MSFT **Form 4** is `2014-08-20`, so the stored row is correct and there is no gap.
- One tell was visible in the JSON before fetching anything: the 2025 form is a **`3`**, and Form 3 is by definition the INITIAL statement of beneficial ownership — a person who has been filing Form 4s against an issuer since 2003 does not file a fresh Form 3 for that same issuer. That is a definitional read of the form, not a measured frequency; the issuer still has to be resolved from the document before the claim is made.
- ⚠ Fetch the RAW `ownership.xml` to attribute a filing to an issuer. The path `…/{accession_nodashes}/xslF345X02/ownership.xml` that appears in `primaryDocument` is the XSL-RENDERED view — an `<issuerCik>` regex against it silently returns `None`, which reads as "the filing has no issuer" rather than "you fetched the wrong representation". Use `…/{accession_nodashes}/index.json` and take the bare `ownership.xml`.
- Prevention: never derive a per-issuer coverage claim from a reporting person's submissions feed. Resolve the issuer from the document, or compare against the issuer's own submissions feed instead. Test: if a sentence says "this holder's latest filing is X" while the subject of the sentence is an ISSUER's ownership, the two nouns disagree and the claim is unverified.
- ⚠ **PENDING SKILL EDIT** — belongs in `.claude/skills/data-sources/sec-edgar.md` as §7.4.1, immediately before §7.5. Writes to `.claude/skills/**` were **DENIED on this worktree again** (seventh recorded occurrence, tracked as #2403), so it is parked here. Apply on a session that has permission.
## A health sentinel whose two sides come from different populations detects nothing (#2337, 2026-08-20)

- Symptom: none, which is the point. `finra_short_interest_refresh` logged a WARNING whenever `rows_resolved / rows_parsed < 0.50`, its module docstring calling it a "universe drift / FINRA shape regression sentinel". It fired on every fire for the whole life of the job, and by the time #2234 wrote the FINRA backfill runbook the alarm had been demoted in prose to something the operator is told in advance to ignore: *"⚠ Expect `match rate ~26% below 50% threshold` warnings — that sentinel is miscalibrated"*. An alarm with a documented "ignore this" note attached is strictly worse than no alarm, because it still costs a reader's attention and it occupies the slot a working detector would have.
- Root cause: the ratio's numerator and denominator are governed by **different populations**. `rows_resolved` is bounded by OUR universe (`build_preloaded_symbol_resolver` selects `instruments WHERE is_tradable = TRUE`); `rows_parsed` is FINRA's — every US-reported symbol, including OTC, preferreds, ETFs and share-class siblings. Nothing links the two, so the ratio has no healthy value anyone could have written down in advance, and the 0.50 that was written down is simply above the whole operating range.
- Measured, full population — every stored payload, re-parsed read-only via `scripts/audit_2337_finra_match_rate.py` (34 files / **715,915** rows): match rate **25.47%–26.58%**, below the floor on **34 of 34** files. It is also drifting monotonically DOWN (26.58% → 25.47% across the corpus) as FINRA's universe grows faster than ours, so re-baselining buys a few years and then repeats.
- ⚠ **The sibling had the same arm and it is worse there.** `finra_regsho_daily_refresh.py` carries a byte-equivalent copy over the same resolver. Its aggregate pools six tapes whose structural match rates run 2.08% (`FORF`, the OTC/ADF tape) to 73.51% (`FNQC`), and the pooled ratio lands **on** the floor: min 49.11 / max 51.74 over 74 stored days, **28 of 74 below**. A sentinel firing 38% of the time *looks* discriminating, which is the more dangerous failure — filed as #2795 rather than folded in.
- Prevention: before writing or accepting a ratio-based health check, **name the population on each side of the division and confirm they are the same one**. If they are not, the check is uncalibratable and no threshold rescues it; split the ratio into the classes it pools and alarm on the class whose healthy value is knowable BY CONSTRUCTION rather than fitted. Here `skipped_invalid_row` is that class — a well-formed pipe-delimited file carries every required field on every row, so its healthy value is exactly 0 (census: 0 of 715,915), and it is where a column-shape regression actually lands. Boundaries at none-at-all and all-of-them need no derivation; only the graded middle does, and where no published formulation exists (FINRA documents the file, not our match against it) fix it by construction and freeze the constant with its derivation next to it — `_RESOLVED_RETENTION_FLOOR = 0.90` against a corpus whose worst consecutive drop over 33 pairs is 0.07%.
- ⚠ Corollary for the census that calibrates the alarm: have it call the SAME predicate production counts, never a re-implementation. `required_row_fields` was extracted for exactly this, because a census that classifies rows slightly differently from ingest mis-calibrates the threshold it exists to derive, and the divergence is invisible in both outputs. Same shape as the census/rule-table entry above ("express them once as a pure function and have both the census and production call it").
- ⚠ A test can pin the WRONG side of a boundary and still pass. `test_retention_exactly_at_floor_is_silent` originally built its "at the floor" case as `ceil(prev * floor)` — 5145/5716 = 0.90010, which is *near* the boundary, where `<` and `<=` agree. The revert probe flipping the comparison was NOT CAUGHT. Integer counts rarely land exactly on a float threshold: choose counts that divide exactly (900/1000 is the same double as `0.9`) and assert that they do, in the test, before asserting the behaviour.
- Enforced in: this entry; `app/jobs/finra_short_interest_refresh.py` (the `_RESOLVED_RETENTION_FLOOR` derivation block + `evaluate_file_sentinels`); `scripts/audit_2337_finra_match_rate.py` (re-runnable full-population census); `tests/test_finra_short_interest_sentinels.py` (6/6 revert-probed, including the boundary probe above).

## A "first bar of the period" rule over a UNION calendar is decided by the corpus's RAREST row (#2797, 2026-08-20)

- Symptom: `s2-cross-sectional-momentum` had fired **zero** signals in production, all-time, under every version — 26,203 `not_fired` and 20,301 `not_evaluable` rows and no `fired` row. The prevention entry above it ("An output whose EMPTINESS is a legitimate outcome cannot be aged") had already *measured* that zero and correctly reasoned that a scan can legitimately fire nothing. It never asked why this one did, so the zero was recorded as healthy and became the premise of a freshness check. It was a bug.
- Root cause: S-2 rebalances on *"the first bar whose calendar month differs from the previous bar's"*, evaluated over the panel's **union** calendar (`load_union_calendar` — every date on which ANY instrument has a loadable bar). `price_daily` carries weekend rows. Full population, validated universe, 2026-08-20: **3,669 weekend bars across 389 instruments on 329 distinct dates — 0.0998% of 3,673,648 bars — controlling 13 of 73 rebalance dates (17.8%)**:

```sql
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT instrument_id), count(DISTINCT price_date)
  FROM price_daily WHERE extract(isodow FROM price_date) >= 6;  -- 3669 / 389 / 329
```

- The general shape: **a union is a MAX and "first of the period" is an ARGMIN over it, so the two compose into "the rarest row in the corpus decides the boundary for everyone".** A junk date does not need to be common, plausible or even loadable by the strategy's own members — it only needs to sort first. One instrument's artefact on Sat 2026-08-01 consumed the whole month; Mon 2026-08-03, with 5,380 eligible names against the Saturday's 9, never rebalanced at all.
- ⚠ **The failure is silent in the direction that hides it.** The junk instruments were not frontier-eligible, so the scan wrote *no row of any kind* for 2026-08-01 — not a `thin_cross_section` refusal, not a `not_fired`. An absent period and a quiet period render identically, so no count, no alarm and no dashboard could distinguish them. The only detector was asking why a legitimate-looking zero was there.
- ⚠ **A period rule interacts with identity churn, and the product of the two can be a strategy that never fires at all.** `write_window_indices` bounds a cold start to ONE bar by design (spec §11 forbids backfilling signals — it would reintroduce look-ahead), so every new `strategy_version` restarts at the frontier. S-2 rebalances monthly and moved through **four** versions in 24 days (≈ one per 6 days). A strategy whose identity churns faster than its decision cadence has a low probability of any version surviving to a decision date, independently of this bug. When a cadence is coarser than daily, check the version's expected lifetime against it before concluding a zero is the market talking.
- Prevention: when a rule selects the first/last member of a period from a pooled calendar, **state which rows are eligible to be that member and cut the ineligible ones BEFORE the period rule runs** — not after, because the boundary is already spent by then. Cite the source rule for the cut (here: the validated universe is US-listed stock (§4.0) and US equity venues hold no regular weekend sessions per the NYSE/Nasdaq holiday-and-hours calendars, so a weekend row cannot be a session the spec means). Then verify on the full population that the surviving boundaries all have healthy participation — `scripts/ab_2797_s2_weekday_rebalance.py` re-derives the pre-fix rule verbatim as its control arm and refuses to pass if the cut moved a date whose panel was already healthy.
- ⚠ **A docstring that delegates a warning to another module is a CLAIM ABOUT THAT MODULE — grep it.** `s10_rebalance_dates` had already found and fixed this exact exposure and wrote: *"S-2 shares the exposure and that is noted there, not silently fixed here — editing its calendar would move its identity."* It was not noted there; `grep -n weekend s2_cross_sectional_momentum.py` returned nothing. The sentence was the only record of the exposure and it lived in the module that did not have it, which is why a known, already-solved bug then ran for two weeks in the one that did. Deferring a fix is legitimate; recording the deferral somewhere other than the affected code is not. Also weigh the deferral's stated cost against the ledger before accepting it — "editing its calendar would move its identity" sounds decisive and was free: S-2 and S-10 had **0** fired signals, **0** promotions, **0** preregistration declarations and **0** live-gate assessments between them.
- Enforced in: this entry; `app/services/strategies/s2_cross_sectional_momentum.py::rebalance_dates` (the cut, the source rule and the measurement); `app/services/strategies/s10_relative_strength_leader.py::s10_rebalance_dates` (the corrected claim); `scripts/ab_2797_s2_weekday_rebalance.py` (full-population A/B, control re-derived not simulated); `tests/test_2797_s2_weekday_rebalance.py` (the 2026-08 regression on its own dates, plus the behavioural anti-drift binding between the two duplicated implementations).

### A DATE literal in a migration is another copy of a Python constant, and nothing ties them (#2697, 2026-08-21)

- First seen in: PR #2757 (2026-08-21), flagged by the review bot in two consecutive rounds — `sql/359`'s `strategy_results_metric_axis_namespace` hardcodes the in-sample boundary as `DATE '2021-06-29'`, and `sql/360`'s control-support predicate hardcodes `EVALUATION_WINDOW_START` and `HOLDOUT_BOUNDARY` the same way. Both mirror Python constants that the test suite already pins against the spec, so a recalibration fails on the PYTHON side while the SQL keeps the old date silently.
- Cause: the Python constant has a spec-pin test (`HOLDOUT_BOUNDARY == SPEC_HOLDOUT_BOUNDARY`), which makes the constant feel governed. It is — but the migration is a THIRD copy, written months later, in a language the pin cannot see. A CHECK constraint that disagrees with the code does not error; it rejects rows the code considers valid, or admits rows it does not.
- ⚠ The failure is silent in both directions and neither is a crash. A too-strict constraint looks like a data problem, and a too-loose one looks like nothing at all until a promotion gate reads a row the code would have refused.
- Prevention: **for every `DATE '...'` (or any constant) literal in a migration, add a test that READS the literal out of the `.sql` file and compares it to the Python constant** — never one that restates the date, which just creates a fourth copy. Scope the regex to the predicate that owns the literal: a migration that also registers reference data carries other, legitimately different dates, and asserting over every literal in the file fails on those. ⚠ Probe it: mutate the SQL literal and confirm the test fails, then restore. A coupling test that cannot fail is worse than none, because it certifies the coupling it never checked.
- Caught by: the review bot, twice — and the second finding was the same class as the first, in the same PR round, one file over. That repetition is the signal to generalise the guard rather than patch the instance.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `tests/test_strategy_result.py::TestTheSpecConstantsAreFrozen::test_the_SQL_migrations_carry_the_same_dates_as_python` (covers `sql/359` and `sql/360`, reads both out of the files).

### A guard that matches a CALL SHAPE misses the same defect behind a different call shape (#2806, 2026-08-21)

- First seen in: PR #2808 (2026-08-21), one day after #2803 fixed what looked like the whole of this defect. `/strategies/overview` still reported `share_unavailable_reason: "never_scanned"` for **all ten** strategies while `strategy_scan_watermark` carried frontier `2026-08-19` for all ten, written that morning. The operator's Strategies page had a working scanner behind it and said the strategies had never run.
- Cause: `universe` is part of `StrategyIdentity`. The live scan stamps `SCAN_UNIVERSE` (`survivor_only`); stored results are on `BACKTEST_UNIVERSE` (`survivorship_free`). The two version sets are **disjoint**, so binding the result basis to a scan relation cannot merely miss rows — it matches none, permanently. #2803 rebound the three queries executed as `cur.execute(_X_SQL, scan_params)` inside `app/api/strategies.py` and shipped a guard for them. It did not reach `load_attribution`, `load_fire_rate` and `load_owned_pnl`, which live in `app/services/strategy_monitoring.py` and take their versions as a **keyword argument**.
- ⚠⚠ **The #2803 guard already named the right table and still could not see the call.** `_SCAN_RELATIONS` listed `strategy_signal_daily_counts` from the day it was written; the guard matched `cur.execute(NAME, params)` pairs in `inspect.getsource(get_strategy_overview)`, and a keyword-argument loader in another module has no such pair. The guard was correct about WHAT must be protected and encoded HOW the one known instance happened to be written. That is the general trap: **a guard keyed on syntax protects the instance, a guard keyed on the relation protects the rule.**
- Measured, full population (dev, before the fix): version-set intersection **0**; of **56,835** `strategy_signals` rows, **0** matched the result basis and 33,655 the scan basis; of **428** `strategy_signal_daily_counts` rows, **0** and 216. A/B of the three loaders on both bases: `fire_rate` 0 → 10 keys, `attribution` 0 → 8, `owned_pnl` 0 → 0 (correct — no deployments exist).
- ⚠ **Both halves fail closed to the SAME symptom, so fixing one looks exactly like fixing neither.** The query binding and the dict lookup key (`pnl_by_strategy.get(key, …)`) each produce an empty card. Any fix of this shape needs a guard on the read-back key as well as on the bind, or a half-fix ships looking complete.
- Prevention: **derive the guarded set from the code under guard, never from a literal list.** The replacement walks `strategy_monitoring` for `load_*` functions, extracts the `_*_SQL` constants each one references, and requires a scan basis for any whose SQL names a scan relation — so a fourth loader is covered without anyone remembering to extend anything. Test: if a guard enumerates its subjects, ask what a subject written in a different style would look like to it; if the answer is "invisible", the enumeration is the bug.
- ⚠ Corollary, and it is the older lesson (#2803) restated because it recurred one file over: **a test that seeds through the same constant the reader uses is self-consistent and proves nothing.** #2803 fixed exactly that in three DB tests. #2806's DB test had the seeding right — on the scan basis — and simply never asserted the fire-rate block reading that same table, so the surface stayed uncovered by a test that appeared to cover it.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/api/strategies.py` (the three scan-basis bindings and the `scan_key` read-back, each with the reasoning at the call site); `tests/test_2803_scan_card_version_basis.py::test_every_loader_over_a_scan_relation_is_called_on_the_scan_basis` and `::test_the_scan_basis_loaders_are_read_back_at_the_scan_key` (both derive the loader set, both revert-probed); `tests/test_api_strategies.py::test_scan_health_reads_durable_daily_counts_after_detail_retention` (asserts the fire-rate block off the row it already seeded; revert-probe reproduces `never_scanned` end-to-end against a real DB).

### A derived guard scoped to ONE FUNCTION is still an enumeration (#2814, 2026-08-21)

- First seen in: PR for #2814 (2026-08-21), the day after #2806. `GET /strategies/signals` returned `{"items": [], "next_cursor": null}` on dev while 33,655 fired rows sat in `strategy_signals`. `/strategies`' card block said "s7-trend-pullback fired 167 entries on 2026-08-19" and the activity feed directly beneath it — the only place the page names the *instruments* — was empty. Third occurrence of one defect.
- Cause: identical to #2803/#2806 — `app/api/strategies.py::get_fired_signals` bound `_current_versions()` (result basis) to `_FIRED_SIGNALS_SQL`, which reads `strategy_signals`. `signal_ledger` is that table's only writer and stamps `SCAN_UNIVERSE`.
- ⚠⚠ **#2806's own prevention rule was applied to half the fix and the other half stayed enumerated.** "Derive the guarded set from the code under guard" produced a genuinely derived walk over `strategy_monitoring`'s `load_*` functions — and left the `app/api/strategies.py` side as three SQL constants named literally, read out of `inspect.getsource(get_strategy_overview)`. `strategy_signals` was already in `_SCAN_RELATIONS` and `_FIRED_SIGNALS_SQL` already read it on the wrong basis while that guard was green. The guard was not looking at the wrong table; it was looking at the wrong **function**. **Test: name the axis your derivation ranges over, then ask what sits one step off it. "Every loader in that module" still fixes the module. "Every constant in that function" still fixes the function.**
- Measured, full population (dev, before the fix): `strategy_signals` holds 22 distinct `strategy_version`, of which **0** match `_current_versions()` and 8 match `_current_scan_versions()`; `universe` is `survivor_only` on **56,835 of 56,835** rows. A/B of `_FIRED_SIGNALS_SQL` on one connection, both bases: **0 rows → 50** (the page limit).
- ⚠ **Nine passing DB tests covered this endpoint and none could fail.** Every one seeded `strategy_version=_current_versions()[strategy_id]` and the reader filtered on `_current_versions()` — the #2806 corollary verbatim, one file over again. The fixture also hard-coded `universe='survivorship_free'` into a table where no production row carries that value. **A fixture constant that no writer in `app/` produces is the tell; grep the value, not the column.** Seeds now construct the identity the scanner constructs (`STRATEGY_MANIFEST[...].identity(universe=SCAN_UNIVERSE, ...)`), deliberately not `_current_scan_versions()`, so seed and reader cannot be the same constant.
- Prevention: the API-side guard now derives over the **module** — every module-level `_*_SQL` in `app.api.strategies` that reads a scan relation and binds `%(versions)s`, matched to whichever function executes it — with a floor asserting the four known constants stay in the derived set, and a companion assertion that the three result-store queries stay OUT (a guard that cries wolf on a correct binding gets muted, which is how this came back twice).
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/api/strategies.py::get_fired_signals` (scan basis, reasoning at the call site); `tests/test_2803_scan_card_version_basis.py::test_every_scan_relation_query_is_executed_on_the_scan_basis` (module-derived; revert-probed both ways — rebinding to the result basis fails it, and renaming the table in the SQL trips the floor rather than silently shrinking coverage) and `::test_a_result_basis_query_is_not_swept_into_the_api_scan_guard`; `tests/test_strategy_monitoring.py::test_fired_signals_read_the_scan_basis_the_ledger_actually_writes` (asserts both arms — scan-basis row returned, result-basis row not — because "returns rows" also passes against a reader filtering on nothing).

### A per-INSTRUMENT bar date read as a per-SCAN calendar invents coverage that never happened (#2811, 2026-08-21)

- First seen in: #2811's own diagnosis (2026-08-21), which is the point — the wrong causal claim was written INTO the ticket and its follow-up comment, and would have been the next session's premise. The ticket asked *"why was 2026-08-03 skipped while 07-31 and 08-04 were written"* and framed it as a caught-up window omitting one interior bar. There is no such omission.
- Cause: `strategy_signal_daily_counts.signal_bar_date` is written **per instrument**. `write_window_indices` bounds a cold start to the last bar *strictly before the frontier* **in that instrument's own date sequence**, so a sparse series yields an older date than a dense one. Measured on dev: every census bar date before 2026-08-06 was ONE instrument — JTKWY→07-28, MARK→07-31, SICP→08-04, TRVN→08-05, each `row_count = 1`, all from the single cold start at 08-09 14:43 against frontier 08-07. `count(distinct strategy_id)` over those rows renders as four strategies covering four days.
- ⚠⚠ **The aggregate that hides it is the one that looks most like coverage.** `GROUP BY signal_bar_date` over a per-instrument relation produces a date axis, and a date axis reads as a calendar. Nothing about the query says "one of these days is four instruments and the next is 11,042". The tell is `row_count` — and it was in the data the whole time, at 1.
- ⚠ **Do not repair this by asserting a contiguous "left edge" instead.** A cold start writes each instrument's last pre-frontier bar, which can be arbitrarily old, so the written set is not an interval either. The honest statement names the SCAN RUNS (`job_runs`: the first `strategy_signal_scan` of any kind was 2026-08-09 06:45), not a range of dates.
- Prevention: **before treating a date column as a calendar, check whether the producer writes it per entity — and if it does, require a population floor before a date counts as a day.** The fix takes the floor from the producer's own declaration (`StrategyEntry.min_participants`, `MIN_CROSS_SECTION = 10` for S-2) rather than inventing one: below it the strategy refuses with `thin_cross_section` and provably cannot fire, so the date is not an opportunity. Without that floor the fix reproduces its own root cause one layer up — a single sparse instrument landing on a rebalance date would set `decision_days = 1` and re-enable the fake share.
- ⚠ The operator-visible half, and the reason this was a bug and not a note: **a periodic strategy is `not_fired` on every bar that is not a decision date** (`strategy_registry` rule 3, correctly — the data was present and the CALENDAR excluded it). So the share's denominator fills with bars the strategy never judged, and a version that has never reached a decision date reports `0.0000` with **no reason at all**. Measured: S-2 `0/3,277`, S-10 `0/5,689`, both rendering as confident measured zeros. This generalises #2797's *"when a cadence is coarser than daily, check the version's expected lifetime against it before concluding a zero is the market talking"* from a note-to-a-human into a mechanism.
- ⚠ **The reader must not RECOMPUTE a producer's calendar, even from the same functions.** Recomputing resolves a historical `strategy_version` against today's universe, corpus and quarantine state — a bar backfilled earlier in a month silently moves which date was "first of the month", with no census row and no version changing. That is #2809's shape (the card recomputed a frontier with `MAX` where the scan used the mode, and called all ten strategies stale). The scan publishes what it used; the card reads it.
- ⚠ Publication is gated on the CORPUS, not on the run having work. Tying it to plan formation would have shipped inert: on the day this landed every version was already `up_to_date` at frontier 2026-08-19, so the card would have kept reading the never-measured zeros as measured ones until the corpus next advanced.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `sql/362_strategy_decision_calendar.sql`; `app/services/strategy_signal_scan.py::publish_decision_calendar` and `::_publish_decision_calendars` (published before the `not plans` return, deliberately); `app/services/strategy_monitoring.py::_panel_floor` and `::load_fire_rate`; `tests/test_strategy_fire_rate.py::TestDecisionDayPartition` and `::TestProducerInvariantsAreAsserted`; `tests/test_strategy_fire_rate_db.py::TestDecisionCalendarPartition::test_one_sparse_instrument_on_a_rebalance_date_is_not_an_opportunity`; `tests/test_2811_decision_calendar_db.py`.

### A `raise` inside a per-item derivation called from an AGGREGATE endpoint turns one bad row into an empty page (#2811, 2026-08-21)

- First seen in: PR #2812 (2026-08-21), flagged by the review bot as a WARNING on a diff that had already passed Codex checkpoint 2. `derive_fire_rate` was given three producer-invariant asserts (`fired_days <= decision_days <= scanned_days`, numerator <= denominator) that `raise ValueError`. It is called once per `(strategy_id, strategy_version)` inside `load_fire_rate`, whose result populates **every** card on `/strategies/overview` — so one inconsistent census row would 500 the whole page rather than spoiling one card.
- Cause: the assert was written from the DERIVATION's point of view, where raising is correct and the alternative (a silently wrong number) is worse. What was not considered is the CALLER's shape. A pure function that raises is fine; a pure function that raises *inside a loop building an aggregate response* has its blast radius set by the loop, not by itself.
- ⚠ **The repo already had the answer one module over and it did not travel.** `strategy_signal_scan._commit_strategy` states the identical contract for the writer — *"One strategy's failure does not stop the others. That is why this returns a result carrying the error instead of raising"* — and the reader was written without it. When adding a hard failure to a per-entity function, look for how the WRITER of the same entity handles its own failures.
- Prevention: **catch per item, and NAME the refusal in the response rather than only in the log.** The fix contains the failure to its own card and adds `invariant_violated` to both `ShareUnavailableReason` and `WeeklyRateUnavailableReason` — both, because the surrounding contract is *"a value is None if and only if its reason is not"*, and refusing one field while leaving a confident number in the other is the same defect one field over. A `logger.warning` alone was the review bot's NITPICK and it is right: a corruption visible only in logs is one nobody sees.
- ⚠ **Say so when the branch is unreachable, and do not fabricate an input to reach it.** All three invariants hold by CONSTRUCTION in the current fold, so no census row can trigger the raise today; the guard is for the fold this becomes later. The test therefore patches the raise in rather than manufacturing an impossible row shape — a test that constructs an input the producer cannot emit proves the branch, not the isolation. The first attempt did exactly that and passed for the wrong reason (`no_decision_date_scanned`, because the off-calendar fire was already excluded by the partition).
- Caught by: the review bot, on a diff Codex checkpoint 2 had already reviewed twice. Codex attacked the SCHEMA and the corpus semantics; the bot attacked the blast radius. Different lenses, and the diff needed both.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_monitoring.py::load_fire_rate` (the per-version `except ValueError`, with the unreachability stated at the call site) and its two reason enums; `tests/test_strategy_fire_rate_db.py::TestOneCorruptVersionDoesNotBlankThePage` (asserts the healthy sibling is still measured; revert-probed).
### The residual of a two-condition impossibility guard was TWO instruments — and the condition that reaches them is a COUNT, not a magnitude (#2232, 2026-08-20)

- First seen in: taking #2232's residual, handed over by the 2026-08-08 run as *"`AVAL = 7` and the other issuer-side XBRL errors that DO file a cover fact. No discriminator exists for them yet and magnitude is falsified; the honest next step is to look for one, not to widen this guard."*
- **Size the residual before searching for a discriminator for it.** Full population, 2026-08-20, `PYTHONPATH=. uv run python -m scripts.audit_2232_denominator_residual` (4,451 live denominators): the arm-2 surface — some disclosed holder exceeds the denominator — is **347**, and the ratio `max_holder / denominator` is **bimodal with an empty decade**: 276 in 1–10×, 54 in 10–100×, 5 in 100–1,000×, **0 in 1,000–10,000×**, then 12 above. Ten of those 12 are already suppressed by arm 1 (no cover-page DEI fact). **The residual is the other two: `HQ` and `AVAL`.** The empty decade is the finding — it says the shipped conjunction already isolates the right cohort, so what was left was a boundary case and not a class.
- **Three discriminators died before the one that worked, and each died on the full population rather than on reasoning.**
  1. **ASC 260-10-55-12 retroactive restatement.** A genuine reverse split restates the EPS weighted-average share count in every period presented, so cover-vs-weighted-average should agree for a real split and diverge for a tagging error. It does — `GWAV` cover 829,631 = `WeightedAverageNumberOfSharesOutstandingBasic` 829,631, same accession. It reaches neither residual instrument: `AVAL`, `MOB` and `PAVS` are 20-F IFRS filers with NO `us-gaap` weighted-average concept at all, and `HQ`'s weighted average is 1, agreeing with its wrong cover. It also false-positives — 22 of the 320 cover-fact instruments exceed 10× on that ratio because a ±200-day window straddles the pre-split filing (`PW` at exactly 10.0, `XPON` 10.9, `DBGI` 11.5).
  2. **"the holder exceeds every share count the issuer has EVER reported."** Threshold-free and attractive: staleness, deemed attribution and unadjusted pre-split numerators are all bounded by some historical count. Fires on **134 of 4,451** — 131 of them at ≤54×, i.e. ordinary short-fact-history noise. And it misses `AVAL` outright: its largest disclosed holder is 1,000,000 against a maximum historical cover of 15,240,124,702.
  3. **An exchange listing-standard floor** (Nasdaq 5405(b)/5505(b) ≥1,000,000 publicly held shares; NYSE American ≥500,000). Published and citable, and still the falsified magnitude axis wearing a citation: of the 10 live sub-500,000 denominators with a cover fact, **8 are real** post-reverse-split or small-float counts — `PW` 367,120 (a 1-for-10 reverse split, confirmed by its weighted average of 3,672,274), `SPRC`, `RUBI`, `NEXR`, `SVRN`, `CMND`, `WORXD`, `PAVS`.
- **What works is a pigeonhole, and its floor is measured rather than chosen** — but only over the ONE channel whose holders each occupy a share no other counted holder occupies. Form 13F is additive across filers by design (Special Instruction 5 routes an overlapping manager to a 13F-NT or to a disjoint COMBINATION report; Column 7 lists only managers the report is filed on behalf of) and Column 5 reports whole shares, so `13F managers > shares outstanding` is a genuine impossibility. Fires on **3 of 4,451** — `AVAL` 88/7, `GLXY` 493/100, `MWH` 199/100 — the last two already suppressed by arm 1, leaving **`AVAL` as the one residual instrument it reaches**. Nearest non-firing instrument arm 1 does not already take is `NVR` at `managers/shares = 0.000398`, ~31,600× below `AVAL`, and no real small-float issuer is near it.
- ⚠⚠ **The FIRST version of arm 3 counted every channel, and it was unsound. Codex checkpoint 2 caught it; both legs of its P1 were then confirmed on the data rather than argued.** (1) *Overlap* — Rule 13d-5(b)(1) deems every member of a group to own all the group's securities, so N distinct Section-16 / 13D-G identities legitimately restate ONE block. That is #2230's entire mechanism, i.e. the guard's premise was contradicted by an open ticket on the same tracker. (2) *Fractions* — `_build_slice` enforces `shares > 0`, not `>= 1`, and the fractions are real: `ownership_insiders_current` holds **13,017 of 170,941** rows with a fractional share count, smallest positive **0.0015** (`select count(*) filter (where shares <> trunc(shares)), min(shares) filter (where shares > 0) from ownership_insiders_current`). Institutions and blockholders have 0 fractional rows and a minimum positive of exactly 1. Narrowing to 13F and to `shares >= 1` costs the guard `HQ` — it has ZERO 13F managers, all nine of its disclosed holders being Section 16 / 13D-G — and that cost is stated in the docstring, in the census output and in the truth table rather than absorbed.
- **Why a count and not an amount:** the three open numerator defects all inflate share AMOUNTS while leaving the manager COUNT at its true value — #2229 staleness carries a dead position at its old size, #2230 deemed attribution repeats one block under several reporting persons, #2231 leaves a pre-split numerator unscaled. None can manufacture more 13F filers than the company has shares. **When magnitude has been falsified as a discriminator, ask whether a DIFFERENT observable on the same rows still separates the classes — here the cardinality did what the size could not.** ⚠ And when it does: **name the channel the new observable is sound in.** "Each holder occupies a share" felt axiomatic and was false for two of our three channels; the check that surfaced it was asking, per source, *what does this form's own rule say about overlap and about fractions* — not re-reading the code.
- Cross-source, SEC EDGAR direct: `AVAL`'s FY2025 20-F (`0001104659-26-044493`) is the issuer's own error, not ours and not a §7.17 stripping artefact. SEC's rendered cover (`R1.htm`) shows `Entity Common Stock, Shares Outstanding` = **7**, undimensioned, and `companyconcept/CIK0001504764/dei/EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding.json` serves the same 7 (against 7,542,263,255 the year before). The SAME filing's audited equity note (`R297.htm`) reports total shares outstanding **23,743,475,754**.
- ⚠ **Incidental, filed as #2800: even the "good" `AVAL` cover values are the PREFERENCE class alone.** `R297` splits 23,743,475,754 into ordinary 16,178,324,920 + preference 7,565,150,834, and the cover series (7,541,763,255 → 7,542,263,255 → …) moves by exactly the `CommonStockConversionToPreferredStock` figures `R298` reports (500,000 for FY2024, 22,887,579 for FY2025). So the undimensioned cover value tracks the preference class, and our denominator was ~3.15× too small for years before the typo landed on top of it. `_detect_dual_class_denominator` cannot catch it — gate 1 requires a us-gaap denominator and this one is `dei`, and gate 2 requires ≥2 in-universe siblings.
- ⚠ **A defensive filter the caller can never reach cannot be revert-probed, and the probe says so.** `count_pie_wedge_holders` was first written with `if h.shares > 0`, guarding against a zero-share Form 4/13D row. Removing it was **NOT CAUGHT** — because `_build_slice` has dropped zero-and-negative-share holders since #1916 Finding A, so no fixture can put one in front of the counter. The filter was deleted and the upstream guarantee asserted directly instead (`test_upstream_drops_zero_share_holders`, which IS caught when `_build_slice`'s drop is removed). **A NOT CAUGHT verdict on a defensive branch usually means the branch is dead, not that the test is weak — check which before adding a stronger test.**
- ⚠⚠ **A control worktree "detached at origin/main" is a SNAPSHOT, and with two loops merging it goes stale inside one session — the A/B then attributes the sibling's behaviour change to yours.** The control here was detached at `origin/main` at the start of the run; PR #2792 (bound the insiders wedge by the Form 4 retention cutoff) merged while the arms were draining, so the control had that bound and the treatment branch, still based on the pre-#2792 commit, did not. The compare reported **294 instruments changed for a reason other than the guard, including all five golden-panel instruments** — `AAPL` insiders 9,782,902 → 17,631,265, `MSFT` 2,621,605 → 459,504,753 — none of it mine, all of it #2792 read backwards. `main` moved a second time (#2797) before the re-run. **This is a different failure from the known stale-base one: there the review bot comments on a file you did not touch and you notice; here you get a plausible NUMERIC result with the wrong sign attached to your name.** Prevention: what has to hold is that **the two arms share a base**, not that either is current. So record BOTH SHAs before launching (`git -C <control> rev-parse HEAD` and the branch's merge-base), and check they match when the arms finish — `main` moving on afterwards only narrows what the A/B covers, whereas the arms disagreeing voids it. On the re-run both arms sat at `71a2ce5a` and `main` had already moved to `566df70b`; that A/B is valid. A golden panel that "MOVED" on a suppression-only change is the tell, because a guard that can only remove wedges cannot make one grow.
- ⚠ **pytest exit 2 is INTERRUPTED, not FAILED, and this repo prints no counts line to fall back on.** The first probe harness ran `pytest -x` under the repo's `-n 4` xdist config; every mutation returned exit **2** and was scored CAUGHT. Exit 2 is `EXIT_INTERRUPTED` — `-x` stopping the session — and it is also what a collection error returns, so it does not distinguish "the test failed" from "the file no longer imports". Same family as the archived exit-4 usage-error trap. Re-run without `-x` and gate on exit **1** (`EXIT_TESTSFAILED`) exactly; do not parse `N failed`, because `addopts = "-q … -n 4"` here emits no summary counts line at all.
- ⚠ **`verify-issue-link` reads the PR body from the WORKFLOW EVENT PAYLOAD, so editing the body does not fix a failure and `gh run rerun --failed` replays the same stale text.** This PR opened with *"Deliberately does NOT close #2232"* — the negated-closing-keyword class `scripts/check_pr_issue_link.sh` already documents from the #2740/#2493 incident, so the gate was right and the phrasing was mine to fix (*"#N stays OPEN after this merges"*). What cost the extra round was the retry: the corrected body passed the gate **locally** (`PR_TITLE=… PR_BODY="$(gh pr view N --json body -q .body)" bash scripts/check_pr_issue_link.sh` → exit 0) while CI kept failing on the payload captured at creation. Only a new `pull_request` event — i.e. a push — clears it. **Verify a body-only CI fix by running the gate script locally against the live body, then push; do not rerun the job and wait.**
- Enforced in: this entry; `app/services/ownership_rollup.py::denominator_is_partial_class` (arm 3 + why the per-class short-circuit does not extend to it) + `count_additive_institutional_holders` (carries the per-channel overlap/fraction argument and the 13,017-row measurement) + the caller's pre-filter comment ("must stay a strict SUPERSET"); `scripts/audit_2232_denominator_residual.py` (re-runnable; scores candidates through the production function rather than restating it, prints the all-channel count beside the 13F one so the narrowing stays visible, and names what no arm reaches); `scripts/ab_2232_partial_class_denominator.py` (population extended with a deliberately WIDER arm-3 surface, so over-firing would show); `tests/test_ownership_partial_class_denominator.py`; `tests/test_ownership_rollup.py::TestPartialClassDenominator::test_more_managers_than_shares_suppresses_despite_a_cover_count` (the only test that can see the caller's pre-filter). 6/6 revert-probed.
- ⚠ **Second unreachable-filter probe in the same diff, and the fix was to make the TEST able to fail rather than to delete the filter.** Dropping the `denominator_basis == "pie_wedge"` check came back NOT CAUGHT, because every memo overlay today carries a category outside `_INSTITUTIONAL_CATEGORIES` — so the category filter alone happens to exclude them. That is a coincidence of the current taxonomy, not a guarantee, and the function is pure over an arbitrary slice sequence. Adding an `institutions`-category slice with `denominator_basis="institution_subset"` to `test_memo_overlays_are_excluded` pins the contract instead of the coincidence, and the probe then CAUGHT it. **Distinguish the two NOT CAUGHT cases: a filter the caller cannot reach (delete it, assert the upstream guarantee) from a filter no FIXTURE reaches (construct the fixture).**
- ⚠⚠ **Two implementations of one gate rule do not fail loudly when they diverge — they produce a PR that can never merge, and both halves report success.** The doc-only classification exists twice: inline in `.github/workflows/claude-review.yml` and as `is_doc_only` in the engine's `safe_merge.sh`. On 2026-08-22 they disagreed on `.autonomy/**`: the workflow skipped the engineering review (*"Doc-only diff — engineering review skipped to save tokens"*) and `safe_merge.sh` then refused to merge with `REFUSE -- latest review is not an APPROVE`. Neither said "we disagree". The workflow has no `workflow_dispatch` and fires only on `pull_request`, so a re-push re-classifies doc-only and skips again — **there is no sequence of actions that produces the APPROVE the merge gate is waiting for.** PR #2848 sat unmergeable by construction. ⚠ `safe_merge.sh:20-22` asserts *"This function is THE single doc-only source: the review workflow sources this file and calls it"* — false for this repo, and that docstring is why the divergence went unnoticed: anyone reading it concludes the two cannot disagree. **A comment claiming single-source is not single-source; grep the consumer.** ⚠ Verifying the first fix surfaced a SECOND live divergence in the same pair (`LICENSE`/`CHANGELOG`/`NOTICE`: the workflow called them doc-only, `safe_merge`'s `doc_only_paths` normalizes entries with `p="${p%/}/"` so an extensionless FILE is structurally inexpressible there) — and `NOTICE` exists in this repo, so that trap was live too. **When a gate pair disagrees, converge on the STRICTER side**: the errors are not symmetric — too lenient costs a PR that can never merge, too strict costs one review nobody needed. Enforced in: #2849 (fix + the remaining consolidation), `.autonomy/config.yaml::merge_gate.doc_only_excludes` (declared rather than left to an engine-only default, so the value is visible to everything that must agree with it), and the precedence comment in `claude-review.yml`.

### A REAL citation that governs a DIFFERENT question is the invented citation's disguise
- First seen in: #2602 item 4 (Codex checkpoint 1, 2026-08-22)
- Symptom: the F-0 reconciliation tolerance needed a source rule and none exists, so the spec derived it from **SEC Reg NMS Rule 612** minimum pricing increments ("$0.01 at or above $1.00, $0.0001 below", 17 CFR 242.612) and presented that as the governing rule. Rule 612 is real, correctly quoted, and load-bearing on a **different question**: the increments on which NMS stocks may be **quoted**, not how far two feeds valuing the same holding may legitimately differ. It also does not reach the CFD and non-US products this account can hold, and a 2025 amendment adds $0.005 tiers with compliance deferred, so the "frozen" constant had an unmodelled effective date too. `CLAUDE.md`'s existing rule — "do not invent a citation" — did not fire, because nothing was invented: the failure mode is a *correct* citation aimed at the wrong decision, which reads as source-rule compliance to every reader including the author.
- Prevention: after finding a candidate rule, state in one sentence **what decision the rule itself governs** and check it is the decision you are making. If the rule's subject is a different actor (a venue quoting a price) from yours (two feeds agreeing on a valuation), it is background, not governance. Where the honest answer is that no rule governs, `CLAUDE.md` already says what to do — say so explicitly, fix the constant **by construction**, freeze it in a version id, and state what a widening would require. ⚠ Also state what the constructed bound deliberately does NOT absorb: the withdrawn version silently implied that anything past one tick was an error, when extended-hours prints and uncredited dividend cash both legitimately exceed it. A bound whose exclusions are unwritten will be widened by whoever first meets one.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `docs/proposals/ta/2026-08-22-f0-reconciliation-verdict.md` ("Source rule", which records the withdrawal rather than quietly dropping it); `app/services/account_equity_evidence.py::RECONCILIATION_RULE_VERSION` and `app/services/portfolio_eod.py::MARK_ROUNDING_PER_UNIT` (both docstrings carry the withdrawal and the version-bump rule).

### A declared-but-unwired symbol is a claim with no subject — in BOTH directions
- First seen in: #2817 / #2823 (a WRITER with no reader), and again inverted in #2844 PR #2852 (a CONSTANT with no writer)
- Symptom: three instances of one shape in this repo now. `strategy_result_regime_cohorts` had a writer since #2726 and no reader, so item 6's per-regime evidence was *invisible* rather than missing; `strategy_result_folds` the same since #2240. #2844 hit the mirror image: `SANDBOX_POLICY_VERSION` was defined and its docstring said it was what a stored refusal is *"interpreted against"* — but nothing in the module's blast radius persists it, so the sentence was true of no row that exists. All three read as working machinery: the symbol is defined, typed, exported, and grep-able, and every test around it passes because nothing asserts the other end.
- Prevention: for any symbol whose value is its **connection** — a version stamp, an audit code, a persisted policy id, a table a job writes — name the OTHER end in the same change and grep for it before merging. `grep -rn "<SYMBOL>" app tests` returning only its own definition is the whole test, and it is one command. If the other end genuinely belongs in a later change, do not ship the symbol early to "prepare": ship it WITH the column or row that carries it, so the version and the thing it versions arrive together. ⚠ Applies symmetrically — a reader with no writer is starved, a writer with no reader is invisible, and a constant with no persister is decorative. Self-review prompt: *"who consumes this, and does that consumer exist on this branch?"*
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `app/services/strategy_capital_sandbox.py` (the comment where the constant used to be, recording why it was removed rather than wired); `app/services/strategy_result_regime_cohorts` readers added in #2817; `strategy_result_folds` readers in #2823.

### A merged REBUILD is not proof the original branch is redundant, and `git cherry` cannot tell you
- First seen in: #2846 worktree audit / #2859 (2026-08-22)
- Symptom: five worktrees from 2026-08-15 held 192 committed-but-unpushed commits. Because nothing was on the remote, no `gh pr list` / branch check / in-flight scan could see them, and on 08-21 two of the tickets were **rebuilt from scratch** and merged as #2825 and #2826. The issues closed. The audit ticket then listed both worktrees as *"merged (#2825) → verify, delete"* — the natural inference, and wrong: the rebuilds are not supersets. **15 of 16** symbols on `fix/2766-first-paper-enable` and **156 of 333** on `feature/2770-operator-promotion` are absent from `origin/main`, including eleven live/paper authority-boundary tests with no behavioural equivalent (concept-grep over main's three strategy test files returns 0 files for six of seven families). Deleting on the table's say-so would have destroyed guard tests for the exact surface #2843 was changing that day.
- ⚠ **`git cherry` is worthless here and fails in the reassuring direction.** It matches patch-ids, so a from-scratch reimplementation shares none: every commit reads `+` (not upstream) whether the work landed or not. Running it on all five branches returned `already-upstream=0` uniformly — a result equally consistent with "nothing landed" and "everything landed differently", i.e. no information at all. `git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD` is no better: the three-dot base is the week-old merge-base, so the diff is dominated by main's own evolution.
- Prevention: **before deleting any branch whose ticket closed via a rebuild, check symbol-level presence in `origin/main`** — extract names added relative to the merge-base and grep each against the remote:
  `git diff origin/main...HEAD --unified=0 | grep -E '^\+\s*(def |async def |class )'`, then `git grep -q "<name>" origin/main` per hit. A **zero** is strong evidence of supersession; a non-zero is a list of things to look at, not a verdict (a renamed symbol reads as missing, and a name that exists elsewhere reads as landed). Where the absences are service functions, check whether main replaced the shape with something better before porting — here `validate_*_evidence_bundle` was correctly superseded by `evidence_refusals` / `GOVERNANCE_GATE_VERSION v2+edge-evidence`, while the **tests** for the same behaviours were simply lost.
- ⚠ **Push before you reap, not after you decide.** `git push --no-verify -u origin <branch>` on every branch first makes the acceptance clause ("zero unpushed commits destroyed") true by construction rather than by judgement, and costs one command per branch. Note the pre-push hook will legitimately reject week-old branches on formatting — archival preservation is the one place `--no-verify` is right, because nothing is being landed.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; #2859 (the eleven dropped tests + the porting plan); the #2846 audit comment (per-worktree method, limits and verdicts).

### A cost model's NAME is not its stamps — read the closure constants
- First seen in: #2840 step 2 (2026-08-22), caught by `freeze_preregistration`'s freeze-time gate
- Symptom: the S-H declaration was built with `declared_carry_unmodelled=True, declared_fx_unmodelled=True`, reasoned straight off `COST_MODEL_ID` — `static-p75-insession-v3+split-adjusted-max+carry-fx-structural-zero-long-x1-real-usd`. "Structural zero" reads as *"we did not model it"*. It is the opposite. `cost_model.CARRY_CLOSURE` is `structural_zero`, a **closure state** meaning the cost does not EXIST for the declared lane — an unleveraged long on the underlying pays no overnight financing, and USD in / USD held / USD out has no conversion event. `unmodelled` is a separate closure, and #2720 flipped both markers to `False`. The wrong stamps propagated into a merged PR body, a merged test docstring and an on-issue handoff before anything failed, because every one of them was internally consistent.
- ⚠ The consequence was not cosmetic. `structural_promotion_refusals('survivorship_free', True, True)` returns `('carry_unmodelled', 'fx_unmodelled')`, which made `falsification_only` look **forced** by `ineligible_trial_not_declared_falsification`. With the real stamps the refusal list is **empty** and the purpose is a free choice between `falsification_only` and `capital_candidate` — a strategy-identity decision that had been hidden behind a fake constraint. Verifying a function's OUTPUT while inventing its INPUTS is not verification.
- Prevention: never hand-write a `declared_*` stamp. Import the constant (`from app.services.cost_model import CARRY_UNMODELLED, FX_UNMODELLED`) so a closure change moves the declaration with it, exactly as the strategy identity is computed from the manifest rather than pasted. More generally: **an id string is a label, not a source rule** — when a decision turns on what a constant MEANS, open the module that defines it and read the docstring, the same way `CLAUDE.md` requires for an SEC Item.
- ⚠ What made this cheap was a gate that refuses on the mismatch instead of trusting the declaration: `result_ledger.freeze_preregistration` compares the declared pair against `(CARRY_UNMODELLED, FX_UNMODELLED)` for any strategy in `STRATEGY_MANIFEST` and raises **before** the INSERT, so no immutable row was burned (`sql/333` bars UPDATE and DELETE — recovery would have meant a new `strategy_version` and a second charge on the shared trial register). Worth copying: where a value must match a module constant, assert it at the write site, not in the caller.
- Enforced in: this prevention log; `scripts/freeze_2840_sh_regime_gate_declaration.py::build_declaration` (reads both constants, and its docstring carries why `falsification_only` is a choice rather than a consequence); `tests/test_2840_sh_declaration.py::TestTheDeclaration::test_the_carry_and_fx_stamps_are_read_from_the_cost_model` and `::test_falsification_only_is_a_choice_and_the_test_says_which`.

### Extracting a helper does not remove its copies — grep the signature, or the dedup is cosmetic
- First seen in: #2868 PR #2872 (2026-08-23), caught by the review bot
- Symptom: a page split extracted three shared string→number formatters into `frontend/src/lib/strategyFormat.ts`, and the extraction's own docstring cited the `information-architecture` skill's *"extract it once and share — never fork a fifth copy"* rule. Two of the three consumers then kept their private `function number(value: string | null)` verbatim. `grep -rn "function number(value: string | null)" frontend/src` returned **three** definitions on a branch whose commentary claimed one. Nothing failed: typecheck passes (each copy is well-typed), every test passes (the copies are currently identical), and the new lib module is genuinely imported elsewhere — so the diff reads as a completed dedup while the drift surface is unchanged.
- ⚠ The rule was not missing. It existed, it was cited by name in the same file that broke it, and it still did not fire — because a naming convention is not a check. What was missing is the one command that turns it into one.
- Prevention: when a change extracts a helper into a shared module, **grep its exact signature across the tree before pushing** and confirm the definition count is 1 — `grep -rn "function <name>(<first param>" <src root>`. Do it as the last step of the extraction, not as a review response: the copies are usually left behind by the mechanical part of the move (a file gets its imports rewritten but its private block survives above the first component), so the author is the cheapest person to catch it. Same command works for the mirror case — an extraction that leaves the ORIGINAL behind while every caller now imports the new one.
